text: When the magnitude or direction of its velocity changes, the vehicle accelerates. In the frame of reference moving with it, an inertial force is considered to act opposite to that acceleration.
Given the same initial speed and constant braking force, a greater mass undergoes less deceleration and requires a longer distance to stop.
For the same acceleration, the inertial force is proportional to mass, so it is smaller for the lighter vehicle.
For the same acceleration, the inertial force increases in proportion to the vehicle's mass.
In the vehicle's frame of reference, the inertial force is opposite to the acceleration, that is, the change in velocity over time.
During braking, inertia tends to maintain motion: in the vehicle's frame of reference, the inertial force points forward, opposite to the deceleration.

The quiz marks this FALSO, but the wording is ambiguous: the inertial force depends on acceleration, not on velocity alone. It can change when velocity changes, but not necessarily: for example, it remains constant when acceleration is constant.
It is incorrect to exclude mass and consider only velocity: the inertial force is proportional to the mass and the acceleration of the frame of reference.
Inertia does not help braking: it tends to keep the vehicle moving, and the braking system must produce the necessary deceleration.
Inertia does not improve grip on a bend: the vehicle tends to continue in a straight line, and a force toward the center of the bend is needed, supplied by the tires' grip.
Having the same speed is not enough to make inertial forces equal: mass and acceleration also matter; on a bend, the radius matters too.
The coefficient of grip does not directly determine the inertial force, which depends on mass and acceleration. It can, however, indirectly affect the acceleration actually achievable.
The engine supplies the power that, through the transmission and drive wheels, produces the tractive force that propels the vehicle.
Some of the engine's power is lost in mechanical components, for example through friction in the transmission; not all of it reaches the wheels.
The transmission delivers power to the drive wheels, which exert a force on the road surface; the reaction of the surface propels the vehicle.
A combustion engine or an electric motor can supply the power that, transmitted to the drive wheels, generates the vehicle's traction.
The transmission components transfer engine power to the drive wheels, making it possible to generate the traction needed for motion.
The driving force is not a centrifugal force: it is the traction resulting from engine power transmitted to the wheels.
The driving force is not the same as gravity: it is the traction at the wheels that propels the vehicle, while gravity produces weight.
The transmission components carry engine power to the drive wheels; the steering components, on the other hand, are used to direct the vehicle.
The driving force is not the steering force: it is the tractive force at the wheels that propels the vehicle.
The engine's power is not completely absorbed: some reaches the wheels through the transmission, despite losses.
For the same gravitational acceleration, the weight of a body is proportional to its mass: P = m × g.
Weight is the force with which the Earth attracts a body near its surface.
Weight is calculated by multiplying the body's mass by the acceleration due to gravity: P = m × g.
Weight acts vertically and equals mass multiplied by gravitational acceleration: it does not change if the body is tilted.
For the same gravity, loading the vehicle increases its total mass and therefore increases its weight.
The slope does not change the weight, which depends on mass and gravity; its components relative to the road do change.
It is not inversely proportional: for the same gravity, weight increases in direct proportion to mass.
Mass and acceleration are not added together: weight is their product, P = m × g.
The number of axles does not directly determine weight: it depends on total mass and gravity.
The nature of the load does not in itself determine weight: total mass is what matters. Loads of different materials can have the same mass and therefore the same weight.
On a bend, a net force directed toward the center of the path is needed to change the direction of motion.
On a flat bend, grip between the tires and the road provides the lateral force needed to turn.
Centripetal force is the net force directed toward the center that allows a body to follow a circular path.
On a bend, a net force directed toward the center of the path is needed to change the direction of motion.
On a flat bend, grip between the tires and the road provides the lateral force needed to turn.
The quiz marks this VERO, but the wording is imprecise: for the same radius, the force is directly proportional to mass and to the square of speed, not to speed itself.
Going uphill alone does not require a centripetal force: it is needed when the path is curved, including on an uphill slope.
The transmission components do not necessarily generate the centripetal force: on a flat bend, it is supplied by the tires' grip on the road.
The control unit does not generate the centripetal force: on a flat bend, it is supplied by the tires' grip on the road.
It is not inversely proportional to mass: for the same speed and radius, centripetal force is directly proportional to mass.
Going downhill alone does not require a centripetal force: it is needed when the path is curved, including on a downhill slope.
In the frame of reference rotating with the vehicle, an apparent outward force appears, called centrifugal force; in the road's frame of reference, the net force is directed toward the center.
In the rotating frame of reference, the apparent centrifugal force is opposite to the centripetal force. In the road's frame of reference, a net force toward the center remains, as needed to turn.
In the vehicle's frame of reference, the apparent centrifugal force is opposite to the force toward the center; in the road's frame of reference, it is the latter that produces the curved path.
On a bend, if grip is insufficient to provide the necessary lateral force, the vehicle can skid outward.
On a bend, excessive lateral acceleration can exceed the vehicle's stability threshold and cause it to roll over.
In the vehicle's frame of reference, the apparent centrifugal force depends on curvature: for the same speed, it increases as the radius of the bend decreases.
In the vehicle's frame of reference, the apparent centrifugal force increases with the square of speed, for the same mass and bend radius.
In the reference frame of a vehicle taking a bend, the apparent centrifugal force acts outward.
For a given radius, centrifugal force increases with mass and with the square of speed.
For a given mass and speed, a bend with a smaller radius produces a greater centrifugal force: its magnitude is mv²/r.
It is not directly proportional to the radius: for a given mass and speed, it is inversely proportional to it.
The radius matters: for a given mass and speed, the tighter the bend, the greater the centrifugal force.
On a straight path there is no lateral centrifugal force due to a bend; it appears when the path changes direction.
Going uphill does not make centrifugal force greatest: it depends on the curvature of the path and the speed, not on the gradient alone.
An uphill gradient alone does not produce a lateral centrifugal force: a bend is needed. An uphill road can, however, also have a bend.
Braking acts mainly along the path; lateral grip provides the force directed toward the center of the bend. Braking can reduce speed and therefore centrifugal force.
The apparent centrifugal force acts toward the outside of the bend, not toward the inside.
At a given speed, a tighter bend increases lateral acceleration and therefore the force that can contribute to a rollover.
A higher center of gravity reduces rollover stability: the lateral force acts with a longer lever arm relative to the outside wheels.
A greater apparent lateral force increases the moment that tends to lift the inside wheels and can contribute to a rollover.
On a given bend, increasing speed increases lateral acceleration and with it the risk of a rollover.
Missing the periodic inspection does not in itself cause a rollover: that depends on the vehicle's stability and the forces acting on it in a bend. Any defects can affect safety.
A wider track increases the base of support and, for a given center-of-gravity height, improves rollover stability.
Greater weight alone does not necessarily increase the risk: center-of-gravity height, track width and lateral acceleration also matter.
The quiz uses a simplified description: the slip angle is the angle between the direction the wheel points and the actual direction of its motion.
Slip indicates a lateral deviation from the intended direction; for an individual wheel, it is measured relative to its actual direction of travel.
Lateral forces deform the tire and are associated with a difference between the direction the wheel points and the direction of its motion.
The tire's ability to deform affects its lateral response: under a lateral force, the direction of motion can differ from the direction the wheel points.
Lateral force and slip angle are linked: the tire's response changes as the angle changes.
Pressure changes the tire's stiffness and therefore its lateral response and slip.
The load on the wheels changes the tires' lateral response and therefore their slip.
Camber changes the lateral force developed by the tire and affects the relationship between force and slip.
VERO. Incorrect wheel toe can contribute to a vehicle's tendency to deviate, but the deviation can also have other causes.
FALSO. Slip is the angle between the direction the wheel points and the actual direction of its movement, not between two vehicle axles.
FALSO. Slip is linked to tire deformation under lateral forces; it is not necessarily caused by driving forces.
FALSO. The suspension affects the wheels' contact and alignment and can therefore change slip.
FALSO. Inflation pressure affects the tire's lateral stiffness and therefore its response and slip.
FALSO. Power steering assists steering wheel operation; its presence does not imply greater slip, which depends on the tires' response to lateral forces.
FALSO. Slip in a bend is not necessarily measured during the periodic inspection. Checking wheel alignment is distinct from measuring slip angle while driving.
FALSO. Maintenance keeps tires and suspension in good working order, but does not eliminate the normal slip that occurs when a tire develops lateral force in a bend.
VERO. With understeer, the vehicle turns less than requested and follows a wider path.
VERO. With understeer, the cornering response is less than requested by the steering wheel input.

VERO. If available grip at the front decreases, the front wheels can lose grip and the vehicle can run wide in the bend. Poor grip alone, however, does not always cause understeer: grip at the rear also matters.
VERO. With understeer, the front wheels have more slip than the rear wheels and the vehicle tends to run wide.
VERO. Ineffective suspension can alter tire contact with the road and contribute to understeer. The actual effect, however, depends on which components are worn and on the vehicle's setup.
VERO. The definition describes greater slip at the front than at the rear, a characteristic of understeer.
FALSO. A greater rear load does not necessarily increase understeer: the effect also depends on the tires, pressure and load distribution.
FALSO. An uphill gradient does not automatically increase understeer: load distribution, traction and grip also matter.

FALSO. Pronounced understeer causes the vehicle to run wide in a bend and can cause loss of control; it does not guarantee greater stability. A moderate tendency to understeer can, however, make the response more predictable.
FALSO. Understeer does not compensate for slip: it is associated with greater slip at the front than at the rear.
FALSO. Pressure affects the tires' lateral response and can therefore change understeering behavior.
VERO. To regain directional control, gradually adjust the accelerator and steering, seeking to restore grip to the front wheels.
VERO. Correcting understeer applies when the vehicle runs wide in a bend, meaning it turns less than requested.
FALSO. If the vehicle turns more than requested, this is called oversteer; understeer is the tendency to turn less and run wide.

VERO according to the quiz, but the maneuver needs clarification: increasing steering toward the inside can help as long as the wheels have grip. If the front wheels are already slipping, ease off the accelerator and gradually reduce the steering angle until grip returns.
FALSO. Braking hard is not the required correction: ease off the accelerator and steer gently to regain grip at the front.
VERO. With oversteer, the vehicle tends to turn more than requested, following a tighter path.
In oversteer, the rear tends to move outward and the vehicle rotates inward. Pivoting on the front wheels is a simplified image, not an actual fixed point.
The greater rear slip causes the vehicle to rotate further inward, tightening its path.
If the rear slides outward, the vehicle may rotate until it spins. Pivoting on the front wheels is a simplified description.
In the usual model of cornering, oversteer corresponds to greater rear slip than front slip.

A loss of rear lateral grip, which can be encouraged by load transfer or excessive acceleration, can cause oversteer. The wording describes an extreme case: oversteer does not always require a complete skid.
Understeer causes the vehicle to turn less than intended; in oversteer, the rear tends outward and the vehicle turns more.
Running wide toward the tangent is typical of understeer. In oversteer, the rear tends outward and the front points inward.
The stated cause is incorrect: the tightening of the path in oversteer is linked to greater rear slip than front slip.
Difficulty turning enough is characteristic of understeer; in oversteer, the vehicle tends to rotate too far inward.
Countersteering points the wheels in the direction the rear is sliding to help recover the intended path.
The driver countersteers toward the outside of the bend, in the direction the rear is moving, to counter the vehicle's rotation.
Countersteering momentarily points the wheels toward the outside of the bend, in the direction of the rear skid.
If excessive acceleration causes the rear drive wheels to slip, gradually easing off the accelerator helps restore grip and directional control.
The suspension affects load transfer between the wheels and therefore the vehicle's grip and behavior in bends.
Accelerating without steering does not correct the skid: the driver must countersteer and ease off the accelerator to help the vehicle recover.
Braking hard can make the skid worse. Instead, the driver should try to recover with controlled countersteering, avoiding abrupt maneuvers.
Greater rear slip than front slip increases oversteer rather than reducing it.
Steering further inward would increase the rotation. The correction is to countersteer outward, in the direction of the skid.
Pitching makes the vehicle rock back and forth: an inadequately secured load can shift and compromise stability.
The longitudinal rocking of the vehicle body can be uncomfortable for passengers, especially if pronounced or repeated.
Pitching is oscillating rotation around the transverse axis passing through the center of gravity: the front rises and falls relative to the rear.
Suspension stiffness affects the vehicle's oscillatory response and therefore its pitching as well.
It does have effects: pitching changes the vehicle's attitude and causes the loads on the wheels to fluctuate while driving.
It is more than just a discomfort: pitching can vary the load on the wheels and, if pronounced, compromise road holding. It does not, however, mean that grip is lost in every case.
Pitching is a longitudinal oscillation around the transverse axis; it is not the phenomenon that counteracts lateral force in a bend.
Roll is the sideways tilting of the vehicle body: if excessive, the wheels can lift and the vehicle can overturn.
Roll transfers load between the wheels and can reduce stability and overall road-holding capability. The verdict does not mean that the coefficient of grip of every tire always decreases.
In bends taken in quick succession, the liquid's sideways motion can add to the tanker's movement and increase roll.
The suspension and shock absorbers determine how much the vehicle tilts and how quickly sideways oscillations are damped.

The quiz considers it false that tread wear directly determines pitching: longitudinal oscillation depends mainly on acceleration, braking and suspension. Wear can, however, indirectly affect braking and therefore the movement.
It is not true that a loaded tanker is always less prone to pitching: the liquid, especially in a partially filled tank, can move back and forth during acceleration and braking.
Roll is not a stabilizing movement: it tilts the vehicle and changes the distribution of loads on the wheels, increasing the risk of rollover if excessive.
Driving behavior affects roll: taking bends too fast or steering abruptly can increase sideways tilt.
The verdict uses a simplification: the resultant weight is considered to act at the center of gravity. Other forces do not necessarily all act at that point and can cause rotation.
The position of the center of gravity of the vehicle and load together depends on the mass of the load and where it is placed.
Moving the load changes the distribution of mass and can therefore shift the overall center of gravity.

The verdict applies to the same unloaded vehicle with an unchanged reference configuration and attitude: under those conditions, the distribution of mass remains the same. It is not an absolute constant relative to the ground in every attitude.
When the liquid moves in the tank, the distribution of mass changes and the overall center of gravity can also change; this happens while the liquid is moving.
The position of the center of gravity affects stability: for example, a higher center of gravity makes a rollover more likely.

The quiz considers a direct change in the center of gravity due to pressure to be false: it depends on the distribution of mass. Different tire pressures can, however, tilt the vehicle and shift the center of gravity relative to the ground.
Age alone does not determine the position of the center of gravity: what matters is how the mass of the vehicle and load is distributed.
The center of gravity does not necessarily coincide with the center of the drive axle: its position depends on the distribution of the mass of the vehicle and load.

A bend does not in itself shift the center of gravity relative to a rigid vehicle with a fixed load. Roll or a shift in the load can, however, change its position relative to the ground or the vehicle.
The center of gravity is not the coupling point: it is the point that represents the distribution of mass and at which the resultant weight can be applied.
Resistive forces oppose forward motion: for example, air resistance takes energy away from the movement.
When two surfaces in contact slide against each other, kinetic friction opposes their relative motion. Static friction also exists without sliding.
Friction during sliding is dissipative: it converts some mechanical energy into internal energy. Static friction, on the other hand, does not necessarily dissipate energy.
Friction opposes relative sliding, or the tendency to slide, between surfaces in contact.
When surfaces slide against each other, friction dissipates mechanical energy, producing heat; static friction does not necessarily produce heat.
Dissipative friction does not increase efficiency: it converts some useful energy into heat. Grip between the tire and the road is nevertheless necessary to move and control the vehicle.
Inertia, not friction, maintains uniform motion in a straight line when the resultant force is zero. Frictional resistance must be offset by traction.
Friction between the tire and the road makes the force that slows the vehicle possible; it does not oppose braking. Friction in the brakes also helps slow the wheels.
Frictional resistance dissipates energy: if it increases, more energy is needed to move forward and consumption tends to increase.
Friction does not by itself lower the center of gravity: its position depends on the distribution of the masses of the vehicle and its load.
A suitably rough surface promotes tire contact and grip, particularly by helping water drain away. The actual value also depends on the condition of the road surface and the tire.
Ice makes the tire-road contact more slippery and reduces the available grip compared with dry asphalt.

The quiz considers the range from zero to one VERO, as a useful approximation for common road conditions. It is not an absolute physical limit, however: in some conditions the coefficient can exceed one.
It is not limited to the range between one and two: on ordinary roads it can be much less than one and depends on the contact conditions. In some cases it can also exceed one.
Wet conditions generally reduce, rather than increase, grip: the film of water reduces effective contact between the rubber and the road surface.
Loose gravel generally provides less grip than good dry asphalt. The values vary with the condition of both surfaces, so the comparison is not absolute.
It is the force with which the air opposes the vehicle's motion relative to the air itself.
For a given air density, surface area and aerodynamic coefficient, resistance increases with the square of the speed relative to the air.
With the other factors unchanged and the coefficient referenced to frontal area, a larger frontal area results in greater resistance.
The Cx coefficient represents the effect of shape and flow conditions: with other factors unchanged, a higher Cx produces greater resistance.
The deflector on the cab roof, if suited to the vehicle's configuration, guides air toward the load and reduces aerodynamic resistance and the associated Cx.
Resistance increases with the square of the speed relative to the air: with other factors unchanged, the percentage increase in resistance is greater than the percentage increase in speed.
Overcoming air resistance requires energy from the engine, so greater resistance tends to increase fuel consumption.
Aerodynamic resistance is not proportional to the engine's maximum power: it depends instead on speed relative to the air, density, reference area and aerodynamic coefficient.
Weight does not directly determine aerodynamic resistance: speed relative to the air, density, frontal area and aerodynamic coefficient are the relevant factors.
A wet road surface does not directly determine aerodynamic resistance, which concerns motion through the air; water on the road can, however, affect grip and other forms of resistance.
Aerodynamic resistance depends on speed relative to the air: with other factors unchanged, it increases with the square of that speed.
The relationship is directly proportional, not inverse: with other factors unchanged and Cx referenced to frontal area, increasing that area increases resistance.
Cx does not depend directly on weight: it describes the effects of shape and flow conditions with reference to a chosen area.
Kinetic energy equals half the mass multiplied by the square of the speed: at the same speed, it is proportional to mass.
For a given mass, kinetic energy increases with the square of speed: the faster the vehicle, the greater its kinetic energy.
During ordinary braking, friction in the brakes transforms the energy of motion mainly into heat.
The more energy there is to dissipate, the greater the distance needed to stop, for a given braking force.
It does not decrease: under the same conditions and with the same braking force, more kinetic energy requires a longer braking distance and therefore increases the stopping distance.
Cx concerns aerodynamic resistance; it does not directly determine kinetic energy, which depends on mass and the square of speed.
Reaction time does not determine kinetic energy: for the same mass and speed, it remains unchanged. A longer reaction time does, however, increase the distance traveled before braking.
During braking that slows the vehicle, kinetic energy decreases because speed decreases.
A steeper slope may require a lower gear: uphill it helps with traction, while downhill it increases the braking effect of the engine.
On a steep descent, a low gear is selected beforehand so that engine braking helps control speed.
A lower gear provides greater torque multiplication at the wheels and therefore more tractive force, for the same driving torque.
Higher gears have a lower reduction ratio and allow higher speeds without bringing the engine to an excessive speed.

With a heavier load, more traction may be needed, especially uphill or when accelerating; if the current gear is not sufficient, shift down. It is not necessary to shift down automatically every time the weight increases.
Higher gears provide less engine braking. On a steep descent, select a low gear before starting downhill to control speed.
Shifting to a higher gear reduces torque multiplication: for the same engine torque, a lower gear provides more traction at the wheels.
A tight bend requires an appropriate speed, not necessarily a higher gear. Slow down and select the appropriate gear before the bend.
On a steeper slope, it is not advisable to automatically select a higher gear: a lower gear may be needed for traction uphill or engine braking downhill.
Changing gear does not by itself change Cx, which describes the aerodynamic characteristics of the vehicle and the airflow.
The rear overhang is the distance between the rear axle and the rear end of the vehicle.
In a turn, for the same maneuver and geometry, a longer rear overhang tends to make the rear swing farther outward.
For the same ground clearance, a longer rear overhang reduces the departure angle and may touch the ground when the vehicle leaves a descent.
At the start of an uphill slope, it is the front overhang that matters: if it is long, for the same ground clearance, the front of the vehicle may touch the ramp.
For scraping at the rear, it is the rear overhang that matters, not the front overhang: a longer rear overhang reduces the departure angle.

The quiz marks this as false: at the start of an uphill slope, the risk to the front of the vehicle depends mainly on the front overhang and ground clearance. A long wheelbase can, however, increase the risk of the middle of the vehicle touching the ground at a change in slope.
The distance between the two axles is the wheelbase. The overhang is the portion that extends beyond an axle toward the end of the vehicle.
FALSO. A longer rear overhang does not necessarily reduce pitch, the longitudinal oscillation of the body. The response also depends on mass distribution and the suspension.
Rear overhang alone does not cause increased understeer: cornering behavior also depends on load distribution and tire characteristics.
This is the Highway Code's definition of a road: an area for public use intended for the movement of pedestrians, vehicles and animals.
A motorway is one of the road types in the technical classification: it is designated type A.
A motorway has independent carriageways or carriageways separated by an uncrossable median, and it has no intersections at grade.
A major non-urban road has no intersections at grade: junctions are arranged without crossings at the same level.
Use is restricted to certain categories of motor vehicles; suitable spaces are provided for any other road users who may be permitted.
The quiz indicates VERO, but the wording is incomplete: the carriageways may be independent or separated by an uncrossable median.
A major non-urban road must have service areas with parking spaces and access points equipped with acceleration and deceleration lanes.
It is not enough for an area to be passable: under the Highway Code definition, it must be for public use and intended for traffic.
Three lanes in each direction are not mandatory: the minimum required is two traffic lanes on each carriageway.
Not all motor vehicles are allowed on motorways: for example, mopeds are prohibited.
Intersections at grade are not a feature of major non-urban roads: these roads must have none.
Not all categories of vehicles are allowed: for example, mopeds are prohibited on major non-urban roads.
Major non-urban road refers to a technical category, not necessarily a state road: the administrative classification also depends on its use and the connections it provides.
The major non-urban road category does not require roads to connect provincial capitals exclusively: it is defined by the road's characteristics, not by those connections alone.
There is no general ban on all dangerous goods on these roads: goods that are permitted may be transported in compliance with the applicable conditions and any specific restrictions.
Separate carriageways are not required: a secondary non-urban road is defined as a road with a single carriageway.
It is false that shoulders are not mandatory: they are included in the definition of a secondary non-urban road.
Secondary non-urban roads are not required to be free of intersections at grade, so such intersections may be present.
On a major non-urban road, access points to adjoining properties must be coordinated.
A secondary non-urban road has a single carriageway with at least one lane in each direction.
Shoulders are among the required features of a secondary non-urban road.
The quiz indicates VERO: secondary non-urban roads may have intersections at grade, but they are not mandatory on every road.
The quiz indicates VERO: if an urban through road has intersections at grade, they must be controlled by traffic lights; such intersections are not mandatory.
The administrative classification divides roads into state, regional, provincial and municipal roads, based on their use and the connections they provide.
Connecting regional capitals is one of the criteria for classifying a non-urban road as a state road.
One criterion for classifying a non-urban road as a state road is that it connects Italy's main road network with that of neighboring countries.
Connecting provincial capitals in the same region is one of the criteria for classifying a non-urban road as a regional road.
A non-urban road may be classified as provincial when it connects the provincial capital to the municipal capitals in the same province.
Connecting a municipal capital with its outlying settlements is one of the criteria for classifying a non-urban road as a municipal road.
It does not have a single carriageway: an urban through road has independent carriageways or carriageways separated by a median, each with at least two traffic lanes.
The types listed are based on technical and functional characteristics. The administrative classification instead distinguishes state, regional, provincial and municipal roads.
State roads are not owned by the municipality: the Highway Code identifies the state as the owner of state roads.
A state road is not required to cross at least three regions: one sufficient criterion, for example, is that it connects Italy's main road network to that of a neighboring country.
A connection between capitals of different regions is a criterion for state roads; a connection between provincial capitals in the same region is a criterion for regional roads.

The provincial designation concerns the road's administrative role and connections, and does not rule out intersections at grade. An urban through road may have them if they are controlled by traffic lights.
Municipal refers to an administrative classification, not a restriction to motor vehicles: the road is also intended for pedestrians and animals, subject to any specific restrictions.
Normally, vehicles must travel on the right-hand side of the carriageway, close to its right edge, even when the road is clear.
Unless signs indicate otherwise, when there are multiple lanes in each direction, use the rightmost available lane; the lanes to the left are reserved for overtaking.
Unless signs indicate otherwise, on carriageways with multiple lanes in each direction, use the rightmost available lane and reserve the lanes to the left for overtaking.
The usual rule is to use the rightmost available lane; the lanes to the left are for overtaking, unless signs indicate otherwise.
The truck exceeds 5 tonnes: unless signs indicate otherwise, on a motorway with at least three lanes it may use only the two closest to the right edge.
The bus is less than 7 meters long, and the 5-tonne threshold applies to vehicles used to transport goods. It may use the left lane to overtake, unless signs indicate otherwise.
There is no general ban on reversing in built-up areas for vehicles over 3.5 tonnes. The maneuver must be performed without danger or obstruction, yielding to vehicles traveling normally.
The bus is more than 7 meters long: unless signs indicate otherwise, on a motorway with at least three lanes it may use only the two closest to the right edge, even if it weighs less than 5 tonnes.

There is no general ban based on the 7.5-tonne threshold: vehicles may travel on tracks at road level without obstructing or slowing trams, provided traffic conditions allow and signs do not indicate otherwise.

It is not true that you must always pass on the left: if the traffic island is to the right of the road's center line, unless signs indicate otherwise you may pass on either side, staying in your own direction of travel and without obstructing passengers.
There is no general ban based on the 12-tonne threshold. Traveling in parallel lines is permitted under the specified traffic conditions or when authorized by traffic officers.
There is no general ban based on the 12-meter threshold. Traveling in parallel lines is permitted under the specified traffic conditions or when authorized by traffic officers.
In built-up areas, drivers may choose the lane best suited to the direction they intend to take at the next intersection, regardless of traffic intensity.

In built-up areas, the rightmost available lane is the rule, unless signs indicate otherwise; however, drivers may choose the appropriate lane for the direction they intend to take at the next intersection.
When there are two separate carriageways, use the one on the right, designated for your direction of travel.

With only one lane in each direction, there is normally no room for two lines of traffic in the same direction. The ban is not absolute: the law also provides for cases authorized by traffic officers and the stretch before a controlled intersection.
Traffic officers may authorize traffic to travel in parallel lines even when the usual traffic density conditions are not met.
The right-hand lane is not reserved solely for slow vehicles: unless signs indicate otherwise, everyone uses the rightmost available lane, and the lanes to its left are used for overtaking.
The right-hand lane is not reserved for vehicles entering or leaving: it is normally the driving lane for everyone.
You cannot simply choose any lane: normally, overtaking is done on the left, using the lanes to the left of the driving lane.
The right-hand lane is not reserved for buses and trucks: unless signs indicate otherwise, it is normally the driving lane for everyone.
Wheelbase and overhangs affect the space a vehicle occupies when turning: the rear follows a different path from the front and may swing out sideways.
When turning right, the rear wheels follow a tighter path than the front wheels: check that they do not hit the curb or other road users.
A bus takes up a lot of space when turning: waiting until the necessary area is clear allows the maneuver to be completed without endangering other road users.
When passing pedestrians or cyclists, leave adequate lateral clearance, taking into account the size of the vehicle and the possible movements of other road users.
There is no general requirement for vehicles over 7 meters long to move left. To turn right, position yourself as close as possible to the right-hand edge, checking that the maneuver is safe.
Heavy vehicles are not required to use the left lane of a roundabout. The choice depends on the direction to be taken, the signs and the space needed.
Low speed does not permit driving onto the sidewalk. Plan the turn while checking the path of the inner rear wheel and protecting the space used by pedestrians.

A length over 7 meters does not require a vehicle to remain in the right-hand lane at all times. Like other vehicles, it normally uses the rightmost available lane, but may use the left lane to overtake and in other permitted cases.
If roadworks prevent vehicles from passing each other and obstruct your direction of travel, stop and let oncoming traffic pass, while obeying any different instructions from signs or officers.

If an obstacle prevents vehicles from passing each other, the driver who encounters it in their direction of travel and cannot keep close to the right-hand edge must stop and let oncoming vehicles pass.

On a steep road, if passing is difficult, the driver going downhill normally stops, pulling over to the right or using a passing place. If the driver going uphill has a passing place available and reversing would otherwise be necessary, that driver stops in it instead.

The driver going uphill who has a passing place available must stop in it if the road is so narrow that reversing would otherwise be necessary. The mere presence of a passing place therefore does not make the rule unconditional.
If reversing is necessary, the truck and trailer, as a combination of vehicles, has priority over the bus, so the bus must reverse.

The driver going uphill does not always have priority: if a passing place is available and the narrow section would otherwise make reversing necessary, that driver must stop in the passing place and let the downhill vehicle pass.
It is not the truck and trailer that must reverse: if the maneuver is necessary, the vehicle combination has priority over the bus, which must reverse.
It is not the bus that must reverse: when the maneuver is necessary, the bus has priority over the truck, whose driver must therefore back up.

VERO. If the oil pump does not work properly, lubrication pressure may be insufficient and cause the warning light to come on.
VERO. An insufficient oil level can cause a drop in pressure and turn on the warning light.
VERO. If the warning light stays on, stop safely, switch off the engine and check the level with the dipstick according to the vehicle's instructions.
FALSO according to the quiz: the warning light indicates a pressure problem, not directly a missed oil change. Neglected oil can, however, indirectly contribute to lubrication failures.
FALSO according to the quiz: the warning light indicates abnormal oil pressure; it does not directly measure the oil's fluidity. Unsuitable viscosity can nevertheless affect lubrication and pressure.
FALSO. The oil in the pneumohydraulic converter belongs to the braking circuit; the engine oil warning light concerns pressure in the engine lubrication circuit.
FALSO. Do not continue at maximum engine speed: insufficient pressure can damage the engine. Stop safely and switch it off.

FALSO. Excess pressure indicates a fault that must be repaired; it is not resolved by avoiding the service brake and relying on the retarder.

FALSO. Water takes up space in the reservoir, so it reduces rather than increases the volume available for air.

In a dual-circuit system, the separation limits the effects of a break to the affected circuit: the other retains residual braking, though not necessarily full normal braking.

The type of gearbox does not prevent use of the duplex valve: it belongs to the pneumatic brake control system, which is separate from the transmission with an epicyclic gearbox.
Running the engine at high speed does not repair the duplex valve. A fault in the brake control requires stopping safely and having the vehicle checked.
A clogged filter restricts intake air and can affect combustion, especially in the diesel engines considered by the quiz.
A clogged filter can reduce the air available for combustion and contribute to black smoke, particularly in a diesel engine; the effect is not necessarily the same in every engine.
If the filter is clogged, less air reaches the engine: it may lose power and run less efficiently.
The engine air filter is not the braking system filter: if clogged, it restricts air for combustion and does not directly cause brake inefficiency.
Clogging restricts airflow; it does not in itself imply that foreign matter enters the combustion chamber. That risk applies, for example, to a damaged or improperly fitted filter.
White smoke is not the typical effect attributed to a clogged air filter: less available air can instead contribute to black smoke, especially in diesel engines.
A clogged cabin air filter can reduce airflow into the cabin and worsen its air quality; it should be replaced according to the maintenance schedule.
The cabin air filter concerns air for cabin ventilation, not air drawn into the engine: its clogging does not directly reduce vehicle performance.
The filter progressively traps impurities in the oil; if it is not replaced at the specified intervals, it can become saturated and clogged.
A clogged filter can cause the bypass to open, allowing unfiltered oil to circulate: impurities can increase wear and also damage the cylinders.

When the filter is clogged, the bypass may open and allow unfiltered oil containing impurities to circulate. However, accumulated impurities contribute to the clogging; the filter does not create them.

In the system considered by the quiz, clogging does not interrupt the circuit: a bypass valve allows oil to continue circulating without being filtered. The answer assumes that the bypass is present and working.
Black smoke is associated with combustion problems, not directly with a clogged oil filter, which concerns the cleanliness and circulation of the lubricant.
A clogged oil filter affects engine lubrication, not the operation of the brake booster. It can instead allow unfiltered oil to circulate through the bypass.
The fuel filter traps impurities in the fuel, protecting the components of the fuel supply and injection system.
A clogged filter restricts fuel flow and can impair the supply to the pump, if the filter is upstream of it.
A clogged filter obstructs the fuel supply: less fuel may reach the engine and power may decrease.

The fuel filter does not lubricate the cylinders: a blockage instead obstructs the engine's fuel supply.
Clogging does not in itself cause greater injector wear: the filter traps impurities and, when clogged, mainly restricts flow.
VERO. Steering while stationary stresses the tread against the road surface without rolling, causing greater tire wear.

VERO. When stationary, the wheels must be turned against friction with the ground: repeating the maneuver stresses the steering components and can accelerate their wear and thus increase steering play. This does not mean that every turn immediately produces play.
With excessive play, some steering wheel movement is not immediately transmitted to the wheels, making it less precise to maintain the intended path.
Excessive play affects steering response and does not necessarily impair the operation of the front suspension. The affected components should still be checked.
Steering play does not necessarily cause premature wear of the rear tires; the main problem is less precise steering.
Holding the steering wheel with both hands helps with control, but does not eliminate mechanical play: the steering must be checked and repaired or adjusted.
Incorrect wheel toe makes the tread scrub unevenly and can produce asymmetric wear.
Excessive pressure can concentrate the load in the center of the tread, which tends to wear more quickly.
With insufficient pressure, the shoulders of the tread tend to wear more than the center.
An unbalanced wheel can cause vibrations and uneven tire wear.
Incorrect wheel toe does not reduce the risk of skidding: it can make steering less stable and encourage the vehicle to drift.
An unbalanced wheel does not shorten braking distance: it can instead cause vibrations and uneven wear.

Under the quiz's criterion, imbalance mainly causes vibrations, while drifting from a straight path is associated with wheel alignment or differences between tires. Drifting can nevertheless have several causes.

The quiz indicates FALSO: steering shimmy is commonly associated with wheel imbalance. The wording is ambiguous, however: a technical document also identifies incorrect alignment as a possible cause of oscillation.
Incorrect wheel toe can make straight-line driving less stable and encourage deviation from the intended path.
Different pressures on the same axle can cause the tires to respond differently and make the vehicle pull to one side.
An unbalanced front wheel can cause vibrations felt as oscillations of the steering wheel.
If underinflated, dual tires can deform until they touch: rubbing damages their sidewalls.
Excessive pressure tends to wear mainly the center of the tread; wear at the edges is typical of insufficient pressure.
Insufficient pressure tends to wear mainly the edges of the tread; wear in the center is typically associated with excessive pressure.
FALSO. Dual tires must also be inflated to the pressure specified for the vehicle and load, without arbitrarily reducing it.
FALSO. Insufficient pressure increases, rather than decreases, the risk of hydroplaning.

VERO. If the belt driving the alternator breaks, the alternator is no longer driven and does not recharge the battery.
VERO. If the warning light remains on while the engine is running, it indicates a possible problem with the charging circuit, not necessarily with the battery itself.

VERO. In the traditional system, the air for braking is supplied by the engine-driven compressor, not the alternator. The statement does not rule out indirect effects on electronic systems that depend on the power supply.

FALSO. It is the battery that is recharged by the generator, not the dynamo. The rectifier converts the alternating current produced by the alternator to supply the electrical system.
FALSO. The pump circulates coolant; it does not recharge the battery, which is the alternator's job. A pump failure can, however, have an indirect effect if it damages a shared belt.
FALSO. The battery warning light indicates a possible charging problem, not excessive pressure in the battery fluid.

FALSO. In the traditional system, the air for braking comes from the engine-driven compressor, not the alternator. An electrical fault may, however, have indirect effects on any electronic systems present.
VERO. The transmission selects different ratios between the rotation of the engine and that of the drive wheels.
VERO. Selecting a gear ratio adjusts the force available at the wheels to the resistance to motion, for example when climbing a hill.
FALSO. There is no direct proportional relationship: a more flexible engine can cover a wider operating range with fewer gear changes. The number of gears also depends on the vehicle's design.
FALSO. Low gears multiply torque at the wheels more and provide more tractive force at low speeds; high gears allow higher speeds with less multiplication.
VERO. A wide interval between the engine speeds at maximum torque and maximum power generally allows the engine to adapt better to changes in load without changing gear.
VERO. In the model used by the quiz, the useful stability range lies between the engine speed at maximum torque and that at maximum power.
VERO. Within the stability range, the engine can respond to an increase in resistance with an increase in torque, reducing the need to change gear.
VERO. Choosing the appropriate gear allows the engine speed to remain within the optimal operating range as vehicle speed changes.
VERO. The limits of the range considered are identified by the engine speeds at which the curves reach maximum torque and maximum power, respectively.
VERO. When climbing with a load, keeping the engine in the optimal range shown on the tachometer helps ensure that the necessary torque is available.
VERO. A lower gear multiplies torque at the wheels more, making more tractive force available for the climb.
VERO. When climbing, change gear to bring the engine back into its useful speed range, choosing the gear according to the load and gradient.
FALSO. The upper limit considered is the engine speed at maximum power, not minimum power; the lower limit is the engine speed at maximum torque.
Falso: the stability range is a range of engine speeds useful for operating under load, not a range in which no fuel is consumed.
Falso: within the stability range, the engine can adapt to changes in load without necessarily requiring a gear change.
Falso: the width of the range depends on the characteristic engine speeds of the torque and power curves, not on the specific fuel consumption value alone.

Falso: the engine speed at maximum torque is not an upper limit that must not be exceeded. When climbing, choose a gear that leaves the engine with a reserve of engine speed and force suited to the load.
If engine speed falls too far below the speed at maximum torque, a lower gear brings the engine back to a more useful speed and increases the force available at the wheels.
A gear suited to the load and gradient keeps the engine operating more efficiently and can reduce fuel consumption.
VERO. Choosing a gear that keeps the engine close to its most efficient speed helps limit the fuel needed for the work required, as permitted by the load and driving conditions.
On a descent, a low gear increases the effect of engine braking and helps control speed.
Falso: keeping the engine at maximum speed all the time does not reduce emissions. To limit fuel consumption and emissions, use a suitable gear and avoid unnecessarily high engine speeds.
Falso: changing gear often does not guarantee lower fuel consumption; what matters is choosing the right gear and driving smoothly, avoiding unnecessary gear changes.
Falso: aerodynamics affect resistance to motion. Greater resistance increases the fuel required and therefore CO₂ emissions.
Falso: for the same engine torque, a low gear multiplies the transmitted torque more and increases the tractive force at the wheels.

The quiz considers fuel consumption excessive when the engine is kept at too high a speed under load. Note: when the accelerator is released, some engines cut off fuel delivery, so engine speed alone does not determine consumption.
If resistance increases, more tractive force is needed to maintain the same speed; otherwise the vehicle slows down.
For the same engine torque, low gears multiply the transmitted torque more and therefore increase the tractive force at the wheels.
An excessive load increases the energy needed for movement and fuel consumption; as a result, CO₂ emissions increase.
Falso: tractive force is not constant. For the same engine torque, it varies with the selected gear ratio and is greater in low gears.
Falso according to the quiz: to increase tractive force, select a lower gear. ‘Higher ratio’ is ambiguous: if it refers to the numerical reduction ratio, this increases in lower gears.
Falso: increasing the load does not in itself increase the driving force available; instead, it increases the force needed for movement. To obtain more tractive force, you can shift to a lower gear.
Falso according to the quiz: to increase tractive force, select a lower gear. ‘Higher ratio’ is ambiguous: if it refers to the numerical reduction ratio, this increases in lower gears.
In general, it is best to use the highest gear that allows the engine to respond without strain, while maintaining control of the vehicle.
VERO. In general, it is advisable to select a gear that keeps the engine in its efficient operating range without placing excessive strain on it at too low an engine speed.
For the same engine torque, a lower gear multiplies the torque at the wheels more, increasing tractive force.
A low gear when driving downhill allows engine braking to be used, helping to control speed.
When driving downhill, a low gear uses engine braking and helps keep speed down; the brakes are also used if necessary.
A low gear increases engine braking and helps control speed downhill; it does not in itself increase braking distance. Braking distance also depends on speed and grip.
A low gear uses engine braking and reduces the need to use the service brakes; it does not increase brake pad wear.
If engine speed drops too low, a higher gear would reduce it further. Instead, select a lower gear suited to the speed and load.
The absolute prohibition is wrong: when climbing, especially with a load, a low gear may be needed to maintain adequate tractive force.
A higher gear is not always suitable for climbing with a load: select the gear according to the gradient and conditions, shifting down if necessary.
To use engine braking on a long descent, select an appropriate lower gear, not a higher one.
The force on the piston passes through the connecting rod to the crank on the crankshaft, producing torque that turns it.
Torque is the product of the force and its perpendicular moment arm relative to the axis of rotation.

The quiz indicates VERO, but the two do not generally coincide: efficiency depends on both engine speed and load. The torque curve alone is not enough to show that maximum efficiency occurs precisely at the speed of maximum torque.
Maximum torque is normally reached at a lower engine speed than maximum power: power depends on both torque and engine speed. The exact position of the peaks depends on the engine.
Force and length are not added together: torque is the product of the force and the perpendicular moment arm.
The brakes apply braking torque to the wheels; driving torque, by contrast, originates in the engine from the force transmitted by the pistons to the crankshaft.
The speed at maximum torque does not necessarily indicate maximum consumption: consumption also varies with load and must be assessed on the engine map, specifying how it is measured.
The two maxima normally do not coincide: power depends on torque and engine speed and can continue to rise after the torque peak.
The torque curve shows the torque delivered at different engine speeds.
The power curve shows power at different engine speeds; at each speed it also depends on the torque delivered.
In the typical pattern considered by the quiz, torque rises to a maximum and then falls; the actual shape depends on the engine and may include an almost flat section.
VERO in the general model used by the quiz: power rises with engine speed to a maximum and then falls. The shape and the range that can actually be used depend on the engine.
The curve does not relate torque to vehicle weight: it shows how torque varies with engine speed.
The power curve does not describe torque in relation to vehicle dimensions: it shows how power varies with engine speed.
The stated pattern is reversed: in the typical curve used by the quiz, torque rises to a maximum and then falls, although there may be flat sections depending on the engine.
FALSO. In the general model the curve follows the opposite pattern: power rises to a maximum and then falls, with details depending on the engine.

The general threshold for goods transport is over 3.5 tonnes, including any trailers, subject to exceptions. From 1 July 2026, the regulation also covers international or cabotage transport over 2.5 tonnes, under the specified conditions.
The regulation covers passenger transport in vehicles built or adapted for more than nine people, including the driver, subject to the specified exclusions.

VERO. The regulation applies to transport within the Union by bus and, for goods, by vehicles over 3.5 tonnes, subject to specific exclusions.

VERO, with a clarification: AETR applies to international transport leaving the EU, EEA and Switzerland under the specified conditions, including those concerning the state of registration; a general reference to any other state is not enough.
The regulation covers transport between the European Union and European Economic Area states if it falls within its scope and is not excluded.
For national regular services without a tachograph that are governed by the regulation, the driver carries an extract from the duty roster and a copy of the service timetable.
Periodic inspection of the tachograph does not exempt the driver from driving limits: these apply when the transport falls within the scope of the regulation.

For transport between Italy and France that is subject to European rules, the EU regulation on driving times applies, not the AETR. The type of service may nevertheless determine whether exclusions apply.
Limiting driving and ensuring rest also helps protect drivers from the risks associated with fatigue.
Breaks and rest periods reduce the risk of driver fatigue compromising the safety of other road users.
The rules also aim to improve drivers' social conditions by limiting driving and ensuring rest.
Reducing emissions is not the purpose of these rules: they aim to improve social conditions and road safety.
Restraining wages is not the purpose of these rules: they aim to improve social conditions and road safety.
Reducing vehicle wear is not the purpose of these rules: they protect social conditions and road safety.
A person who drives even for a short period is also a driver: the definition does not require a minimum duration.
A person on board to drive when needed is also a driver, even if they are not at the wheel at that moment.
During a break, the driver neither drives nor performs other work: the period is exclusively for recuperation.
Loading and unloading are work other than driving and therefore count as other work.
Checking tyre pressure is an activity for vehicle safety and maintenance, so it counts as other work.
Rest is an uninterrupted period during which the driver is free to dispose of their time.
There is no need to cover 100 km: a person who drives even for a short period is also a driver.
A person on board to drive when needed also falls within the definition of a driver.
During a break, the driver may neither perform other work nor drive: the period is intended for recuperation.
Cleaning the vehicle is work other than driving and counts as other work.
Customs formalities connected with the transport are work other than driving and count as other work.
Not driving is not enough: during rest, the driver must be free to dispose of their time without performing other work.
Other work also includes work performed for another employer, inside or outside the transport sector.
A regular daily rest period can consist of at least 11 consecutive hours.
A regular daily rest period can be split into at least 3 consecutive hours followed by at least 9 consecutive hours.
A reduced daily rest period lasts at least 9 consecutive hours but less than 11.
A regular weekly rest period lasts at least 45 hours.
A reduced weekly rest period lasts less than 45 hours, but at least 24 consecutive hours, under the conditions set out in the regulation.
Daily driving is the total driving between two daily rest periods or between a daily rest period and a weekly rest period.
Seven hours is not enough: a regular daily rest period is at least 11 consecutive hours, or it can be split into at least 3 hours followed by at least 9.
Six hours is not enough: a reduced daily rest period lasts at least 9 hours and less than 11.
Twenty-four hours is the minimum for a reduced weekly rest period; a regular one lasts at least 45 hours.
Daily driving is normally limited to 9 hours and can reach 10 hours no more than twice a week.
Weekly driving cannot exceed 56 hours; the limit for two consecutive weeks also applies.
Total driving over two consecutive weeks cannot exceed 90 hours.
After 4 and a half hours of driving, a break of at least 45 minutes is required unless a rest period is started; the break can also be split according to the applicable rules.
After 4 and a half hours of driving, a break of at least 45 minutes or a rest period is required; split breaks are permitted under the specified conditions.
During a break, the driver may neither drive nor perform other work: the time is exclusively for recuperation.
Maintenance is work and cannot be performed during a break, which must be used for recuperation.
The break is not optional: after 4 and a half hours of driving, a break of at least 45 minutes is required unless a rest period is started.

The presence of a second driver does not permit driving for more than 4 and a half hours without the required break. With multiple drivers, the break can be taken while the other driver is driving, under the specified conditions.
Other work cannot be performed during a break: it is reserved for recuperation.
The normal threshold is 4 and a half hours of driving, not 4 hours: at that point, a break of at least 45 minutes or a rest period is required.
An extension to 10 hours is permitted at most twice a week, not three times.
The break can be split into at least 15 minutes followed by at least 30 minutes, distributed over the driving period according to the applicable rule.
A regular daily rest period is normally at least 11 consecutive hours. The question omits split and reduced rest periods, which are permitted under the specified conditions.

A regular rest period is at least 11 hours and a reduced one at least 9. To clarify: at most three reduced daily rest periods are permitted between two weekly rest periods, not simply three days per week.
As a rule, a new daily rest period must be completed within 24 hours of the end of the previous daily or weekly rest period. Exceptions are provided, for example when there are multiple drivers.

The normal rule requires a weekly rest period to begin within six 24-hour periods after the end of the previous one. Referring to six consecutive days is a simplification, and exceptions are provided for certain passenger services.
Eight hours is not the general maximum: the normal limit is 9 hours, extendable to 10 at most twice a week.
The 9 hours are the ordinary total daily limit, not 9 consecutive hours: after 4 and a half hours, a break or rest is required.
Four and a half hours refers to driving before a break, not the daily limit. The ordinary daily limit is 9 hours, which can be extended to 10 twice a week.
The limit is 90 hours in total over two consecutive weeks, not 112.

An agreement with the employer does not remove the obligation to take weekly rest, which must normally begin within six 24-hour periods after the previous rest. Note that the limit concerns 24-hour periods, not necessarily calendar days; specific exceptions exist for certain passenger services.
The break is for recovery: during it, the driver may neither drive nor perform other duties.
Exceptionally, the limit may be exceeded to reach a suitable stopping place, only as far as necessary for safety and without compromising road safety; the reason must be recorded.
Rest requires the driver to be free to use their time as they wish. Availability while waiting to resume work is recorded separately from rest.
Daily rest away from base may be taken in the vehicle, at the driver's choice, if it is stationary and has suitable sleeping facilities for each driver.
The weekly driving limit is 56 hours, not 45; the limit of 90 hours over two consecutive weeks also applies.
Feeling fit does not permit a driver to continue without a break: after four and a half hours of driving, a break of at least 45 minutes is required unless a rest period is started.
Being at home does not automatically turn on-call time into rest: rest requires freedom to use one's time, whereas availability is recorded separately.
A ferry is not the only permitted place: daily rest away from base may also be taken in a stationary vehicle equipped with suitable sleeping facilities.
VERO. When a tachograph is mandatory, driving without one entails a fine and suspension of the driving licence as an additional penalty.
VERO. Driving with a tachograph that does not meet the prescribed specifications entails a fine and suspension of the driving licence.

Failure to insert the record sheet or driver card, when required, entails an administrative fine and suspension of the driving licence.

Confiscation is not prescribed solely because the tachograph is not working: driving entails an administrative fine and suspension of the driving licence.
Revocation is the incorrect part: driving with tampered seals entails a doubled fine and suspension of the driving licence.

A repeat violation within two years does not automatically make the court responsible for determining a penalty: for driving with an altered tachograph, Article 179 provides for an administrative fine and suspension of the driving licence.

Failure to insert the record sheet or card results in a loss of points. If the violation occurs during a service for which the CQC is required, the points are deducted from the professional qualification.
For driving with tampered seals, the administrative fine is doubled and the driving licence is suspended.
Driving with an altered tachograph entails a doubled administrative fine and suspension of the driving licence.
The holder of a passenger transport licence or authorization who puts a vehicle without the mandatory tachograph into service is subject to an administrative fine.
It is wrong to rule out suspension: driving with tampered seals entails suspension of the driving licence as well as a fine.

Being the holder alone does not entail suspension of the driving licence: putting the vehicle into service entails a fine and, in the event of repeated violations under the conditions set by law, suspension of the licence or authorization.
The tachograph records driving, other duties, availability, breaks and rest separately, according to the activities selected by the driver.
Opening the casing that contains the record sheet is automatically marked on the sheet itself.

The question refers to authorized workshops; the rules also permit authorized installers and vehicle manufacturers to carry out installation and repairs. Periodic inspections are the responsibility of authorized workshops.
The record sheet stays with the driver when changing vehicles, provided it is compatible with the next tachograph; the details of the change are recorded.
The driver does not have to write the approval number: the sheet must include, among other things, the driver's name, vehicle registration number and journey details.
The tachograph card number is not among the details to be written on the analogue record sheet; the driver's name, vehicle registration number and journey details are required, among other things.
The date of the last inspection is not among the entries required of the driver on the sheet; the driver's name, vehicle registration number and journey details are recorded, among other things.
It is false that availability periods are missing: the tachograph records them separately from other activities using the mode switch.
The tachograph records speed, but does not act as a speed limiter for the vehicle.
The record sheets must be of an approved type suitable for the installed tachograph.
The transport company supplies drivers with a sufficient number of approved record sheets suitable for the device.

The record sheet is normally removed at the end of the working day and is not used beyond its intended duration, normally 24 hours. Returning the vehicle alone does not necessarily coincide with the end of work; authorized early removal is permitted.
The driver records the vehicle registration number before the first journey and also that of any subsequent vehicle used with the same sheet.
Not all vehicles over 3.5 tonnes are subject to the requirement: the type of transport and the exemptions provided by law matter.
It is false that the tachograph prevents speed limits from being exceeded: it records speed but does not limit the vehicle's movement.
A photocopy cannot replace an approved, compatible record sheet: a suitable sheet supplied by the company must be used.
The chamber of commerce does not supply the record sheets: the transport company gives them to the driver.
Do not wait 36 hours: the sheet cannot be used beyond its intended duration, normally 24 hours, and is generally removed at the end of work.
While stopped, the driver selects the actual activity, such as other duties, availability or rest, so that it is recorded separately.
The record sheet belongs to an individual driver: when drivers change, the records must appear on the sheet of the person actually driving.
Before the first recorded journey, the driver notes the initial odometer reading.
Before the first journey recorded on the sheet, the driver enters the vehicle registration number on it.
At the start of using the sheet, the driver writes their surname and first name on it.
The place where use of the sheet begins is entered on it.
The date on which use of the sheet begins is entered on it.
When changing vehicles, the record sheet stays with the driver if it is compatible with the new device; the registration number, odometer readings and time of the change are entered on it.
Changing vehicles does not automatically require a new disc: the driver may continue using their sheet, recording the new vehicle's details, provided it is compatible with the device.

The sheet is not completed only at the end of work: some information, such as the name and the starting place and date, must be entered at the beginning of use; other details are completed at the end.
The driving licence and CQC numbers do not have to be entered on the disc. The required details include the driver's first and last name, dates, places, registration numbers and odometer readings.
A mandatory break does not in itself require the sheet to be replaced: the disc remains in use and also records breaks and rest periods, within its recording capacity.

During the malfunction, the driver records periods that were not properly recorded, including driving and rest, on the sheet or on a separate sheet to be attached, together with their identifying details and signature.

The repair must be made as soon as circumstances permit; if the base cannot be reached until more than a week after the malfunction, it must be made en route. The time limit stated in the quiz does not permit waiting seven days regardless of circumstances.

If the vehicle returns to base within a week of the malfunction, the repair may be made on its return, provided circumstances do not permit an earlier repair. The week runs from the malfunction, not necessarily from the start of the journey.

During the malfunction, the driver manually records periods that were not properly recorded, with identification and a signature. They may use the disc, including its reverse, or a separate sheet to be attached: the reverse is not the only option.

The quiz marks the statement as VERO, but the wording requires caution: in the event of a malfunction, the driver must record periods that were not properly recorded, identifying themselves and signing. The provision on malfunctions does not expressly impose a general obligation to record the kilometres travelled.
The disc makes it possible to distinguish records of different activities, including driving, availability and rest, using the markings and traces provided for each period.
The obligation to manually record periods that were not properly recorded applies during the malfunction, even on short journeys. The one-week threshold concerns repair en route.
A malfunction does not automatically require the journey to be stopped immediately. Unrecorded periods must be noted and the tachograph repaired as soon as possible, including en route when required.

A malfunction does not automatically require an immediate stop or reporting the times to the inspectorate as described. Instead, the driver records the unrecorded periods and the company arranges for repair as soon as possible.

A tachograph malfunction does not require a temporary driving permit from the Chamber of Commerce. The driver records the unrecorded periods and the company has the device repaired as soon as possible.

Discs for the last three months are not required. For roadside checks, the driver must be able to present the sheets for the current day and the previous 56 days, along with the other required documents.

The requirement to retain sheets for inspection does not depend on the length of an individual transport operation. Sheets for the current day and the previous 56 days are required for activities subject to recording.

The driver enters the symbols for the countries where the working period begins and ends, and records non-driving activities using the selector or manual entry when necessary. The quiz's reference to the ‘place’ should be understood with this clarification.
The digital tachograph records card insertion and withdrawal events in its memory, associating them with the data needed to reconstruct card use.
Speed is measured and stored by the digital tachograph; it is not a value the driver has to enter manually for each journey.

The memory records information about data transfers to an external device. The technical specification cited provides in particular for data on the last transfer in the specified modes, not necessarily a complete history of all transfers.

The driver card is used for every day of driving, from the time the driver takes over the vehicle, and should not normally be withdrawn before the end of the working period, except where withdrawal is authorised or necessary.
In Italy, tachograph cards are issued by the Chambers of Commerce, which national legislation designates as the issuing authorities.

Average speed is not entered manually by the driver into the tachograph: the device records movement data, while manual entries concern, for example, activities and the countries where work begins and ends.
Routine vehicle maintenance is not among the activity and movement data recorded by the digital tachograph. Speed, distance and driver activities are among the data recorded.

The card is not used only while driving and should not automatically be withdrawn for every break or rest period. It normally remains inserted during the working period to record other activities too, unless withdrawal is authorised or necessary.
The driver card is personal: each driver must use their own, even when taking turns in the same vehicle.
A Chamber of Commerce card is not one of the four types: the fourth is the control authority card, alongside the driver, company and workshop cards.
The driver card is personal and cannot be lent, even to a colleague from the same company.
There are four types of tachograph card: driver, company, workshop and control.
The four types correspond to the different users: driver, company, workshop and control authority.
The card identifies an individual driver and is personal: it must not be used by anyone else.
The driver uses their own card from the moment they take over the vehicle, to record their activities.
With two drivers on board, each inserts their own card in the correct slot, distinguishing the person driving from the second driver.
The tachograph signals card-related anomalies, such as an invalid combination of cards or insertion while driving.

The second driver does not have to wait for their turn to drive: when on board as the second driver, they also insert their card in the appropriate slot so that their respective activities are recorded.
Incorrect insertion does not stop the vehicle: the tachograph detects and signals the anomaly while recording activities and movement data.
The tachograph is not intended to warn of speed cameras: it records and displays data about the vehicle and the drivers' activities.
There is no need to wait 24 hours: the card may be withdrawn when the daily working period ends or when withdrawal is otherwise authorised.
Loss of the card does not always require an immediate stop: the driver may continue temporarily under the prescribed conditions, making the printouts and requesting a replacement card.
The tachograph warns the driver about continuous driving time before and upon reaching four and a half hours. The warning should not be understood as a universal check of every driving limit.
At the end of the day, the card is withdrawn while the vehicle is stationary, after the relevant data has been recorded.
Loss of the card must be reported to the police, including for the purpose of requesting a replacement.

If the card is lost, the required printouts are made at the beginning and end of the journey, with the required details added and the printouts signed; the documents must be available for inspection. The final printout alone does not fulfil all the requirements.

The quiz says VERO, but the prescribed limit is 15 calendar days, not working days. Driving may continue for longer only to return the vehicle to base, if it can be shown that the card could not be presented or used during that period.
The out-of-scope function indicates use excluded from the rules on driving times; it does not physically switch off the tachograph or erase data.
The card must be inserted before setting off. The device may detect insertion while driving as an anomaly: the verdict does not mean it is physically impossible to insert it.
A colleague's card cannot be used: it is personal. If the card is lost, a replacement is requested and the rules for temporarily driving without a card are followed.
The out-of-scope function concerns uses excluded from the rules, not malfunctions. If the tachograph is damaged, the prescribed repair and recording procedures apply instead.

For professional goods transport, the appropriate licence for the vehicle and the CQC goods qualification are required, subject to exemptions. The quiz says VERO, but for vehicles over 3.5 tonnes and up to 7.5 tonnes, a C1 licence may be sufficient instead of C or CE.

Professional passenger transport by bus requires the appropriate driving licence and a passenger CQC, unless an exemption applies. The quiz says D, but D1 may be sufficient for buses that fall within the limits of that category.
Professional scheduled public transport requires a bus driving licence and a passenger transport CQC.
The CQC is issued by the Motorizzazione Civile, the authority responsible for professional qualifications.

The quiz considers the exemption for own-account transport when the person is not employed as a driver. However, the contractual job title alone is not enough: the conditions for the exemption must be met, such as transporting materials used by the driver and driving not being their principal activity.
The Chamber of Commerce does not issue the CQC: it is issued by the Motorizzazione Civile.
A D or DE licence alone does not exempt the holder from the CQC requirement: the corresponding qualification is also needed for professional transport subject to that requirement.
