The KB certificate is not the qualification required for a scheduled bus service: a passenger transport CQC is needed along with the appropriate licence.
It is incorrect to rule out the CQC: the passenger transport qualification is required for professional driving of buses on scheduled services.
There is no general exemption for school buses: the CQC is required for drivers who needed the CAP KD, whether operating on their own account or for others.
The CQC does not necessarily expire at the same time as the driving licence: the qualification has its own five-year validity period and renewal process.
The CQC qualification is valid for five years and must be renewed periodically.

The VERO answer reflects the previous rules: after more than two years, periodic training and a reinstatement exam were required. Today, as a general rule, a CQC expired for more than three years requires a review exam instead of the course, subject to transitional rules.
Ordinary renewal of the CQC requires attendance at a periodic training course. Different rules apply if it has been expired for more than three years.
The CQC has a points balance that is separate from and additional to the driving licence's balance.
The CQC qualification is required for professional driving of vehicles in the relevant categories, including for an Italian transport company, subject to the applicable exemptions.
A driver from a third country employed by a company established in the Union is also subject to the qualification requirement for the vehicles concerned, unless an exemption applies.
Proving that you have worked as a driver does not replace renewal: the periodic training required for the CQC is normally needed.

It is not renewed by taking a new initial training course. The previous rule required periodic training and a reinstatement exam; today, after more than three years of expiry, a review exam normally applies.
The CQC starts with 20 points, not 30; this balance is separate from the driving licence's balance.
Turning 60 does not automatically prevent renewal of the passenger CQC. To continue driving buses after that age, drivers must meet the medical requirements and obtain the required certificate.
The CQC is an additional professional qualification and does not replace the driving licence: if the licence is suspended, the CQC alone does not authorise driving.

The quiz marks this VERO, but ‘every’ injury is too broad: an occupational accident requires a sudden, violent cause arising in connection with work; harm that develops gradually may be an occupational disease.
A fall while climbing into the cab during work is a sudden event connected with the work activity; the fracture may therefore constitute an occupational accident.
An injury caused by a sudden event during maintenance carried out for work may constitute an occupational accident; the connection with work and the sudden, violent cause matter.
An injury caused by a sudden event during loading or unloading carried out for work may be an occupational accident.
A sudden hand injury while coupling a trailer for work may constitute an occupational accident because it occurs in connection with the work activity.

An accidental fall into the tank during work is a sudden, violent cause connected with the activity. Whether the case is recognised as an occupational accident also depends on the consequences of the injury.

Negligence in using protective equipment does not automatically rule out an occupational accident: the connection with work matters, except in cases of a risk voluntarily assumed for personal reasons.
Breaking safety rules does not automatically rule out an occupational accident. The connection with work and any risk voluntarily assumed for personal reasons must be assessed.

Drinking alcohol is not in itself an occupational accident: there is no injurious event caused by a sudden, violent cause in connection with work. Any subsequent accident must be assessed in light of its circumstances.
Damage to goods concerns property, not an injury to a worker. An occupational accident, on the other hand, concerns personal injury connected with work.
A tourist's injury during a journey is not, for that reason alone, an occupational accident: there must be a connection with the injured person's work activity.

An accidental fall from the loading platform during work is a sudden, violent cause arising in connection with work. Whether the case is recognised as an occupational accident also depends on the consequences of the injury.
The definition requires an event caused by a sudden, violent cause in connection with work and resulting harm to the person, such as incapacity, impairment or death.
A musculoskeletal injury caused by sudden exertion while changing a tyre may constitute an occupational accident; the event and its consequences must be established.
Accidental contact with corrosive material during work may be a sudden, violent cause of injury to eyesight. The consequences must be assessed in the individual case.
A road accident during professional activity may constitute an occupational accident: the injury results from a sudden event connected with work.

It is not excluded simply because it happened in the depot at the end of a shift: an activity connected with finishing a shift may also be work-related. The circumstances and any injury must be checked.
The vehicle does not have to be moving: an injury caused by a sudden, violent cause during loading or maintenance can also occur in connection with work.
Incorrect driver behaviour accounts for most established or presumed causes in ISTAT statistics. The proportion depends on the data and circumstances recorded.
A speed that is too high or unsuitable reduces the time available to react and is among the recurring circumstances of accidents.
Failing to give way can create a conflict with other road users and is among the behaviours most frequently recorded in accidents.
Distraction takes attention away from the road and is among the behaviours most frequently recorded in accidents.
An insufficient following distance can prevent a driver from stopping in time and is a recurring circumstance, particularly in rear-end collisions.
Fatigue can reduce attention and responsiveness, increasing the risk of an accident.
Ineffective suspension can compromise stability and the wheels' contact with the road, contributing to an accident.
Worn tread reduces the ability to drain water and can worsen grip, increasing the risk of losing control.
Ineffective brakes can prevent a vehicle from slowing down or stopping effectively and contribute to an accident.
Tachograph failure is not among the most recurring causes of accidents. Behaviours such as distraction, failing to give way and excessive speed are more frequent.
Injection pump failure is not among the most recurring causes of accidents. Distraction, failing to give way and excessive speed are among those recorded more often.
The absence of a fire extinguisher does not in itself cause a road accident: an extinguisher is used to tackle a fire, so its absence can make the consequences of a fire worse.
The quiz marks this FALSO because a pump failure affects engine cooling, not driving directly. However, it can cause overheating and a breakdown, so an indirect risk cannot be ruled out.
The quiz marks this FALSO because a clogged filter mainly affects engine operation. A loss of power can nevertheless indirectly create a dangerous situation.

FALSO. The mere fact that a vehicle uses diesel, LPG or methane does not automatically increase the risk of a road accident: driving and the vehicle's condition also matter. The systems require precautions specific to the fuel.

For stays of up to three months, an EU citizen may use an identity card valid for travel abroad. ‘Without restrictions’ must be understood within the limits set by law, for example on public order grounds.
A residence card from the police headquarters is not required: for a short stay, an EU citizen only needs an identity document valid for travel abroad or a valid passport.
An EU citizen does not need an entry visa: a passport or an identity card valid for travel abroad is sufficient.
A valid passport and visa allow a person to request entry, but do not automatically guarantee it: the other applicable conditions must also be met. In some cases a visa is not required.

Foreign nationals may be subject to the checks provided for at the border, including customs, currency and health checks where applicable. Not all of these checks are automatically carried out on every person.
A visa is an authorization relating to entry and, depending on its type, to a stay; it does not automatically guarantee admission at the border.
Italy and France are among the countries affected by irregular residence. The comparison depends on the year and the indicator used: the quiz specifies neither.
The quiz describes entry without meeting the required conditions. Irregular migration also includes a stay that becomes irregular after lawful entry, so the definition is incomplete.
Facilitating irregular entry can expose people to exploitation and trafficking; demand for undeclared work can fuel the phenomenon. Not all irregular migration involves trafficking.
A visa is not a signature on an entry stamp: it is an authorization issued for entry or a stay, depending on the type of visa.

The quiz marks this FALSO: the main sea route referred to is the central Mediterranean route towards Italy, not the Tyrrhenian coast as such. Routes change over time and do not rule out individual arrivals elsewhere.
It is incorrect to limit the phenomenon to lawful entry or the absence of permanent residence: it concerns entry or a stay without meeting the required conditions, including after lawful entry.
Not all EU countries are part of the Schengen area: Ireland is outside it.

The quiz incorrectly assigns the carrier responsibility for checking financial means: its obligation concerns the required travel documents. Means of subsistence, on the other hand, are a condition that border authorities may check.
Non-EU countries also participate in the Schengen area, including Norway and Switzerland.
As a rule, internal borders are crossed without border checks on people. In circumstances provided for by law, checks may be temporarily reinstated.
The carrier must check that the foreign national it transports has the travel documents required for entry; this obligation applies in the cases specified by law.

The quiz marks this VERO, but the wording is imprecise: in the cases provided for, the obligation falls on the carrier and concerns the person refused entry. The law specifies the country of departure or the country that issued the travel document, not the country that issued the ticket.

The quiz marks this VERO, but ‘only’ is imprecise: a valid passport is also accepted. The declaration of presence is optional; without it, a stay of more than three months is presumed, although evidence to the contrary can rebut this presumption.

The quiz marks this VERO, but expulsion is not automatic for everyone without a permit or with an expired permit: the law distinguishes between cases and provides for time limits, exceptions and safeguards.

There is no general obligation to take the person to the prefecture: in the specified cases of refusal of entry, the carrier must take responsibility for the person and return them in accordance with the law.
The absence or expiry of a permit does not lead to immediate regularization: the situation is assessed under the rules on residence and, where applicable, expulsion.
It is false that this is only an administrative offence: facilitating irregular entry constitutes a criminal offence punishable by imprisonment and fines.
Heartbeat detectors can be used during vehicle checks to find hidden people.
Parking in a supervised area and locking the vehicle reduces opportunities for unauthorized access; the vehicle should still be checked before setting off again.
A thorough check of the bus and any trailer helps identify unauthorized access or hidden people before reaching the border.

The question simplifies the situation: the carrier must check the required documents and report the presence of people with irregular status. Financial penalties apply for a violation; suspension or revocation is provided for in more serious cases.
Facilitating irregular entry is punishable by imprisonment and a fine; in cases specified by law, the vehicle used for the offence is also confiscated.
The check described in the references uses carbon dioxide detectors, not oxygen detectors: the probe measures CO₂ that can build up from breathing.

The quiz marks this FALSO, but the wording is ambiguous: checking passengers’ documents may be appropriate and, in the specified cases, is among the carrier’s obligations. To prevent people from hiding on board, the vehicle must also be checked and secured.
As a rule, no border checks on people are carried out at Schengen internal borders; police checks and exceptional temporary reinstatement of border checks remain possible.
Free movement within the Schengen area is accompanied by common rules and checks at its external borders.

The quiz indicates that an exception is possible: a country may temporarily reinstate checks at internal borders in response to a serious threat, subject to specific conditions. The entire treaty is not suspended.
There are common rules for borders and short-stay visas and a common European framework for asylum. Asylum rules, however, do not simply coincide with the Schengen Agreement.
It is false that systematic checks at external borders are abolished: the absence of border checks applies in principle to internal borders; checks are provided for at external borders.
It is false that Schengen normally strengthens checks at internal borders: border checks there are generally abolished, subject to exceptional temporary reinstatement.
It is false that drivers are granted tax relief: Schengen mainly governs border crossings and the absence of routine checks at internal borders.
It is false that the absence of checks always makes an identity document unnecessary: countries may require people to possess or carry identity documents and may conduct police checks.
As a rule, internal borders can be crossed at any point without border checks on people. Police checks and temporary reinstatement of border checks are possible.
Poland is a member of the European Union and part of the Schengen area.
Slovenia is a member of the European Union and part of the Schengen area.
Latvia is a member of the European Union and part of the Schengen area.
It is false that the driver must show the agreement: it is a set of rules, not a personal travel document. Identity documents may, however, be requested during permitted checks.
It is false that Serbia is an EU member and part of Schengen: it is a candidate for EU membership and is not among the Schengen countries.
It is false that Ireland is in the Schengen area: it is an EU member but maintains its own border policy.
It is true that Ukraine is not an EU member, but false that it is in Schengen: it is a candidate for EU membership and is not among the Schengen countries.
It is false that all EU members are in the Schengen area: for example, Ireland is an EU member but does not apply Schengen border rules.
Ireland is part of the European Union, but not of the Schengen area without internal border checks: it applies its own border policy.
In the quiz's terminology, the term refers to a citizen of a non-EU country who entered without meeting the entry conditions. The irregularity concerns the entry, not the person themselves.

The quiz points to the risk that criminal networks may facilitate irregular entry and exploit the people involved. However, the wording is too broad: irregular immigration does not necessarily involve trafficking or exploitation; facilitation and trafficking are distinct phenomena.

The quiz refers to the Italian offence of illegal entry and stay: in the cases provided for, it is punishable by a fine. The rule has exceptions and should not be understood as applying indiscriminately to every irregular migration situation.
It is wrong to call an EU citizen an irregular immigrant merely because they lack a document: EU citizens enjoy freedom of movement and are subject to specific rules on travel documents.
It is wrong to say that only a warning is provided for: in Italy, illegal entry or stay constitutes an offence punishable by a fine in the cases provided for by law.

It is too absolute to rule out any risk: facilitating irregular entry can involve criminal networks and create security risks. This does not mean that every person who entered irregularly is dangerous.

It is wrong to say that irregular entry is permitted: EU countries set entry and stay conditions, and crossing the external Schengen borders is subject to checks. The protections provided for people seeking protection remain in place.
Entering for work does not make irregular entry lawful: the applicable entry and work conditions and procedures must be followed.

Generally, there are no systematic checks on people at borders between EU countries in the Schengen area, and goods circulate within the customs union. Police checks and temporary reinstatement of border controls are possible.

Schengen generally removes checks on people at internal borders, while the EU customs border may involve formalities and checks on goods and cash. Not every check is automatic, and money is not always prohibited: declaration requirements may apply.

The quiz distinguishes between borders for people and customs borders: an EU country outside the Schengen area without border controls may check travellers, while there are normally no customs checks between EU countries on goods in free circulation.

Customs checks and formalities may apply at the EU's external border, as may restrictions on certain goods and cash declaration requirements. The quiz's word 'always' is too absolute: not every traveller is physically checked, and declaring money is not the same as prohibiting it.

At external Schengen borders, people are subject to border checks, including document checks. 'Always' should be read as a general rule: in exceptional circumstances the code allows checks to be relaxed.

It is wrong to say that there are always customs checks between EU countries in Schengen: within the customs union, goods in free circulation normally cross these borders without systematic customs checks.

It is wrong to rule out checks on people as well: identity checks may be carried out at borders with an EU country that does not participate in the Schengen area without border controls, although customs union rules apply.

The quiz reverses the two types of checks: there may be checks on people when crossing to or from an EU country outside the Schengen area without border controls, while there are normally no customs checks on goods in free circulation between EU countries.
There is no general ban on vehicles carrying goods: they may cross the external border by complying with customs formalities and any restrictions on the goods.

The quiz reverses the checks: checks on people are not normally carried out at internal Schengen borders, but customs formalities for goods and cash may apply with Schengen countries outside the EU. Exceptions to the rules on checks on people are possible.

EU citizens have the right to enter Italy with a valid identity document or passport, without a visa. This freedom is not absolute: restrictions provided for by law are allowed, for example on public policy grounds.
For stays of up to three months, an EU citizen must have a valid identity card or passport; they do not need to meet the additional conditions for longer stays.

The quiz identifies public policy, security and public health grounds that may justify restrictions. However, 'only' is too absolute: removal may also follow when the conditions for the right of residence are no longer met, subject to the safeguards provided for.

An EU citizen does not have to apply for a residence permit as a third-country national would. For stays longer than three months, however, they must meet the applicable conditions and may be required to register as a resident.
In exercising freedom of movement, an EU citizen may enter another member state with a valid identity card or passport without an entry visa.

Freedom of movement allows EU citizens to move within member states, but it may be restricted in the cases provided for, for example on public policy, security or public health grounds, subject to the applicable safeguards.
An EU citizen's right of entry may be restricted on public policy grounds, subject to the conditions and safeguards provided for by law.
It is wrong to require an EU citizen to have a visa: a valid identity document or passport is enough to enter another member state; the relevant conditions apply to their stay.
Religion is not grounds for removal. Restrictions on freedom of movement are permitted only in the cases provided for, such as public policy, public security or public health.
A valid passport or equivalent document and crossing the border at an authorised point are entry requirements; the other applicable conditions must also be met.
An entry or transit visa is required when the regulations provide for one; possessing it alone does not guarantee entry, as the other requirements must also be met.
The normal deadline for applying for a permit is eight working days after entry. The wording is general: a permit is not required for some short stays.
The absence of a threat to public policy, security, public health or international relations is one of the entry conditions; the other requirements must also be met.

The requirements include sufficient means for the stay and return; a return ticket can help demonstrate that the means for the journey are available. Exceptions are provided for, for example for entry for work.
It is wrong to say that there are no checks: at external borders, third-country nationals are subject to the prescribed checks, along with any other checks applicable to their case.
A residence permit is not required for visits, business, tourism or study for up to three months; the obligation to declare one's presence in the prescribed manner remains.
An alert in the SIS for refusal of entry is ordinarily an obstacle to entry; exceptions are possible in the cases provided for by law.
Having relatives with no criminal record does not remove the formalities: the applicable entry conditions must be met, including a document and a visa when required.
The normal deadline is not 30 working days: when a permit is required, the application must be submitted within eight working days of entry. A permit is not needed for some short stays.

A passport and, when required, a visa are documents needed for entry. The question is too general: the other requirements must also be met, and the visa is normally requested from the representation responsible for the applicant's place of legal residence.

A visa authorises its holder to present themselves for entry in accordance with its validity; it is normally affixed to the travel document as a sticker. Entry remains subject to verification of the requirements.
A visa is normally issued by the Italian representation responsible for the applicant's place of legal residence, after the requirements have been checked.
Nationals of certain countries are exempt from the visa requirement for short stays for the purposes listed, up to 90 days; the other entry conditions still apply.
The quiz marks VERO, but the absolute wording about extensions is out of date: in special cases the Questura may decide on an extension during a stay in Italy.
It is wrong to specify stays longer than 120 days: the exemption considered by the question concerns short stays of up to 90 days, not longer stays.
The stated limit of 150 days is wrong: a uniform Schengen visa covers short stays of up to 90 days in any 180-day period, within the limits of the visa issued.
The 60 days are wrong: under the historical rules referred to by the quiz, a collective visa was provided for transit or a stay of no more than 30 days.
A visa is not issued by a court: the authorised Italian diplomatic and consular offices are responsible, according to territorial rules.
An Italian visa does not grant free movement in all European countries: its validity depends on the type of visa and the territory for which it is valid, subject to conditions and limits on the stay.
The quiz marks VERO because the rules also provided for a collective passport for groups. The Italian provision was subsequently repealed.
The minimum of one hundred people is wrong: under the historical rules, a collective passport was provided for groups of 5 to 50 people and for specified purposes. The provision was later repealed.

An identity card valid for travel abroad is accepted in many countries, but not at every border: a passport is required for some destinations. Before departure, check which document the destination country requires.
The quiz considers the Sicilian coast, including Lampedusa and Pantelleria, among the areas of entry by sea. The significance of individual routes can change over time.
The quiz considers the Adriatic coast of Puglia an area affected by arrivals by sea. The volume of flows varies over time.
The quiz includes Trieste and Tarvisio among the areas of entry by land. Routes and their volume change over time: the eastern border is affected by the Balkan route.
The Ionian coast of Calabria sees arrivals by sea, including in the Roccella Ionica area. The significance of the routes can vary over time.
Gorizia is on the eastern border affected by the Balkan route. The relative importance of the different entry points varies over time.
FALSO. The quiz does not identify Rome and Fregene as one of the main entry areas. An important route to Italy instead crosses the central Mediterranean; routes can change over time.
The historical quiz gives FALSO, but the answer needs context: Sardinia also sees arrivals by sea, particularly on the route from Algeria. The relative significance of the routes changes over time.
FALSO. Milan is an inland city and is not an entry border into Italy; it can be a destination or a later transit point. One entry route instead reaches Italy across the central Mediterranean.
The historical quiz indicates FALSO: the western Ligurian coast was not among the main landing points. In 2011–2016 arrivals were concentrated mainly in Sicily; routes can change over time.
The historical quiz indicates FALSO: Versilia was not among the main landing areas. In 2011–2016 arrivals were concentrated mainly in Sicily; routes can change over time.
Passive millimeter-wave scanners can produce images that help identify people hidden in vehicles. How clearly the images can be read also depends on the load and the person's position.
A heartbeat detector can identify a hidden person by sensing the small movements their heartbeat produces in the vehicle.
Carbon dioxide detectors measure the air in the cargo compartment and can help identify people hidden on board.
The technologies used in vehicle checks include gamma-ray scanners, alongside other detection tools.
Dog units can supplement other checks to find people hidden in vehicles.
'WWW rays' are not an inspection technology: the web does not allow anyone to see inside a vehicle. Searches instead use, for example, CO2 detectors and physical checks.
Sound waves are not used to force people out of a vehicle. Checks instead rely on detection tools and inspections, such as CO2 probes and dogs.
Checks for hidden people are not normally carried out using satellites: the vehicle is searched through inspections and tools such as CO2 detectors and motion sensors.
Explosive charges are not used to frighten hidden people. Checks instead use detection and search techniques on the vehicle.
Completely unloading the goods is not inevitable: detection tools such as CO2 probes or heartbeat detectors can also be used to search for people. Further checks may still be necessary.

The driver must implement and document vehicle security measures: failures to do so may result in penalties. The verdict is general: ‘incontrovertible evidence’ is not always required, and criminal liability does not automatically follow from the mere presence of hidden people.

The company must also organize effective measures to prevent unauthorized access and may be penalized for its own failures. The verdict is general: the mere lack of ‘incontrovertible evidence’ does not automatically establish criminal liability.
A security plan helps prevent unauthorized access: it includes securing the vehicle, checks during the journey and recording the checks. The precise requirements depend on the country being crossed.

The carrier must check the documents required of the passengers concerned. The obligation under Schengen rules applies to air and sea carriers and, on the road, to groups transported by bus: it should not be applied indiscriminately to every form of transport.

The carrier that brought the person to the external border must take responsibility for them if entry is refused. At the authorities' request, the carrier must return them to the country they came from or to another third country permitted by the rules.

It is wrong to limit liability to the driver: the carrier can also be penalized for breaching its own obligations. Criminal liability still requires the elements of the offense to be established; it does not arise automatically from a lack of conclusive evidence.

It is wrong to exclude the company: the carrier can also be penalized for breaching its own obligations. The elements required for criminal liability must be established; it does not arise automatically from a lack of conclusive evidence.
It is false that imprisonment is ruled out: the law also provides for imprisonment for facilitating illegal entry, as well as confiscation of the vehicle in the cases specified.
Penalties do not apply only to the driver: whoever engages in the conduct specified by law is liable, whatever their role.
It is false that this is not an offense: facilitating illegal entry is a criminal offense punishable by imprisonment, among other penalties.
Keeping watch over the vehicle, especially in high-risk areas, reduces the possibility of unauthorized access. In practice, supervision, locks and regular checks are used together.
Checking vulnerable parts may reveal unauthorized access; if the presence of people is suspected, the relevant authorities must be notified immediately.
People can hide in various parts of the vehicle: checking the interior, roof, area behind the cab and axles helps identify unauthorized access.
When transporting passengers, it is useful to check the interior and the passengers to identify anyone who may have boarded without authorization.
Even minor damage or signs of forced entry can indicate unauthorized access and call for a more thorough check.
A broken lock may indicate that someone opened the cargo compartment without authorization: the vehicle must be checked and the suspicion reported.
It is false that the company can neglect to inform drivers: instructions and training on checks and reporting are part of prevention. The specific procedures depend on the applicable rules.
It is false that padlocks and seals are prohibited: they protect access points and make any tampering recognizable.
The vehicle must not be abandoned to avoid involvement: if there is a suspicion, notify the authorities while staying safe.
Ten minutes is not a safe threshold: even a short unattended stop can allow access. The vehicle must be secured and checked after stops.

A special customs regime does not prevent inspection: during operations and in locations specified by law, the police may check vehicles and goods if there are reasonable grounds relating to the specified offenses.

The carrier may also be liable if it participates in illegal transport. Note: knowledge alone is not automatically enough; an act of participation and the other elements of the offense must be established.
A breach of the carrier's obligations can, in the most serious cases specified by law, result in suspension or revocation of its authorization to carry out transport activities.
The law punishes those who engage in the specified conduct to bring about illegal entry. Liability requires the elements of the offense to be established.

The quiz refers to imprisonment and confiscation of the vehicle used for the offense. The reference to 15 years comes from the historical wording of the question: the applicable penalties and conditions must be checked in the current law.
It is false that a special customs regime rules out checks: under the conditions laid down by law, vehicles and goods carried can be inspected even under that regime.
It is false that only foreign nationals are penalized: the law also punishes those who engage in the specified conduct to facilitate their illegal entry.

It is false that reporting this is in itself an offense of informing on someone: the carrier is required to report the presence on board of foreign nationals with irregular status to the border police.

The official verdict is FALSO because reporting is not merely recommended: the carrier is required to report any foreign nationals with irregular status on board to the border police. However, the word 'recommend' makes the wording ambiguous.
Carriers' obligations are not established solely by bilateral agreements with the country of origin: there are also common European provisions, supplemented by national rules.
An adjustable driving position accommodates drivers of different builds and allows them to reach the controls while maintaining a suitable posture.
An ergonomic driving position limits awkward postures and unnecessary effort, reducing strain on the muscles and skeleton.
A driving position suited to the driver helps limit fatigue during prolonged driving without eliminating the need for breaks.
Accessible, well-adjusted controls prevent awkward movements and excessive effort while driving.
Ergonomics does not specifically aim to address fuel consumption: it adapts work and tools to people's characteristics, improving safety and comfort.
A company's accounts concern its financial management; ergonomics instead studies how to adapt work, tools and the environment to people.
Keeping the cabin above 28 °C at all times does not guarantee ergonomics: the temperature needs to be comfortable, taking into account the environmental conditions and the individual.
Ergonomics does not depend on rarely using the indicators, which must be operated when necessary: what matters is being able to reach and use the controls easily.
Controls and instruments within the driver's reach allow them to operate without stretching or adopting strained postures.
Ergonomics aims to make work safer and more comfortable by adapting it to the individual; it does not eliminate every risk on its own.
Tools and devices designed for the user encourage suitable postures and reduce unnecessary movements and effort.
Having a stereo does not make the driving position ergonomic: the seat, space and controls must be suited to the driver.
A navigation system alone does not make the driving position ergonomic: what matters is the adjustability of the seat and the arrangement of the space and controls.
An anti-robbery communication system does not determine the ergonomics of the driving position, which depend on how well it physically suits the driver.
Posture is the position assumed by the body: when driving, it describes how the driver positions themselves at the controls.
A suitable posture helps prevent work-related musculoskeletal disorders, although it cannot on its own guarantee freedom from illness.
The upper body should be supported and kept from leaning forward. Upright does not mean rigid or perfectly vertical: the backrest may be slightly reclined.
Poor posture can place excessive strain on muscles, tendons and joints, especially if maintained for a long time.
Poor posture, especially when prolonged, can contribute to back and spinal problems.
A well-adjusted position limits unnecessary tension and effort and can therefore reduce driver fatigue.
The legs should not have to be fully extended to reach the pedals: the seat should be adjusted so that the knees remain slightly bent.
The knees must not hit the steering wheel: the driving position should be adjusted so the legs have room and the controls can be used easily.
The back should not be held away from the backrest: it should be supported, particularly in the lower back area.
Driving with the upper body bent forward is not correct posture: the back should be supported by the backrest, which may be slightly reclined.
Correct posture does not require the legs to become tired: the seat and controls should be adjusted to allow easy movement and limit tension.
It is false that poor posture spares the muscles: it can also tire the muscles of the back, neck and shoulders.
The back should be supported by the backrest, adjusted to support it along its full length. This is one element of correct posture, along with adjusting the other controls.
The seat should be adjusted so the pedals can be pressed all the way down while keeping the knee bent, without having to fully extend the leg.
The top edge of the head restraint should be adjusted to approximately the height of the top of the head, so that it better supports the head in a collision.
After adjusting the seat, adjust the mirrors from the normal driving position so that you can check the view without moving in the seat.
Adjusting the seat helps the driver reach the pedals and controls comfortably and support the back; the other available elements should also be adjusted.
With the seat properly adjusted, the right foot can move from the brake to the accelerator by pivoting on the heel, while maintaining control of the pedals.
When not operating the clutch, the left foot can rest on the designated footrest to the left of the pedals.
At shoulder height, the head restraint is too low: its top edge should be adjusted to approximately the height of the top of the head.
Correct posture makes it easier to reach the controls and improves comfort, but it does not necessarily reduce gear changes, which depend on driving conditions.
Good posture does not authorize exceptions to driving and rest times: the relevant rules apply, along with only the exceptions they provide for.
A good driving position does not replace the right mirror: the mirrors must be adjusted and used to check the areas to the sides and rear.
Excess weight can increase the load on the back and contribute to pain or injury; this does not mean that every overweight person will suffer harm.

The quiz marks this as true: excess weight and vibrations can both contribute to back problems. However, the increased risk is not automatic for every driver, nor does it prove that every jolt causes harm.
Stress can be accompanied by muscle tension and make it harder to maintain a relaxed, comfortable posture.
Fatigue reduces the ability to drive safely: it can slow reactions and contribute to errors or brief episodes of falling asleep.
A large, heavy meal can make a person drowsy, reducing alertness while driving.
Stress can contribute to fatigue and impair driving, increasing the risk of errors and accidents.
Heavy traffic can be stressful; stress can interfere with driving and increase the risk of dangerous behaviour. Not every traffic jam necessarily causes an accident.
It is false that regular exercise is in itself a cause of stress and accidents: suitable activity can instead reduce anxiety and improve sleep. Excessive exertion can still cause fatigue.
Sleeping for eight consecutive hours is not in itself a cause of stress: adequate sleep supports recovery and alertness, although sleep quality and individual needs also matter.
Prolonged fasting does not guarantee better performance: hunger and lack of energy can impair concentration.
Regularly driving beyond the prescribed limits can lead to a buildup of fatigue and stress, compromising safety and increasing the risk of an accident.
Fatigue can slow the response to events: the driver takes longer to react to a hazard.
Fatigue can reduce attention and concentration, making it harder to follow what is happening on the road.
Fatigue does not sharpen vision: it can instead narrow awareness of what is happening to the sides.
Opening the window when tired is not mandatory: it is not a reliable remedy. You need to stop safely and rest.
Raising the temperature does not resolve fatigue. If you are tired while driving, you must stop safely and rest.
Limiting driving time and observing rest periods reduces prolonged exposure to fatigue and promotes recovery; it does not eliminate every risk of illness.
Breaks interrupt prolonged exposure to driving and promote recovery. They contribute to prevention, without on their own guaranteeing freedom from illness.
Getting enough sleep reduces drowsiness and the risk of fatigue-related accidents while driving.
Limiting night driving as much as possible helps reduce disruptions to sleep and biological rhythms. The extent of this measure depends on how work is organized.
Keeping regular sleep hours as far as possible helps limit disruption to the sleep-wake cycle; getting enough sleep remains important.
Driving for six hours without a break does not prevent illness: it increases fatigue. For transport subject to the EU regulation, the prescribed breaks must be observed.
Smoking more cigarettes does not improve health: smoking increases the risk of many diseases.
Listening to the radio at high volume is neither a way to improve health nor a reliable remedy for drowsiness: you need to rest.
Twelve hours of uninterrupted driving do not improve health: they increase fatigue and conflict with the breaks required for transport operations subject to EU regulations.
Vibrations transmitted to the body through the vehicle, especially over long periods, can contribute to back and musculoskeletal disorders.
Exposure to excessive cold or heat and drafts can affect well-being and, if intense or prolonged, health. The risk depends on the conditions of exposure.
Dust and harmful substances can be inhaled during work and harm health; the risk depends on the substance and the exposure.
Sitting in the same position for a long time can contribute to pain and musculoskeletal disorders, especially in the back and neck.
It is not true that relaxation exercises should be avoided: moving and stretching the muscles during breaks can counter stiffness caused by maintaining the same posture for a long time.
The seat belt must not be left loose: it should fit snugly against the body, with the diagonal section across the shoulder and chest and the lap section low across the pelvis.
Removing the head restraint does not protect the neck: it should be kept in place and adjusted correctly to reduce the risk of neck injuries in a collision.
Suitable sunglasses can reduce glare: they are not generally discouraged. However, they should not be worn at night or in insufficient light.
Driving at night can strain the eyes because of darkness and glare; eye strain can make it harder to see and drive safely. It does not necessarily imply an eye disease.
When driving for work, a person can be involved in a road accident and suffer injuries or trauma.
A fire in the vehicle or its load can expose the driver to injuries such as burns or harm from smoke inhalation.
The driver may inhale pollutants, such as exhaust gases and particles. With sufficient exposure, some substances can cause poisoning or other harm.
When climbing into or out of the cab, a person can slip or fall and suffer a sprain; maintaining three points of contact is helpful.
Maintaining poor posture for a long time while driving can strain muscles and joints and contribute to musculoskeletal disorders.
Relaxation techniques can help reduce tension; they should be practiced without becoming distracted from driving, for example during a stop.
It is wrong to limit sleep to four hours: before a long journey, you need enough sleep because lack of sleep contributes to drowsiness at the wheel.
Vibrations transmitted to the whole body, if prolonged, can damage the spine, especially the lower back.
The quiz considers it useful to strengthen the neck muscles to support the area under strain. Exercise does not eliminate vibrations, however: exposure must also be reduced.
Strengthening the muscles that support the lower back can help the back; it does not replace measures that reduce vibrations transmitted by the vehicle.
It is false that prolonged exposure to vibrations cannot cause occupational diseases: vibrations can contribute to spinal conditions, whose work-related origin must be assessed in each case.
Supplements do not eliminate vibrations or guarantee protection from their effects: the risk is reduced by addressing exposure, for example through the seat and vehicle.
Painkillers do not eliminate exposure to vibrations or prevent harm: vibrations must be reduced at their source, and the seat and vehicle must be properly maintained.
Heavy traffic requires continuous attention and can increase the driver's physical and mental tension.
Working during rest periods takes time away from recovery: accumulated fatigue can contribute to physical and mental stress.
Irregular schedules can disrupt sleep and make it difficult to eat regularly, contributing to fatigue and stress.
Excessive, prolonged noise in the workplace can contribute to the driver's tension and stress.

The quiz considers it false that using air conditioning is in itself a cause of stress: a comfortable temperature can improve conditions in the cab. An unsuitable setting can nevertheless cause discomfort.

The quiz considers it false that attending refresher courses is in itself a cause of stress: training can help workers manage workplace risks. How it is organized can nevertheless affect a worker's workload.
Breaks are not in themselves a cause of stress: stopping driving allows recovery from fatigue. If drowsiness occurs, you must stop safely and rest.
Getting too little sleep increases sleep pressure and can cause involuntary sleep, even while driving.
During an episode of involuntary sleep, the driver temporarily loses control and may cause an accident.
Fatigue and lack of sleep contribute to drowsiness and brief episodes of involuntary sleep while driving.
A large meal does not protect against involuntary sleep: it can bring out drowsiness already caused by insufficient rest. You need enough sleep before driving.
Nearsightedness is not in itself a specific cause of involuntary sleep: relevant factors include insufficient sleep, fatigue and sleep disorders.
Tranquilizers do not prevent involuntary sleep: they can actually cause drowsiness. If you feel sleepy, you must stop safely and rest.
Closing the windows limits the entry of outside noise and improves the cab's sound insulation.
Excessive noise in the cab can disturb the driver and contribute to stress, reducing their well-being.
Insufficient fresh air can make the environment unpleasant and reduce the driver's well-being.
Smoke lingering in the vehicle cabin pollutes the air and can cause discomfort, impairing well-being and driving performance.
Open windows do not improve sound insulation: they generally let more noise into the cabin.
It is false that good ventilation encourages involuntary sleep: fresh air improves comfort, but does not replace rest when you are tired.
Turning up the radio adds sound: it can mask other noises, but it does not improve soundproofing, which involves reducing the transmission of noise.
It is false that the filter is irrelevant: a contaminated filter can contribute to contaminants in the cabin air. It should be checked and replaced according to the maintenance instructions.
Personal protective equipment is worn to protect workers from health or safety risks during work, including a driver's activities.
Protective gloves are available for mechanical, electrical and chemical risks. The type must be suited to the risk: no single glove protects against every hazard.
Suitable goggles and face shields can protect against fragments and corrosive splashes; protection must be chosen for the specific risk, and goggles may be needed under a face shield.
It is false that retroreflective vests are not personal protective equipment: high-visibility vests protect wearers by making them more visible to vehicle drivers.
It is wrong to exclude falling from the loading platform from occupational risks: while working on the vehicle, the driver can fall and be injured.
It is wrong to exclude injuries from handling loads from occupational risks: loading and unloading can expose the driver to injury.
Before and during a journey, easily digestible meals are preferable to avoid feeling weighed down by a long and difficult digestion.
Light foods that provide energy are suitable in moderate portions: even on a long journey, there is no need to eat excessively.
Drinking water regularly helps maintain hydration, especially in hot weather; it is advisable to drink in small sips.
A balanced diet includes a variety of foods, including fruit and vegetables, and an adequate intake of water.
It is advisable to limit fried and very fatty foods, which can make digestion more difficult during a journey.
It is advisable to limit foods and meals that may cause drowsiness, because alertness is essential for safe driving.
Large meals that are difficult to digest can make you feel weighed down and cause drowsiness; light meals are preferable during a journey.
It is false that a few large meals are advisable: it is better to spread food intake across light meals and small snacks, without eating excessively.
It is false that fatty foods are needed for driving: a balanced, easily digestible diet is preferable, without excessive fat or quantities of food.

It is false that drinking wine during a break before resuming driving is a good choice: alcohol may still be present when driving resumes and reduces attention and driving ability. The professional drivers concerned are prohibited from driving after drinking.
It is false that a proper diet consists only of red meat: it should be varied and include other foods, such as fruit and vegetables.
It is false that a driver should drink alcohol to aid digestion: alcohol slows digestion and reduces attention and concentration while driving.
It is false that drinking large amounts of coffee is good practice: too much caffeine can cause problems and does not reliably eliminate the risk of drowsiness.
It is false that you should avoid drinking water during a journey: maintaining adequate hydration helps prevent dehydration.
Some medicines can cause drowsiness, making driving less safe.
Some medicines, when combined with alcohol, can impair the abilities needed for driving.
Some medicines cause side effects, such as drowsiness or blurred vision, that make driving risky.
Some medicines can slow reactions: the driver takes longer to respond to a danger.
Some medicines can cause drowsiness and reduce the alertness needed for driving.
It is false that medicines never interact with alcohol: some combinations can impair driving.
It is false that side effects occur only on an empty stomach: taking some medicines with food can reduce certain problems, but does not necessarily eliminate every unwanted effect.
It is false that tranquilizers can be used to exceed the prescribed limits: driving times and breaks must be observed, subject to exceptions provided by law.
It is false that stimulants must be taken to exceed the prescribed limits: driving times and breaks must be observed, subject to exceptions provided by law.
Alcohol can intensify the sedative effect of tranquilizers such as benzodiazepines and further impair reactions.
With some antibiotics, alcohol can worsen effects such as dizziness, making driving less safe; the interaction depends on the medicine.
Alcohol and drugs can impair judgment; alcohol can also encourage aggressive behavior and cause people to underestimate dangers.
Alcohol and drugs can impair judgment, leading people to overestimate their driving abilities.

Alcohol and drugs impair judgment and can lead people to overestimate their own abilities and the vehicle's limits. The question refers to vehicle performance, but the effect concerns the driver's assessment, not an actual increase in performance.
It is false that alcohol and drugs improve concentration on long journeys: together they can worsen the impairment of driving ability.
It is false that drugs can be used to improve reflexes: they can instead slow reactions and impair driving.
It is false that alcohol and drugs make drivers more clear-headed: they can impair judgment and reaction times.
It is false that alcohol and drugs improve intellectual abilities while driving: they can impair judgment and reactions.
The exception for grappa is false: it contains alcohol, which can interact with some medicines. If the interaction is unknown, avoid alcohol and ask a doctor or pharmacist.
The exception for an herbal digestif is false: if it contains alcohol, it can interact with some medicines. If the interaction is unknown, avoid alcohol and ask a doctor or pharmacist.
Alcohol can initially cause euphoria, even though it is already impairing abilities needed for driving.
Repeated alcohol use can lead to physical dependence, with withdrawal symptoms when its effects wear off.
Alcohol impairs judgment: people may overestimate their abilities without recognizing that their driving is already impaired.
Alcohol can cause a dazed feeling and impair balance and judgment.
True. Alcohol impairs judgment and can cause people to underestimate dangers, leading to reckless behavior.
False. Alcohol does not improve motor coordination: it can impair it, even before intoxication is apparent.
False. Alcohol does not improve perceptual abilities: it can reduce the processing of sensory perceptions and visual ability.
False. Drinking alcohol does not in itself lower blood alcohol concentration: ingested alcohol is absorbed into the blood, and its elimination takes time.
True. Alcohol can narrow the field of vision, especially peripheral vision, making it harder to see what is happening to the sides.
True. Alcohol can increase sensitivity to glare, making driving at night more difficult in the presence of bright lights.
True. Alcohol can increase the time needed to react to a danger, delaying braking, for example.
True. Alcohol can impair the assessment of distances and speeds, encouraging risky maneuvers such as a misjudged overtaking maneuver.
False. Alcohol does not make reflexes quicker: it can instead slow responses to stimuli and dangers.
False. Alcohol does not widen the field of vision to 270°: it can instead narrow it, reducing peripheral vision.
True. Blood alcohol concentration indicates the concentration of alcohol in the blood.
True. Blood alcohol concentration is commonly expressed in grams of alcohol per liter of blood, indicated as g/L.
Vero. A breathalyzer analyzes alcohol in exhaled air and makes it possible to estimate the concentration of alcohol in the blood.
Vero. Blood alcohol concentration can be measured by analyzing a blood sample; it can also be detected through exhaled air.
Falso. Blood alcohol concentration is not a disease: it is the concentration of alcohol in the blood. Alcohol use disorder is a distinct condition.
Falso. Blood alcohol concentration refers to alcohol in the blood, not its concentration in urine.
Falso. A probe in the digestive tract is not used to measure blood alcohol concentration: a blood sample can be analyzed or the concentration can be estimated from exhaled air.
Falso. A psychological test does not measure blood alcohol concentration, which is detected through a blood test or estimated from exhaled air.
Vero. Repeated use of alcohol and some psychoactive substances, including certain medications, can lead to dependence; the risk varies according to the substance and how it is used.
Falso. Coffee neither neutralizes the effects of alcohol nor makes a person sober quickly: the body needs time to metabolize it.
Falso. A glass of water can help with dehydration, but it does not eliminate all the effects of alcohol: it takes time to metabolize it.
Falso. Eating dry foods does not eliminate all the effects of alcohol already consumed. Food can slow its absorption, but it does not make a person sober quickly.
Falso. Repeated use can cause habituation or tolerance: a larger amount may be needed to achieve the same effect. Not all substances and medications carry the same risk.
Vero. Continued alcohol consumption can damage organs such as the liver and heart and contribute to disease; the risk also depends on the amount consumed and the duration of consumption.

Vero according to the quiz. Alcohol can irritate and damage the stomach lining, possibly causing erosions or ulcers. However, the wording is too categorical: gastritis and ulcers do not necessarily develop in everyone who drinks and have other causes as well.
Continued consumption, especially at high levels, can damage the brain and peripheral nerves; damage is not inevitable in every person.

The quiz indicates FALSO: brittle nails are not a specific and inevitable consequence of alcohol. However, the wording is too absolute: nutritional deficiencies, including those associated with problematic consumption, can contribute to brittleness.
It is wrong to say that alcohol prevents cirrhosis: prolonged consumption can instead cause liver damage, including cirrhosis.
Alcohol does not prevent calluses: these form mainly as the skin's response to repeated pressure or friction.

For the professional categories specified by the Code, driving after drinking is prohibited: a blood alcohol level above zero carries penalties. The prohibition concerns driving, not all consumption in private life.
Alcohol abuse can lead to dismissal if the specific circumstances constitute a sufficiently serious breach of the employment relationship; it is not an automatic consequence of any consumption.
Traffic police can check drivers to determine whether they have consumed alcohol, including through preliminary checks and, in the cases provided for, a breathalyzer test.

The quiz indicates VERO, but the mere presence of traces in the blood does not necessarily demonstrate a current effect. Today Article 187 concerns driving after consumption and provides for specific tests: the result must be interpreted according to the applicable procedures.

The quiz indicates VERO, but the word ‘only’ does not describe all current procedures: Article 187 also provides for tests on oral fluid collected according to the guidelines, as well as cases where healthcare facilities are used.

The quiz indicates VERO, referring to analytical testing, but it is inaccurate to speak always and only of laboratory tests to establish a current effect: the current rules concern driving after consumption and distinguish between preliminary checks and toxicological tests.

The quiz indicates FALSO, but ‘only if’ makes the statement ambiguous and the verdict should be read with caution. The presence of traces alone does not prove a current effect; current law governs driving after consumption and the prescribed tests, without automatically equating traces with an effect.
No exception is allowed for meals: the professional drivers specified by law are prohibited from driving after consuming alcohol, and a level above zero carries penalties.
Alcohol is not a remedy for feeling insecure behind the wheel: it can impair judgment, coordination and reaction times, increasing the risk.
Traces of smoke in the passenger compartment are not enough to prove that the driver has taken drugs. The law provides for specific toxicological tests.
Incorrect answers to a questionnaire do not in themselves prove drug use: the assessment follows the procedures set out in Article 187.
Cannabis, amphetamines and heroin include substances classified as controlled narcotic or psychotropic substances.
Marijuana is a preparation of cannabis, which is classified as a controlled narcotic substance.
Ecstasy, commonly associated with MDMA, is classified as a controlled narcotic or psychotropic substance.
LSD is a hallucinogenic substance classified among controlled narcotic or psychotropic substances.
Cocaine is a controlled narcotic substance that stimulates the central nervous system.
Coca-Cola is a beverage and should not be confused with cocaine, which is a controlled narcotic substance.
A beverage does not become a narcotic simply because it contains ginseng or taurine: controlled substances are identified in specific schedules.
Passionflower and calendula should not be classified as narcotics simply because they are plants: the rules concern the substances identified in specific schedules.
Papaya and royal jelly are food products, not narcotics by nature. Controlled substances are identified in specific schedules.

The quiz indicates VERO: some drugs can cause lasting or irreversible brain damage. However, the statement is too general: the effects depend on the substance and the conditions of use, and not every instance of use necessarily causes irreversible damage.
Drug use can cause dependence, especially when repeated: not every instance of use necessarily leads to it.
It is wrong to say that use always leads to violence: violent behavior can occur, but the effects vary.
Alcohol dependence does not automatically result from using other drugs. However, using multiple substances can lead to multiple dependencies.
Ecstasy commonly refers to MDMA, a synthetic psychoactive substance.
Ecstasy is commonly found in pills or tablets, although other forms exist.
The quiz considers it a drug that causes dependence: some people report symptoms of dependence, but research has not yet definitively answered the question of its potential to cause dependence.
Ecstasy can cause fatal complications, for example a severe rise in body temperature.
Ecstasy can contribute to dehydration, particularly during intense physical activity.
Here ecstasy does not refer to a mystical state: it is the name commonly given to a drug containing MDMA.
Taking ecstasy before driving is dangerous: it can impair the perception of movement and the assessment of collision risk.
Ecstasy is not an energy supplement: it is a synthetic drug that can have serious adverse effects.
Ecstasy is not a saffron-based drug: the name commonly refers to MDMA, a synthetic substance.
A feeling of euphoria or well-being may be among the initial effects of ecstasy.
Ecstasy can cause nausea, an increased heart rate, and confused or disorganized thoughts.
Ecstasy neither makes it safe nor permits exceeding driving time limits: it can impair abilities essential for driving.
Ecstasy is not recommended for a tiring journey: it can impair the ability to judge movement and hazards.
Ecstasy is not a dietary supplement: it is a synthetic drug commonly associated with MDMA.
Ecstasy is not a substitute for a meal and is not recommended for drivers: it can impair abilities needed for driving.
Marijuana can impair memory. The quiz wording does not mean that every use causes permanent memory loss.
Marijuana can slow reactions, making it harder to respond promptly to hazards.
Marijuana is not simply a medicine for headaches. Medical cannabis has specific uses assessed by a doctor.
It is false that marijuana shortens reaction times: it can instead slow reactions.
Marijuana does not improve a driver's responsiveness: it can slow reactions and impair coordination.
It is false that this conduct carries no penalty: Article 187 penalizes driving after taking narcotic or psychotropic substances.

The quiz treats drug use as prohibited for professional drivers. In particular, driving after taking narcotics is penalized for all drivers; the word ‘always’ does not distinguish any authorized therapeutic uses.

Drug use can affect a professional driver's fitness to work and employment, potentially leading to dismissal in certain circumstances. This is not automatic, however: the protections provided for the rehabilitation process apply.
There is no occasional permission to drive after taking narcotics: the prohibition also applies to professional drivers.
The distinction between goods and passengers is incorrect: the prohibition on driving after taking narcotics applies to both types of driver.
To obtain and retain a driving licence, a person must meet the physical and mental requirements assessed under the applicable rules.
Fatigue reduces attention and alertness: you must stop safely and rest before driving again.
Strong emotions can impair concentration and control: it is prudent to wait until you are calm before driving.
A sudden illness can unexpectedly impair control of the vehicle: you must wait until you feel well before driving.
If a medicine impairs attention or reflexes, you must not drive. Check the effects listed in the package leaflet and ask a doctor or pharmacist for advice.
The quiz advises against driving after eating very heavy food: a large meal can cause drowsiness. The effect depends on individual circumstances; if you feel sleepy, you must rest.
Being rested and alert helps you notice danger and react promptly; drowsiness, on the other hand, slows reactions.
Resting after arrival does not eliminate the risk during the journey, even if it is short. If your condition impairs your driving, you must stop and rest before setting off again.
Coffee does not make it safe to drive when you are very tired and is no substitute for rest. You must stop safely and rest before continuing.
ABS helps prevent the wheels from locking during braking, but it does not speed up the driver's reaction before they brake.
It is incorrect to assume that digestion increases alertness through greater blood flow to the brain: after a large meal, drowsiness can instead occur, which is dangerous when driving.
FALSO. After a meal, there is no need to set a low temperature as a remedy for drowsiness. If you feel sleepy, stop safely and rest: cold air is no substitute for sleep.
You should not limit water intake as a matter of principle: during a journey it is advisable to stay hydrated and have water available.
It is false that stress has no effect on driving: it can disrupt attention and control. It is prudent not to set out on a journey while stressed.
Falling asleep suddenly is not limited to the night: drowsiness can also occur during the day. At the first signs, you must stop and rest.
Before intervening, assess the hazards and protect your own safety: a rescuer involved in another accident cannot help effectively.
Identifying smoke or flames from a safe position helps you recognize a fire hazard and report it to the emergency services without exposing yourself to danger.

If the injured person cannot be moved, warn other road users of the danger and call the emergency services without exposing yourself to traffic. Do not move a person with traumatic injuries unless there is immediate danger.
Promptly warning approaching vehicles of the danger helps prevent further collisions; use the required warning devices, protecting your own safety first.
Assist the injured and promptly call the emergency services, giving the location and the conditions observed.
The horn alone is not enough to provide a continuous warning of the obstruction to approaching vehicles: use the hazard lights and the required warning devices.
Do not give alcohol to an injured person in shock. Call the emergency services and do not give them food or drink.
Do not call your lawyer before taking any other action: first stop and provide any injured people with the necessary assistance.
Calling the insurer is not the first required action: you must stop and provide any injured people with the necessary assistance.
In the event of an injury or sudden illness, it is advisable to seek medical assistance; if life or safety is at risk, call 112 or 118, who will assess what help to send.
Keeping calm helps you assess the situation and communicate clearly with the emergency services without giving in to panic.
Assist the person and, while waiting for the emergency services, encourage and reassure them, checking whether their condition worsens.
Do not give drinks to an unconscious person: they may be unable to swallow and could choke. Call the emergency services.
Do not immediately move an injured person without considering their injuries: movement can make them worse. Moving them is justified if necessary to remove them from serious and imminent danger.
Do not give alcohol to an injured person: while waiting for the emergency services, do not give them drinks.
A fracture does not in itself require a tourniquet: try to keep the limb still and call the emergency services. A tourniquet is instead used for potentially life-threatening bleeding from a limb.
Do not plug the ear canal: blood coming from the ear after a head injury may indicate a serious injury. Call the emergency services immediately and avoid moving the person.
Do not indiscriminately undress a burn victim: clothing stuck to the skin must not be pulled off, as this can worsen the injuries. Clothing that is not stuck can be removed carefully.
Do not give just any medicine: while waiting for the emergency services, follow the instructions of medical personnel and do not take decisions about medication on your own.
An injured person who cannot move should not be moved unnecessarily, because movement can worsen their injuries. Move them if necessary to remove them from serious and imminent danger.
Normally, you should wait for medical personnel to move injured people, to avoid worsening any injuries. An exception is when they must be moved away from serious and imminent danger.
It is not mandatory to call an ambulance for every accident without injuries: medical assistance is requested when there is a risk to life or safety.
There is no general obligation to call the Carabinieri when there is only property damage. Drivers must nevertheless stop and provide useful information to those who suffered damage.
Leaving to avoid identification is wrong: anyone involved in an accident attributable to their own conduct must stop and provide the required information.
Personal details and useful information must be given to those who suffered damage without making the exchange conditional on the presence of law enforcement.
First aid includes the immediate help that even a bystander can give a victim, by making the scene safe and calling emergency services.
First aid is the immediate help that even a bystander can give an injured person, within the limits of their abilities and by calling emergency services.
First aid is the immediate assistance given to the affected person, including while waiting for emergency responders to arrive.
First aid includes simple, prompt actions, such as assessing the person and calling for help while waiting for medical assistance.
The rescuer must avoid unnecessary actions that could worsen the injured person's condition: for example, they do not move a person who has suffered trauma unless necessary.
Among the first things assessed are vital functions, particularly responsiveness and breathing: these help identify an emergency and call emergency services immediately.

The airway, breathing and circulation are priorities. Checking for a pulse requires training: an untrained person assesses responsiveness and breathing and immediately follows the instructions of 112 or 118, without delaying emergency assistance.
FALSO. Even someone who is not a healthcare professional can provide assistance and call emergency services; the obligation placed on the road user involved is not limited to professionals.
FALSO. A signature is not required to give first aid: if the person is conscious, ask for their consent and respect their wishes.
FALSO. First check that the scene is safe and assess the injured person's condition; asking for identification is not the first action.
FALSO. A road user involved in an accident attributable to their conduct must stop and provide injured people with the necessary assistance.
FALSO. The assistance owed by the driver involved extends to people injured in the accident, not just passengers in their vehicle.
VERO. As a rule, leave the injured person in the position in which they were found to avoid further harm; if the location is dangerous, moving them may be necessary.
VERO. If a spinal injury is suspected, avoid movements that could make it worse. Immediate danger or the need for lifesaving interventions may make moving the person necessary.
FALSO. An absolute prohibition on moving the person until law enforcement arrives is incorrect: immediate danger or the need for lifesaving actions may require moving them.
FALSO. An insistent request does not oblige you to move the injured person: assess the dangers and their condition, avoiding unnecessary movements that could worsen injuries.
FALSO. Do not automatically remove the helmet: the movement can worsen a neck injury. It may be necessary to remove it to perform resuscitation.
FALSO. Intoxication alone does not prohibit moving the injured person: the dangers and possible injuries matter; unnecessary movements should still be avoided.
VERO, in the case of an embedded object: do not attempt to remove it and seek assistance. The wording is general: current guidance permits rinsing for small particles on the surface.
VERO. Avoiding touching or rubbing the eye helps prevent the injury from getting worse.

VERO as a protective measure, but the dressing depends on the injury: for a small object that is not embedded, a sterile eye pad may be used without applying pressure; a penetrating object must be protected without pressure.
VERO in the case of an embedded object: protect the eye without applying pressure and seek medical assistance. Guidance may differ for a small particle on the surface.
FALSO. Do not attempt to remove a penetrating object: protection and medical assistance are needed. A small particle on the surface, however, requires a different assessment.
FALSO. Simply leaving the eye exposed is not the indicated measure: if the object is embedded, protect the eye without applying pressure and seek medical assistance.

FALSO according to the quiz: not every eye containing a foreign object should be rinsed indiscriminately, especially if the object is penetrating. The wording is general: current guidance permits rinsing with clean water for small particles on the surface.
FALSO. Do not attempt to remove a penetrating object with improvised tools: protect the eye without applying pressure and seek medical assistance.
VERO. Watching whether the chest rises and falls is part of assessing breathing, along with listening for and feeling airflow.
VERO. Gently placing a hand on the chest can help you feel its breathing movements, which should be assessed alongside the other signs of breathing.
VERO. Listening near the mouth and nose can help detect airflow; also watch the chest movements and feel for airflow.
VERO according to the quiz: the principle is to feel the airflow. The current procedure indicated by guidelines uses the cheek near the mouth and nose, along with watching the chest and listening.
FALSO. Checking that the chest is uninjured does not show that the person is breathing: you need to watch for breathing movements and listen and feel for airflow.
FALSO. The rescuer can assess breathing immediately and call emergency services; they do not have to wait for a professional to arrive to do so.
It is not mandatory to have taken a course to assess breathing: you can ask the emergency dispatcher for help, and they will guide the assessment.
In mouth-to-mouth breathing, the rescuer breathes in normally and blows air into the injured person's mouth, watching for the chest to rise.
Rescue breaths carry air containing oxygen into the lungs, supporting oxygenation when breathing is ineffective.

If spontaneous breathing is absent, it must be supported promptly. For an unconscious person, the emergency dispatcher guides resuscitation; if you are not trained in rescue breaths, perform continuous compressions.
Absence of breathing requires immediate action: call emergency services and follow their guidance, without delaying compressions on the unconscious person.
Artificial respiration includes rescue breaths that bring air into the lungs and raise the chest.
Giving the injured person a drink does not make breathing easier and can cause aspiration. If someone has difficulty breathing, assess them and call for help.
The aim is not to introduce carbon dioxide: rescue breaths supply air containing oxygen.
Artificial respiration does not mechanically stimulate the whole body: rescue breaths carry air to the lungs to provide oxygen.
Electrodes are part of a defibrillator; artificial respiration is performed by giving rescue breaths, including mouth-to-mouth.
The carotid pulse is checked at the neck to detect circulation. Note: today, a non-medical rescuer assesses consciousness and breathing without delaying CPR to check for a pulse.

The quiz considers the carotid pulse at the neck a sign of circulation. Note: current guidance for laypeople is based on consciousness and breathing; do not delay CPR to check for a pulse or force the neck after trauma.
The capillaries in the eye are not the criterion for checking the heartbeat. Medical personnel can check the pulse; a lay rescuer primarily assesses consciousness and breathing.
Pricking a finger does not check the heartbeat. Healthcare professionals can check the pulse; a lay rescuer mainly assesses consciousness and breathing.
Cardiac massage consists of repeated compressions in the center of the chest, on the lower half of the breastbone.
Chest compressions help maintain blood circulation during cardiac arrest.
In CPR with rescue breaths, trained people alternate compressions and breaths. The statement is absolute: those who are not trained to give rescue breaths perform continuous compressions.
Cardiac massage is not needed in every emergency: it is started when cardiac arrest is suspected, for example if the person is unconscious and not breathing normally.
Do not compress the carotid artery: cardiac massage is performed by compressing the breastbone in the center of the chest.
Rescue breaths are ventilations; cardiac massage consists of chest compressions.
High blood pressure is not a reason to avoid compressions when cardiac arrest is suspected: what matters is recognizing unconsciousness and absent or abnormal breathing.
Answering questions is a sign of consciousness. The statement is general, however: a conscious person may be unable to speak, for example because of severe breathing difficulty.
An appropriate response to a voice is a useful sign when assessing consciousness; the person's other conditions are also checked.
Consciousness indicates that the brain is still receiving blood flow and oxygen. It does not guarantee normal breathing, however: even a conscious person can have severe difficulty breathing.

The quiz considers consciousness a sign that vital functions are present. The statement is too absolute: a conscious person can have severely impaired breathing, so vital functions must still be assessed.
