Traveling toward the exit does not make cabotage permissible: CEMT does not authorize it.
The third loaded journey does not authorize cabotage: CEMT does not permit it.
After no more than three loaded journeys that do not involve the country of establishment, the vehicle must return there, even if empty.
Short-term CEMT authorizations are not valid in Austrian territory.
Not every type of transport is permitted without limits: for example, CEMT does not authorize cabotage and may have territorial restrictions.
No total number of journeys is set for the entire validity period, but the limit of three loaded journeys outside the country of establishment before returning still applies.
The vehicle does not wait until ten journeys have been completed: after no more than three loaded journeys that do not involve the country of establishment, it must return there.
The short-term duration is 30 days, not 90; CEMT covers transport between participating countries, including European countries, and not only outside the EU.
The short-term authorization is valid for 30 days, not 60.

CEMT covers international transport between participating countries and transit journeys, including with an empty vehicle and between countries other than the country of establishment, within the prescribed limits.
CEMT permits international transport between participating countries, subject to any restrictions.
Empty international journeys and transit through countries other than the country of registration are also permitted, subject to the applicable conditions.
Under the paper-based system in the quiz, the authorization had to be kept on board the vehicle. From 2026, the CEMT information document may also be available digitally.
The same authorization may be used by only one vehicle at a time, even if the undertaking has several vehicles.

Under the paper-based system in the quiz, the authorization itself had to be kept on board. From 2026, the information document is generated by the digital system and may be printed or stored on a device.
Under the paper-based system in the quiz, the journey logbook accompanied the authorization. From 2026, the logbook is digital and the journey information document is associated with the vehicle.
Loaded bilateral journeys are not the only ones permitted: CEMT also covers empty international journeys and transport between other participating countries, within the prescribed limits.
CEMT is not limited to bilateral journeys: it also permits transport between participating countries other than the country of establishment, within the prescribed limits.
CEMT is not limited to the EU: it also includes participating countries outside the Union.
The authorization cannot be rented or transferred to another undertaking: it is used by the carrier to which it was allocated.
A journey logbook is required and associated with the authorization. In the current system it is digital and records the journeys made under that authorization.
It is not true that the Community licence must always accompany the CEMT authorization: it may be needed, for example, as authorization to cross a country where CEMT is subject to restrictions.
The certificate of registration in the Register is not a mandatory attachment to the CEMT authorization. The journey logbook and the prescribed vehicle certificates are required, among other things.

For a journey carried out under a CEMT authorisation, the documentation must be available throughout the journey, including empty legs. From 2026, the licence information document may be digital or printed.
Under the CEMT system, the authorization also accompanies an empty journey linked to the loaded journey. From 2026, the licence information document must be available in digital or paper form.

The CEMT authorisation entitles the holder company to carry out permitted international transport between participating countries, with the required documentation and certificates. The quiz describes the paper logbook: from 2026 the CEMT system also uses digital information documents.

The quiz indicates VERO: the CEMT document must be available for checks during the journey. The wording is imprecise: current guidance requires it to be available for inspection when checked, not presented voluntarily at every customs post.
False. Checks are not limited to the customs office of departure: while the licence is in use, the related information document must be available and capable of being presented for inspection.
False. The licence document is not presented only at the customs office of arrival: it must be available and capable of being presented while it is in use on the vehicle.
It is incorrect to say that CEMT is the only possible authorization: for some routes, a Community or bilateral licence may also be used, depending on the applicable system.
False. The journey record alone is not enough: the CEMT licence information document, digital or printed, must also be available on the vehicle.

The quiz means that there is no fixed overall limit on the number of journeys during the period of validity. However, limits still apply to the sequence of laden journeys outside the country of establishment, as do return obligations.
A CEMT licence has a fixed duration: the guide distinguishes between annual and short-term licences.
The standard multilateral CEMT authorisation falls within a quota allocated to member countries. Special authorisations for removals follow a separate system.
The licence is allocated by the competent authority of the country where the business is established.
Under the CEMT system, the motor vehicle must be registered in a member country; for a vehicle combination, the same condition does not apply to every trailer.
In Italy, multilateral authorisations are allocated through a procedure based on a ranking list.
CEMT covers international transport between member countries, possibly involving transit. It does not authorise cabotage, meaning domestic transport within another country.
CEMT does not cover transport originating in a member country and destined for a country outside the system. However, transit through a third country between two members is possible.
There is no overall limit of 100 journeys per licence. Validity is limited by time, and the limits on laden journeys outside the country of establishment must be respected.
There is no overall limit of 50 journeys per licence. Validity is limited by time, and the limits on laden journeys outside the country of establishment must be respected.
The number of permitted journeys is not determined by those made in the previous year. The licence has a fixed duration, and its use is subject to rules on journeys and returns.
A five-year duration is incorrect: the guide provides for annual licences or short-term licences valid for 30 days.
A European body does not issue the licence directly to the business: allocation is the responsibility of the authority in the country of establishment.
A foreign embassy does not issue the CEMT licence: the business obtains it from the authority in its own country of establishment.
An application does not automatically entitle a business to a licence: ordinary authorisations are subject to quotas, and Italy uses a ranking list.
For international transport for hire or reward covered by the EU-Switzerland agreement, the Community carrier must have a certified true copy of the Community licence on board.
Transit through Switzerland falls within the scope of the land transport agreement between the European Union and Switzerland.
For normal transit for hire or reward covered by the EU-Switzerland agreement, no separate Swiss transit authorisation is needed: the Community carrier uses the Community licence.
For normal transit for hire or reward covered by the agreement, no occasional authorisation issued at the border is needed: the Community carrier uses the Community licence.
It is incorrect to say that no documents are needed: for transport for hire or reward covered by the agreement, a certified true copy of the Community licence must be available on board.

The transit in question is governed by the EU-Switzerland land transport agreement, not by a simple bilateral agreement between Italy and Switzerland. Bilateral provisions remain possible for certain triangular transport operations.
Transit is not entirely free of conditions: a Community licence is required for transport for hire or reward covered by the agreement.
There is no liberalisation limited to daytime hours: access follows the agreement and its conditions. Separately, night-time traffic may be subject to bans and exemptions.

The verdict assumes a Swiss, EU or EEA driver: the agreement exempts these citizens from the driver attestation requirement. The carrier's Swiss nationality alone is not enough to establish whether the driver is exempt.

A specific bilateral authorisation from the destination country is not required for every journey: transport covered by the agreement uses the licence provided for under the applicable system. The type of journey remains relevant.
Liberalisation does not eliminate every document requirement: a licence is required for international transport for hire or reward covered by the agreement.

Being a non-EU carrier is not enough to make a driver attestation mandatory: the agreement exempts drivers who are Swiss, EU or EEA citizens. For other drivers, the applicable conditions must be checked.
The CMR covers road transport for hire or reward between two different countries, at least one of which is a contracting party, regardless of the parties' domicile or nationality.
The CMR governs contracts for the international carriage of goods by road, including documents and the carrier's liability.
The official verdict is FALSO, but the statement is ambiguous: the CMR can also apply to dangerous goods when its requirements are met. The specific safety rules are covered by the ADR.
As a general rule, the CMR does not govern purely domestic contracts: it requires the places of taking over and delivery to be in two different countries.
The CMR concerns contracts for the international carriage of goods by road; the specific rules for dangerous goods are contained in the ADR.
The CMR concerns contracts for the international carriage of goods by road; it is not the specific convention for perishable goods, which are covered by the ATP.
The CMR concerns international transport: the places of taking over and delivery must be in different countries.
The convention expressly excludes removals from its scope.
The CMR excludes transport carried out under international postal conventions.
The CMR requires a contract for transport for hire or reward; free transport therefore falls outside its ordinary scope.
Funeral transport is expressly excluded from the CMR.
Not all transport within the EU is excluded: transport between two different countries may fall under the CMR if it meets the required conditions.
Not all transport within the EEA is excluded: the CMR may apply to international transport that meets its conditions.
Not all transport is subject to the CMR: the specified requirements must be met, and there are exclusions, such as removals.
Perishable foodstuffs are not excluded as such: the CMR may apply if the transport meets its conditions.
The quiz uses this abbreviated wording. The full French title is «Convention relative au contrat de transport international de marchandises par route», known as the CMR.
The CMR governs contracts for the international carriage of goods by road, under the conditions set out in the convention.

The official verdict is VERO, but the absolute statement is imprecise: the CMR may apply to an intermodal journey if the loaded vehicle travels part of the way by sea, rail, inland waterway or air without the goods being unloaded, subject to the specified conditions.
On taking over the goods, the carrier checks, among other things, the number and marks of the packages and the apparent condition of the goods and their packaging.
The CMR governs performance of the contract, for example the instructions to follow when transport encounters obstacles.
The CMR applies to combined transport under the conditions of Article 2, for example when the loaded vehicle travels part of the way by train without the goods being unloaded.
FALSO. The CMR also governs the sender's liability, for example for inaccurate particulars in the consignment note.
FALSO. The CMR does not concern only the carrier: it also provides for the sender's liability, for example for inaccurate information in the consignment note.
FALSO. The CMR concerns contracts for the international carriage of goods by road under the conditions set out in the Convention, not purely domestic contracts.
FALSO. The CMR also imposes obligations on the consignee: if the consignee exercises the right to obtain the goods, they must pay the amounts due as shown on the consignment note.

VERO according to the quiz, but the wording is incomplete: merely passing through a contracting country is not enough. The CMR requires carriage by road for payment between two different countries, at least one of which is a party to the Convention and is the country of taking over or delivery.
VERO. When the prescribed conditions are met, the CMR applies regardless of the domicile or nationality of the parties.

VERO. Among the CMR requirements, the contractual places of taking over and delivery must be in two different countries, at least one of which is a contracting country; the carriage must also be by road and for payment.
FALSO. The CMR expressly excludes removal services from its scope.
FALSO. The CMR concerns contracts for the carriage of goods by road for payment; carriage free of charge does not meet this requirement.
FALSO. Funeral transport is expressly excluded from the scope of the CMR.

FALSO according to the quiz: the CMR's specific rule for combined transport assumes that the goods are not unloaded from the road vehicle, subject to the stated exception. However, unloading and transferring the goods does not necessarily exclude the CMR from each individual road leg that meets its requirements.
FALSO. Carriage on one's own account is not in itself a contract for carriage for payment entrusted to a carrier, as required for the CMR to apply.

VERO in terms of liability for loss or damage: the carrier is liable for the period from taking over the goods to delivery. However, the CMR also governs obligations relating to other stages of the contract.

FALSO according to the quiz if it refers to the carrier's liability for loss or damage, which begins when the goods are taken over. The statement is ambiguous: the CMR governs the contract and also obligations that do not begin with taking over the goods.

FALSO according to the quiz if it refers to the carrier's liability for loss or damage: that period begins when the goods are taken over, not when the vehicle is made available. The CMR also governs other contractual obligations.

FALSO according to the quiz if it refers to the carrier's liability for loss or damage: this begins when the goods are taken over, not when the sender judges the vehicle suitable. The CMR also governs other contractual obligations.
VERO. The sender may ask the carrier to check the gross weight or the quantity expressed in another way; the carrier may claim the cost of the check.

VERO according to the quiz: delivery involves the arrival of the goods and their being made available to the consignee, who may request delivery. However, the CMR does not expressly list notice of arrival as a step that is always required.
FALSO. The sender may request a check of the weight or quantity, but the carrier is entitled to claim its cost: it does not necessarily remain the carrier's expense.
FALSO. The sender may also request a check of the gross weight, the quantity expressed in another way and the contents of the packages, not just their number.
FALSO according to the quiz. Delivery is more than mere arrival: the consignee may ask the carrier to deliver the goods and the consignment note against a receipt.
FALSO. Leaving the goods without the consignee taking possession of them is not equivalent to delivery: after arrival, the consignee may request delivery of the goods against a receipt.
FALSO. Informing the sender does not constitute delivery: delivery concerns handing the goods over to the consignee, who may request them against a receipt.

True. If the carrier cannot carry out the instructions under the conditions laid down by the CMR, the carrier must immediately notify whoever issued them: if they came from the sender, the sender must be notified.

True according to the quiz, but the wording is imprecise: before arrival, the carrier asks the person entitled to dispose of the goods for instructions; that person may be the recipient. The carrier does not necessarily have to notify both parties.
False. Being unable to carry out the instructions does not automatically require the goods to be returned: the carrier must immediately notify the person who gave them.

FALSO. If the carrier cannot carry out the instructions under the prescribed conditions, they must immediately notify the person who gave them; there is no automatic obligation to interrupt the journey.
FALSO. If the carrier cannot carry out the instructions under the prescribed conditions, they must immediately notify the person who gave them, not quietly decide based on their own convenience.
False. The sender is not always the only person contacted: before arrival, the carrier asks for instructions from the person entitled to dispose of the goods, who may be the consignee.

False. If carriage cannot continue under the consignment note, the carrier must ask for instructions from the person entitled to dispose of the goods, either the sender or the consignee, as appropriate.
False. The CMR does not require the embassy to be notified: before arrival, the carrier must ask for instructions from the person entitled to dispose of the goods.

The impediment concerns the inability to perform the contract under the conditions of the consignment note. However, the CMR does not define a separate category of 'absolute impediment': carriage may still be possible under different conditions.

If carriage can continue under different conditions and the instructions of the person entitled do not arrive in time, the carrier takes the measures they consider best in that person's interest. The sender is not necessarily the person entitled.
It is false that the carrier has no obligations: if they can continue under different conditions and do not obtain instructions in time, they must act in the interest of the person entitled.

Return to the place of loading is not automatic: the carrier asks the person entitled for instructions and, if carriage is possible under different conditions and instructions are not received in time, acts in that person's interest.

Unloading at the first suitable place is not mandatory. The CMR permits unloading on behalf of the person entitled, but does not require that location; the carrier holds the goods on that person's behalf.
A 10% increase in cost is not a threshold established by the CMR. What matters is the inability to perform the contract under the conditions of the consignment note.
The CMR does not set a 10% time threshold to define an impediment. The criterion is the inability to perform the contract under the conditions of the consignment note.
Losing the consignment note does not automatically make the journey impossible: it affects neither the existence nor the validity of the contract of carriage.
When the consignee has the right of disposal, they may order delivery to another person. That person may not in turn designate a further consignee.
The sender must provide the carrier with the documents and information needed for the formalities to be completed before delivery, thereby enabling the carrier to perform the carriage correctly.
This is false: when handing over dangerous goods, the sender must inform the carrier of the exact nature of the danger and, if necessary, the precautions to be taken.
The consignee may designate another person to receive the goods when they have the right of disposal; the new consignee may not designate another person.

The substitution concerns a delivery order given in exercise of the right of disposal before the goods have been delivered; it is not a right to be exercised after having the goods unloaded and receiving them.

The official verdict is false, but the statement is ambiguous: communicating the order to the driver is not prohibited. The CMR requires the conditions for exercising the right of disposal to be met; it does not say that simply informing the driver is enough.

Completion by the carrier does not automatically relieve the sender of responsibility: if the carrier enters the details at the sender's request, they are presumed to act on the sender's behalf unless proved otherwise.
It is false that the sender is never liable: for example, the sender is liable for damage and expenses caused to the carrier by certain inaccurate or insufficient particulars.

True. The sender is liable for damage and expenses caused by defective packaging; if the defect was apparent or known when the goods were taken over, liability remains when the carrier has made reservations.
True. The sender may be liable to the carrier for damage and expenses caused by defective packaging, subject to the exception for an apparent or known defect accepted without reservation.

True. The sender is liable to the carrier for damage caused by inaccurate or insufficient particulars that the sender is responsible for providing. The rule does not cover every omission indiscriminately: some responsibilities lie with the carrier.

'Always' is incorrect: the sender's liability depends on the cause of the damage and the conditions set out in the CMR. For example, an exception applies to defective packing if the defect was apparent or known and the carrier made no reservations.
False. The sender may be liable for damage and expenses caused by defective packaging, unless the defect was apparent or known to the carrier and the carrier made no reservations.

It is false to automatically place the burden on the carrier and exclude the sender's liability: the sender is liable for damage and expenses due to defective packing, subject to the exception for an apparent or known defect where no reservations were made.

The sender may be liable for damage and expenses caused by defective packing. Liability is excluded if the defect was apparent or known to the carrier when the goods were taken over and the carrier made no reservations.
The sender does have responsibilities regarding packing: they may be liable for damage and expenses caused by defects in the packing, subject to the exception provided for by the CMR.
'Always' is incorrect: the sender is not liable if the defect was apparent or known to the carrier when the goods were taken over and the carrier made no reservations.

False. For particulars the sender is responsible for providing, the sender is liable to the carrier for damage caused by inaccuracies or insufficiencies. The CMR also provides for specific responsibilities of the carrier.

False. For particulars the sender is responsible for providing, the sender is liable to the carrier for damage caused by inaccuracies or insufficiencies; these are not automatically the consignee's responsibility.
It is not true that no one bears responsibility for the damage: the sender is liable for damage and expenses caused to the carrier by certain inaccurate or insufficient particulars.

The sender must make available to the carrier the documents and information needed for customs and other formalities prior to delivery. The CMR specifies that deadline; it does not generally require all of them to be provided before departure.

The documents required depend on the formalities applicable to the carriage: the sender must provide those that are necessary. The phrase 'validity of the CMR' is imprecise: the absence of the consignment note does not invalidate the contract.
The consignment note alone is not necessarily enough: the sender must also make available the documents and information needed for customs and other formalities before delivery.
FALSO. The sender must provide more than just the certificates listed: they must also make available the other documents and information needed for customs and other formalities before delivery.

FALSO. Providing only the documents authorizing the vehicle to cross the border is not enough: the sender must provide the documents and information needed for the formalities to be completed before delivery.

FALSO. The DDT and accompanying document do not determine the validity of the CMR contract: the consignment note is evidence of the contract, which remains valid even if the note is missing or irregular.
FALSO. The consignment note documents the contract, but is not required for its validity: the contract remains subject to the CMR even if the note is missing, irregular or lost.
FALSO. The validity of the CMR contract does not depend on the accompanying document: the contract is documented by the consignment note and remains valid even without it.

VERO according to the quiz, but the wording is imprecise: damage during the non-road leg does not automatically exclude the road carrier's liability. If it is proved to result from an event specific to that leg and not from an act or omission by the road carrier, liability is determined under the rules applicable to the other mode of transport.

VERO. The injured party may bring a claim against the carrier for loss, damage or delay; however, the absence of a cause attributable to the person entitled to the goods does not in itself guarantee compensation, as other grounds for exemption may apply.

FALSO according to the quiz, but the statement is ambiguous: the carrier's liability may also extend to the non-road leg. In specific, proven circumstances, the rules for the other mode of transport apply, without liability being automatically excluded.

FALSO. Liability is not automatically total for all damage caused by third parties: when the conditions laid down for the non-road leg are met, it is determined under the rules applicable to that transport.

FALSO. Starting the journey by road alone does not automatically make the carrier liable for all damage attributable to other carriers: for certain events on the non-road leg, liability follows the rules specific to that leg.

FALSO according to the quiz, but the wording is problematic: if the damage does not result from an instruction by the person entitled to the goods, this particular ground for exemption does not apply. A claim may therefore be brought, subject to examination of other grounds for exemption.

FALSO according to the quiz, but diligence alone does not automatically rule out every claim: the carrier is liable for loss, damage and delay unless it proves a ground for exemption under the CMR, including unavoidable circumstances and consequences that could not be prevented.

FALSO according to the quiz, but a warning alone does not automatically rule out a claim: it must be determined whether the damage was caused by an instruction from the person entitled to the goods and whether that instruction resulted from fault by the carrier.
True. For loss or damage, the carrier's liability covers the period from taking over the goods until delivery, subject to the grounds for exemption provided by the CMR.

True in the sense that the contractual relationship does not limit liability to employees alone: the carrier is also liable for people whose services it uses for carriage, when they act in the course of their duties.
True, with a clarification: the carrier is liable for the acts and omissions of employees and other people whose services it uses for carriage, when they act in the course of their duties.
FALSO. For loss and damage, CMR liability covers the period from taking over the goods to delivery, not the period before they are taken over.
FALSO. Liability for loss and damage begins when the goods are taken over, not merely when the contract is concluded, and lasts until delivery.
False. For loss or damage, the relevant period runs from taking over the goods until their delivery, not merely the vehicle's journey up to its entry into the place of destination.

FALSO. The carrier is not liable only for the goods: it is also liable for the acts and omissions of employees and other persons it uses to perform the transport, when they act in the course of their duties.
FALSO. Liability is not limited to regularly salaried staff: it also covers other persons the carrier uses for the transport, when they act in the course of their duties.
FALSO. Payment under a contract is not the condition set by the CMR: the carrier is liable for the acts and omissions of persons it uses if they act in the course of their duties.
False. Liability does not concern loading staff alone: it includes the acts and omissions of employees and other people whose services the carrier uses for carriage, in the course of their duties.
False. The carrier is liable not only for the driver, but also for other employees and people whose services it uses for carriage, when they act in the course of their duties.
VERO. The contract may provide for an amount to be collected on delivery: if the carrier delivers without collecting it, it is liable to the sender up to the agreed amount.

VERO according to the quiz: if the goods have become unusable, the recipient may no longer have a practical interest in delivery. However, the loss of interest must be assessed in each case; the CMR does not automatically presume it for every alteration.
FALSO. The sender may also entrust the carrier with collecting an amount on delivery, if the transport contract provides for it.

FALSO according to the quiz: the amount to be collected on delivery must be specified in the agreement, so that the carrier knows how much to collect. The CMR provides for liability for failure to collect it, up to that amount.
FALSO. The amount due on delivery is a sum to be collected under the contract; there is no provision for automatically replacing it with any asset of indeterminable value.

FALSO according to the quiz: if the goods can still be used, there may still be an interest in delivery. However, the actual interest depends on the circumstances and the remaining usefulness of the goods, not merely on whether they can physically be used.

FALSO. Exceeding the agreed deadline by up to twenty days alone does not show that the interest in delivery has ceased. The CMR allows goods that remain undelivered thirty days after the agreed deadline to be considered lost.
FALSO. If no deadline was agreed, goods that have not been delivered may be considered lost without further evidence after 60 days from taking them over, not after 50.

VERO according to the quiz: if damage to part of the goods makes the entire lot commercially unusable, the harm may affect the whole consignment. However, classification as a total loss is not automatic: the CMR also covers damage that reduces the value of the entire consignment.
VERO. Damage is harm to the goods that reduces their value; the goods may remain usable. The CMR bases compensation on the reduction in value.
FALSO. A very low price indicates a substantial reduction in value, but does not automatically mean a total loss: the goods may be damaged and still saleable.
FALSO. Failure to declare the value in the consignment note does not cause the goods to be lost; the declaration may affect the compensation limit.
FALSO. The number of consignment notes does not automatically turn damage to part of the goods into a total loss. What matters is the harm to the consignment.
FALSO according to the quiz, but the wording is ambiguous: damage can reduce both the value and the usability of the goods. The CMR links compensation for damage to the reduction in value.
FALSO according to the quiz, but the statement is incomplete and can describe damage: it is harm to the goods, which is relevant under the CMR through the reduction in value.
FALSO. Loss of usability alone does not define every case of damage: damaged goods may retain some usefulness despite having lost value.
VERO. A change in the condition of the goods that lowers their commercial value may constitute damage; compensation is calculated based on the reduction in value.
FALSO. A change that has no effect on commercial value does not cause the reduction in value on which the CMR calculates compensation for damage.
FALSO. Damage is not defined merely by attributing the event to the carrier: what matters is the harm to the goods; the cause affects liability.

FALSO. An instruction from the recipient does not define damage: damage concerns harm to the goods. An instruction from the person entitled to the goods may, however, be relevant to exempting the carrier from liability.

VERO when the goods can be considered lost: the person entitled to them may claim compensation for loss instead of waiting for delivery. If the goods are found and requested, the CMR provides for the compensation for loss to be returned, without prejudice to the right to compensation for delay.
VERO. The goods may be delivered late and the harm caused by the delay may be compensated if proved, within the limits set by the CMR.
VERO. Failure to meet the agreed delivery deadline constitutes delay. If no deadline was agreed, the reasonable time for a diligent carrier is considered.
FALSO. Compensation for loss of the same goods is not retained after their delivery has been requested: it must be returned, without prejudice to the right to compensation for delay.
FALSO. Late delivery does not rule out all compensation: if the person entitled to the goods proves harm caused by the delay, they may claim compensation within the prescribed limits.
FALSO. Delay may give rise to compensation for proven harm; once the prescribed periods have elapsed, undelivered goods may also be considered lost.
FALSO. Delay begins when the agreed deadline is missed, without waiting another 40 days.
FALSO. Delay concerns the time of delivery: it occurs when the agreed deadline or, in its absence, a reasonable time is exceeded.
FALSO. There is no need to wait 70 days: without an agreed deadline, delay depends on whether the reasonable time for a diligent carrier has been exceeded.
VERO. The carrier is liable for total or partial loss and damage between taking over the goods and delivery, as well as for delay, subject to the prescribed grounds for exemption.
VERO. The carrier is exempt if it proves that the loss, damage or delay was caused by an inherent defect in the goods.
FALSO. The carrier's liability is not limited to loss: it also covers damage and delay in delivery, subject to the prescribed exemptions.

The carrier is not liable only for delay: it is also liable for total or partial loss of and damage to the goods between taking them over and delivery, subject to the prescribed grounds for exemption.
A vehicle breakdown does not in itself exempt the carrier from liability for delay.
An avoidable circumstance is not enough: exemption requires circumstances the carrier could not avoid and whose consequences the carrier could not prevent.
Exemption does not apply in every case: the carrier is liable unless one of the grounds provided for by the convention applies.
It is not true that exemption is always ruled out: it is provided for, for example, when the goods have an inherent defect.
The consignment note documents the contract, but its absence, irregularity or loss does not affect the contract's existence or validity.
The consignment note is evidence, unless proved otherwise, of the conclusion and terms of the contract and of the carrier's taking over of the goods.
The contract can be valid even without a completed consignment note: the absence of the document does not affect its existence or validity.
The convention provides for the consignment note as evidence of the contract and its terms; the contract remains valid even if the note is missing.
The CMR provides for three original copies, signed by the sender and the carrier.

In the form referred to by the quiz, there may be a fourth white copy for statistical purposes. The convention, however, requires three original copies: the additional copy is not a mandatory fourth original prescribed by the CMR.
The absence, irregularity or loss of the consignment note does not make the contract void: its validity is unaffected.
A missing, irregular or lost consignment note does not make the contract voidable: its validity is unaffected.
The absence, irregularity or loss of the consignment note does not make the contract ineffective; it remains subject to the convention.
The absence or loss of the consignment note does not affect the validity of the contract of carriage.
The consignment note is not essential to validity: even if it is missing, the contract remains valid and subject to the CMR.

It is false to state that the general retention period for the consignee is two years from the date of transport. Commercial documents subject to Article 2220 of the Civil Code must be retained for ten years; applicability depends on the nature of the document and the party concerned. The retention period must not be confused with the time limit for pursuing a CMR claim.
Preparing three copies is not enough: the CMR also requires the signatures of the sender and the carrier.
Both the sender and the carrier sign; the signatures may be printed or replaced by stamps if the law of the country of issue permits it.
The CMR provides for three originals: the first is given to the sender.
Of the three originals provided for by the CMR, the second accompanies the goods.
Of the three originals provided for by the CMR, the third is retained by the carrier.
The CMR does not require at least four copies: it provides for three originals, and the second accompanies the goods rather than being assigned generally to the owner.
The carrier is not the only one who signs: the consignment note must also be signed by the sender, in the forms permitted by the law of the country of issue.
Two copies are not enough: the CMR provides for three originals, intended respectively for the sender, to accompany the goods, and for the carrier.

The consignment note is signed by both the sender and the carrier. If the law of the country of issue permits it, the signatures may be printed or replaced by stamps: they do not necessarily have to be handwritten.
If the goods are divided into different loads or belong to different categories, the sender or carrier may request a separate consignment note for each load or category.

Taking over involves entrusting the goods to the carrier; at that point the carrier checks the apparent condition of the goods and packaging and the particulars concerning the packages. The CMR does not, however, always assign the physical loading operation to the carrier or require the carrier to check every particular in the consignment note.
It is not limited to a single load: if the goods are divided into different lots, the sender or carrier may request a separate consignment note for each one.
It is not limited to a single category: if goods of different categories are carried, the sender or carrier may request a separate consignment note for each category.
The vehicle is not the only criterion: a separate consignment note may also be requested for each category or lot of goods when there are different categories or lots.

The quiz marks this false because the description is incomplete: on taking over, the carrier must also carry out the prescribed checks on the goods and packages. The statement is ambiguous, however, because it says ‘includes’ and does not exclude those checks; moreover, the physical loading may be performed by the sender.

The quiz marks this false because checking the apparent condition alone does not cover everything involved in taking over: the carrier also checks the number of packages and their marks and numbers. The statement is ambiguous because it says that this check is included, not that it is the only one.

The quiz marks this false because checking the number of packages alone does not cover everything involved in taking over: the carrier also checks the marks and numbers of the packages and the apparent condition of the goods and packaging. The wording is ambiguous because it does not exclude these other checks.
The CMR prescribes mandatory particulars, including the sender, carrier, consignee, places of taking over and delivery, and description of the goods.
The agreed time limit for carrying out the transport appears in the consignment note where applicable.
The parties may agree on the delivery time limit separately from the consignment note: the CMR does not make the note a condition for the validity of the contract.
The delivery time limit may be agreed verbally: the CMR does not make the validity of the contract dependent on the consignment note. Proof of the agreement is a separate matter from its validity.

The quiz marks this false because the CMR requires three originals signed by the sender and the carrier. This does not mean that it imposes a single graphic format; moreover, loss or irregularity of the consignment note does not invalidate the contract.
The content is not entirely unrestricted: the CMR lists the particulars to be included, while allowing the parties to add other useful details.
The parties cannot freely depart from the CMR: subject to the exceptions provided for, a clause that directly or indirectly departs from it is void, without making the other clauses void.
It is wrong to say that the duration must appear only in the consignment note: the time limit may also be agreed separately, since the note is not a condition for the validity of the contract.
It is wrong to rule out a verbal agreement on the time limit: the CMR does not require a consignment note for the contract to be valid, although proving the agreement may be more difficult.
It is wrong to rule out a separate document: the time limit may also be agreed outside the consignment note, which is not a condition for the validity of the contract.

The quiz accepts the re-creation of the consignment note by the sender and carrier in three originals. The CMR provides for those originals to be signed by both and states that loss does not invalidate the contract; it does not expressly regulate the replacement procedure.
Duties may be calculated on the quantity of the goods, on their value, or by combining the two criteria.

Loss of the consignment note does not make it impossible to document the transport: the sender and carrier can prepare a new note. The CMR states that loss does not invalidate the contract, without expressly regulating replacement.

The quiz marks this false: the consignment note is made out with the signatures of the sender and the carrier, not by the consignee alone. The statement is ambiguous because it mentions the consignee's consent without saying that it replaces the required signatures; the CMR does not expressly regulate replacement of a lost consignment note.

The quiz marks this false because the consignment note requires the signatures of the sender and the carrier: the driver does not replace it solely on their own initiative. The statement does not clarify, however, whether the driver is acting on behalf of the carrier; the CMR does not expressly regulate replacement of a lost consignment note.
It is false that customs duties originated for reasons other than raising revenue: initially their purpose was to generate revenue; later they also acquired a protectionist function.
FALSO. Customs duties on trade in goods between member states are prohibited; the common tariff applies to dealings with third countries.
FALSO. When due, a duty is a charge on imports and increases the cost incurred for the goods.
VERO. Customs authorities inspect goods entering or leaving the customs territory of the Union, as well as other operations subject to supervision.
VERO. Customs authorities' duties include protecting the financial interests of the Union and its member states.
VERO. National customs authorities apply EU customs legislation and contribute to common EU policies.
VERO. Customs checks combat unfair and illegal trade and contribute to consumer safety.
VERO. The customs union prohibits import and export duties between member states.

Transporting animals does not in itself require authorization from the road-owning authority: the documents prescribed for the animals are needed. Road authorization may be required for other reasons, such as exceptional transport.
A municipal licence is not the document required because live animals are being transported: the documentation relating to animal transport is needed instead.
Transporting animals does not in itself require authorization for a test drive: the documentation relating to the animals being transported is needed instead.
FALSO: transporting unpackaged food does not in itself require authorization from the body that owns the road; the usual vehicle documents are required.
FALSO: transporting unpackaged food does not require a municipal licence for the service; the documents and authorizations required for the vehicle and the activity apply.
FALSO: authorization for test driving concerns driving for test purposes, not the normal transport of unpackaged food, for which the vehicle registration document is required.

The quiz refers to the former health authorization for vehicles intended for certain foods. These are historical rules: the verdict should not be understood as a current general requirement for every vehicle.
For the quiz, a valid ATP certificate is required to prove the vehicle's compliance. The ATP also allows an equivalent certification plate linked to a valid certificate.
The driver must carry the registration document: it is the vehicle's document and is also required when carrying frozen food.
A municipal licence is not required simply because frozen food is being transported. The registration document and, when applicable, proof of ATP compliance are required instead.
The animal accompanying document concerns animal transport and is not required solely for transporting frozen food. The applicable ATP provisions apply to frozen food instead.
Proof of ATP compliance is not optional when the agreement applies: the certificate must be valid and accompany the vehicle, unless there is an equivalent certification plate.

The quiz refers to the health mark on meat and the documents that allow it to be identified. The mark is applied to the product or its packaging; it is not a separate document to be kept in the cab. The arrangements depend on the product.
The quiz refers to the former health authorization required for certain vehicles that carried meat. These are historical rules, not a current general requirement for every vehicle.
For transport subject to ADR, the vehicle must carry the required safety equipment, selected also according to the hazards of the goods.
For transport subject to ADR, the written instructions must be on board and easily accessible to guide the crew in an emergency, subject to applicable exemptions.
The driver must carry the ADR training certificate with the tanker specialization when the transport is subject to that requirement; ADR exemptions exist.
Transporting meat does not in itself require a municipal licence on board. The driver must carry the registration documents prescribed for the vehicle.
The question reverses the devices: an analogue tachograph uses a record sheet, while a digital tachograph uses a driver card. Records of previous activities may also be required.

The quiz does not regard the former health authorization as optional for the vehicles concerned. However, it refers to historical rules: it does not state a current general requirement for every vehicle carrying meat.
FALSO: the certificate of approval is not optional when ADR requires it for the vehicle used; it must accompany the unit concerned.

The ATP certificate attests to the suitability of equipment for perishable food; it is not required solely because dangerous goods are carried in a tank. ADR requirements apply to those goods instead.
FALSO: a journey log is not required simply because dangerous goods are being transported in a tank. The ADR documents applicable to the transport are required instead.

When the prescribed circumstances apply, the container packing certificate must accompany the transport along with the ADR documents; it is not required for every transport operation that does not use a tank.
The written ADR instructions must also be on board and accessible to the crew for transport operations not using a tank that are subject to this requirement, subject to applicable exemptions.
VERO applies when interchangeable bodies are used: the supplementary certificate relates to their approval. The statement is incomplete if read as a requirement for every non-tanker vehicle.

The statement is incomplete: it does not specify which certificate is concerned. The official verdict is FALSO, but the missing document cannot be identified. In general, ADR certificates required for the particular transport operation must be on board when required: they are not optional; obligations and any exemptions depend on the circumstances.

The health authorization concerns suitability for food transport; it is not an optional ADR document for dangerous goods. For those goods, the ADR documents required in the particular case apply instead.
FALSO: when ADR requires a certificate of approval for the type of vehicle, carrying it on board is not optional; not all non-tank transport requires it.
VERO reflects the system in the old quiz: the form accompanied transport in the cases specified, while SISTRI used tracking devices. SISTRI has been abolished and the FIR and RENTRI rules now apply.
The motor third-party liability insurance certificate is a vehicle document for waste-carrying vehicles too. VERO is outdated regarding the insurance disc, which is now digital.

False as a general requirement for waste: the packing certificate concerns specific shipments of dangerous goods in containers before sea transport. However, the qualification ‘where applicable’ makes the question ambiguous.
False as a rule for all waste: written instructions are required when the transport is subject to the relevant ADR provisions, for example for waste classified as dangerous goods.

The quiz marks this false, but the wording is ambiguous: the separate certificate of ownership is not among the documents normally required on board, so carrying it is optional. Today the single vehicle document replaces the registration document and certificate of ownership.

As a rule, an undertaking that collects and transports waste must register in the relevant category of the National Register of Environmental Operators. The rules provide for some exceptions, so the question should be understood in general terms.
As a rule, waste transported by organizations or undertakings is accompanied by a waste identification form completed with the required information; exceptions are provided by law.
The relevant ADR requirements apply to the road transport of dangerous goods, taking account of any exemptions provided for in the agreement.

Registration in the road hauliers' register alone is not enough: collection and transport of waste normally also require registration in the National Register of Environmental Operators, subject to exceptions.
ADR does not always require an invoice to be kept on board. Transport documents and written instructions are required in the prescribed cases instead.
An ordinary transport document is not necessarily enough: transport subject to ADR requires the prescribed information and other documents, depending on the case and any exemptions.
For transport subject to the Community licence, a certified true copy must accompany the vehicle. The rule must be read in light of its scope and any exemptions.

The vehicle must have third-party liability insurance and the certificate; the true verdict reflects the old rules on the insurance disc, which is now digital. Territorial coverage must be checked for the journey.
False: the registration document is not optional; it must accompany the vehicle during international transport too.
False: a municipal licence is not the general authorisation for international carriage of goods for hire or reward; a certified copy of the Community licence is required in the applicable cases.
False: an ATP certificate is not optional when the transport and vehicle fall within the applicable requirements; however, it is not required for every carriage of goods.

The true verdict applies to a journey made under a CEMT permit, which must accompany the vehicle. Not all transport outside the EU requires a CEMT permit: bilateral permits or other arrangements may apply.
The registration document is a vehicle document that must also be carried during international transport outside the EU.
The true verdict concerns journeys for which the applicable agreement requires a bilateral permit from the country concerned. It is not a blanket requirement for every journey outside the EU.

False if understood as a general requirement for the part outside the EU: the authorisation depends on the applicable agreements. However, the statement is too absolute, because a copy of the Community licence may be needed for the legs where it applies.
False: the pink-striped approval certificate is not always needed for transport outside the EU; it is required when ADR rules prescribe approval for the vehicle and transport concerned.
False: a municipal licence is not the general authorisation for international carriage of goods; depending on the route and agreements, bilateral or multilateral international permits may be needed.
The driver must carry the vehicle's registration document; own-account transport to non-EU countries may also require other documents.

The quiz considers proof of insurance coverage valid abroad necessary. The wording is dated: the Italian insurance sticker is no longer required, and the documents accepted depend on the country being crossed.

The driver must carry a licence valid for the vehicle: C or CE when required. The wording is general: other categories may suffice for lighter vehicles, and further documents may be needed outside the EU.
The quiz indicates FALSO, but the answer requires caution: not all non-EU countries have the same rules. Some own-account routes require a bilateral or CEMT authorization; others are liberalized.
The copy of the Community licence concerns carriage for hire or reward; it is not required for own-account transport that meets the prescribed conditions.

A journey certificate on a DTT form is not required in every case: the documentation depends on the transport route and the applicable rules. For example, the circular distinguishes between liberalized transport operations and those subject to a CEMT or bilateral authorization.
In addition to the unauthorized carrier, the customer, loader and owner of the goods may be penalized if they entrust the transport to a carrier lacking authorization or violating its limits.

Penalties may involve several parties in the transport chain: the carrier and, in the prescribed cases, the customer, loader and owner of the goods. They do not automatically apply to every party in every circumstance.
The carrier is not the only party liable: the customer, loader and owner of the goods may also be penalized for entrusting transport to an unauthorized carrier.
The carrier and loader are not the only parties involved: the client and the owner of the goods may also be liable when the prescribed conditions apply.

The quiz marks this as FALSO because the expected answer also includes the carrier and the client. The statement is ambiguous, however: the loader and owner can indeed be penalized in the prescribed cases.
In transport for hire or reward, the limits of registration in the Register must also be respected: operating beyond the permitted limits constitutes unauthorized operation.
For transport for hire or reward, registration alone is not enough: the conditions of registration must also be respected.
Carrying goods by road for hire or reward without the required registration in the Register constitutes unauthorized operation.
Unauthorised road haulage carries an administrative fine. The rules distinguish operating without registration from transporting goods without the required authorisation or beyond its limits.

Administrative detention for three months is an additional penalty provided for unauthorised operation; confiscation may be ordered for a repeat offence. Cases concerning transport authorisation are governed separately.

The quiz considers loss of good repute a consequence of unauthorised operation. However, it is not automatically lost for every irregularity: the circumstances and the assessment required by the applicable rules matter.

Transporting people irregularly is not in itself the same as unauthorized operation of road freight transport: the latter includes, among other things, carrying goods for hire or reward without the required registration.

Irregular staffing, lack of motor third-party liability insurance, and failure to pay the registration fee are separate violations; they do not automatically constitute unauthorized transport, which also concerns the absence of, or failure to comply with, the required authorization. Registration status must still be checked.

Overloading and driving on prohibited days are separate offences: they do not in themselves define unauthorised transport. The latter concerns operating without registration or transporting goods without the required authorisation or beyond its limits.

Revocation of registration is not the penalty automatically prescribed for every case of unauthorised transport; moreover, if the company is not registered, there is no registration to revoke. A fine and vehicle detention are prescribed in the specified cases.
This is not a disciplinary penalty: unauthorised operation is punished with an administrative fine, with vehicle detention added in the cases prescribed.
It is incorrect to speak of a criminal penalty for this violation: unauthorized road transport for hire or reward is subject to the administrative penalties prescribed by law.

For overloading, the penalties under Article 167 apply to the driver and owner, and also to the customer if the transport is carried out exclusively on their behalf. The question uses ‘jointly and severally liable’ imprecisely: the rule provides for penalties to be applied to each person.

If the written contract provides for arrangements incompatible with the safety rules that were breached, the other parties named may be held liable alongside the driver, within the prescribed limits and after their responsibility has been established.
Not all the parties named are automatically jointly responsible for every violation by the driver: the legal conditions must be checked and each party's responsibility established.
The carrier is not necessarily the only party liable: other parties in the supply chain may also be liable when the conditions laid down by law are met.
The loader is not necessarily the only party liable: depending on the violation and circumstances, the carrier and other parties in the supply chain may also be liable.
For own-account transport using motor vehicles with a total mass exceeding 6 tonnes, a licence is required for each vehicle.
Providing transport to a consignor for payment describes carriage for hire or reward. In own-account transport, the carriage serves the operator's own needs and is ancillary to its main activity.

It is wrong to rule out the need to demonstrate the relationship: in own-account transport, driving must comply with the conditions for the proprietor or permitted staff, which can be checked during an inspection.

The goods must be connected with the company's activity: for example, they must be intended for processing or otherwise for use in that activity. The transport must also be ancillary to that activity.
Using each mode where it is best suited can reduce overall costs by choosing capacity and route according to the load; the savings depend on the particular circumstances.
VERO. Choosing a vehicle suited to the characteristics and quantity of the load allows capacity and resources to be used more effectively, helping contain costs.
A less steep route can reduce engine workload and fuel consumption. Savings are not automatic: distance, traffic and tolls also matter.

Over long distances, an intermodal chain can reduce costs by combining an efficient main leg with the flexibility of road transport. Savings are not automatic: they also depend on connections and transfer costs.
Meeting all requests does not in itself reduce costs: it may require more trips or resources. Services must be organized and the available vehicles used efficiently.
Using road transport as much as possible does not guarantee the lowest cost: on some routes, especially long ones, an intermodal solution may be more cost-effective.
Using rail as much as possible does not guarantee the lowest cost: cost-effectiveness depends on distance, connections and transshipment costs.

Using air transport as much as possible does not guarantee a lower cost: air freight is generally more expensive than road or sea transport, although it is faster. The choice depends on the shipment's needs.
In the historical context of the quiz, uneven growth among modes of transport contributed to imbalance in the system and to congestion.
In the context of the quiz, failure to comply with social and safety rules creates safety and competition problems: the Commission proposed more effective checks and penalties.
Moving goods onto sea routes can take vehicles off congested roads, provided ports and land connections are adequate.
Aviation security measures entail compliance and inspection costs, which are also borne by transport operators. The question refers to the historical framework of European rules.
Rail can carry large quantities of goods with energy and environmental advantages over road transport; the actual result also depends on the load and the energy source.
Insufficient use of roads is not the problem identified: in the quiz's context, imbalance between modes and road congestion also call for alternatives to road transport.
Insufficient use of air transport is not the problem identified: the European context referred to in the quiz identifies imbalances between modes and congestion in airspace too.

The official verdict is false, but the statement is ambiguous: the White Paper noted that short-sea shipping was not being fully exploited. The general problem was imbalance between modes, not a single cause applicable to all shipping.
False. The stated share is too high: according to the European Commission, transport contributes about 5% of EU GDP.
False. International air freight is permitted: it is subject to checks and security measures, not a general ban.
False. Sustainable mobility is also a European objective pursued by the EU transport strategy.
False. Sea transport is not always less economical: for large loads it can be particularly economical.
True. Goods can travel by land, by sea or inland waterways, and by air.
True. Road and rail are among the main modes of land transport.
The availability of goods affects transport planning: knowing where and when they are available helps in choosing a suitable service.
True. The cost of the different modes is one of the economic factors to consider when choosing transport.
True. Distance affects the organisation and cost of the journey and therefore the choice of mode.

False according to the quiz if the comparison concerns inland transport, where road transport predominates. However, the statement is ambiguous: when sea transport is included, Eurostat data for 2024 show that water transport predominates in tonne-kilometres.

A long distance does not mean rail always predominates: the choice depends on traffic flows and the territory. The question does not specify a geographical area; in Italy, overall land transport is predominantly by road.
FALSO. Road and rubber refer essentially to the same mode; land transport also includes rail transport.
FALSO. The modes can also complement one another: for example, road transport can serve the first and last legs of a journey whose main leg is by rail.
VERO. In general, rail is safer than road when comparing land transport modes; this does not rule out individual rail accidents.
VERO. In general, rail uses less energy than trucks per tonne of goods transported and kilometre travelled.
VERO. In general, rail produces fewer greenhouse gas emissions than road transport per unit of goods transported and distance travelled.
VERO. Rail requires tracks and terminals, whereas road transport can cover the legs to the sender and recipient more flexibly.
FALSO. Rail is not generally less safe: among land transport modes, it has a safety advantage over road transport.
FALSO. In general, rail transport has lower greenhouse gas emissions than road transport per unit transported and distance travelled.
FALSO. Rail is less flexible for door-to-door transport: road transport is often needed to connect the sender and recipient to terminals.
FALSO. In general, rail requires less energy than trucks per tonne-kilometre, not more.
VERO. Rail generally offers an environmental advantage, with lower greenhouse gas emissions per unit transported than road transport.
VERO. Rail offers a safety advantage over other land transport modes, although it is not free from accidents.
VERO. For goods, rail generally uses less energy than trucks for the same number of tonne-kilometres.
VERO. When land transport modes are compared, rail generally has a safety advantage.
The quiz considers it false that rail guarantees a speed advantage: for goods, waiting times and transfers can lengthen delivery times. The comparison depends, however, on the route and service.
It is incorrect to describe energy consumption as a general disadvantage: rail is among the most efficient modes per unit of transport.
Safety is not a general disadvantage of rail: European railways are among the safest.
Rail does not provide general network coverage: trains are restricted to tracks, and another means of transport is often needed to reach the origin and destination.

The quiz considers the improvement of inland waterways a requirement of the water transport system. The wording is imprecise: inland navigation and maritime transport are distinct modes, although they can be integrated at ports.
Moving goods from roads to sea routes can ease traffic and therefore road congestion.
The quiz considers it true that procedures can make air transport more burdensome: goods require security checks or a secure supply chain. Their complexity and duration depend on the shipment.
It is false to exclude sea transport from combined transport: a sea leg can be integrated with other modes. In the question, “multimedia” should be understood as multimodal.
It is false that major investment is unnecessary: port infrastructure and services require action to remove bottlenecks and improve capacity.
It is false that short-sea shipping never relieves congestion: it can move by ship some of the goods that would otherwise travel on congested roads.
It is false that air transport is unaffected by checks: security checks are part of the supply chain and can affect timing; they are not necessarily lengthy in every case.
The quiz considers the general adequacy of access infrastructure false: airports' logistics connections may have shortcomings. The situation varies from airport to airport.
It is false that the European air system is free from fragmentation: airspace management remains divided, and this also affects cargo flights.
The vehicle can collect the goods from the sender and deliver them directly to the recipient, if the locations are accessible by road.
Flexible routes and direct delivery can make road transport timely. However, VERO does not mean that it is always faster: that depends on the route and the service being compared.
The road network can serve places without direct rail, port or airport connections, provided they are accessible to the vehicle.
It is false that the loss of human life is insignificant: road accidents cause many deaths every year.
It is false that road transport is much safer than other modes: the risk of death per distance traveled is higher than for rail, at least when comparing passengers.
It is false that road transport does not pollute: vehicles produce emissions that affect air quality and the climate.
Road transport offers flexibility in choosing routes and can make direct deliveries, helping provide timely service; actual times also depend on traffic.
The vehicle can collect and deliver goods directly at the sender's and recipient's locations, when those locations are accessible by road.
The flexibility of road transport makes it possible to organize routes and loads to make better use of vehicles, for example by reducing empty trips.
The road network can directly reach places without rail, port or airport connections, provided they are accessible to the vehicle.
Traffic queues are not an advantage: they slow the journey and can delay deliveries. One advantage of road transport is the flexibility of the service.
The possibility of traffic congestion is not an advantage: it can slow the journey and delay deliveries. Flexibility of routes, on the other hand, is an advantage.
An increase in greenhouse gases is a negative environmental impact, not an advantage of road transport.
Road transport is widely used for goods: in the EU it predominates in inland transport. The comparison nevertheless depends on the area, period and unit of measurement considered.
Over the long term, road freight traffic has grown, and the increased activity has contributed to emissions. Trends in individual pollutants also depend, however, on the technologies and fuels used.

The comparison must be understood in terms of goods carried and distance traveled: in general, heavy vehicles emit more greenhouse gases per tonne-kilometer than ships. Other pollutants and individual journeys may yield different results.
Integration of the borderless European market has encouraged cross-border road transport, which has grown over time. Removing barriers is one factor in that growth, not the only cause.
Road freight traffic contributes to congestion, especially in international corridors where long-distance flows and local traffic converge.

The quiz marks this false, but the ranking depends on what is measured: considering tonne-kilometres across all modes in the EU, Eurostat does indeed place sea transport ahead of road transport. The wording does not specify the criterion.
It is false that bracket tariffs are mandatory: freight transport prices are left to negotiation between the parties, subject to safety principles.

It is generally false that road transport pollutes less than rail: per tonne-kilometer, heavy vehicles normally emit more greenhouse gases. The comparison nevertheless depends on the pollutant and transport conditions.
It is false that all of Europe is completely liberalized: even in the EU, access to international transport and cabotage remain subject to conditions.
Road transport offers a flexible service that can adapt routes and delivery to the customer's needs; timeliness and efficiency nevertheless depend on travel conditions.
The road network can also reach places without a railway station or line, provided they are accessible to vehicles.
A road vehicle can collect goods from the sender and deliver them directly to the recipient: this is door-to-door service.
A return load uses the vehicle on the journey back as well, reducing the distance travelled empty and improving vehicle utilization.
Road transport can be carried out for the needs of one's own business or, for payment, on behalf of third parties, subject to the respective conditions.
It is false that road transport makes it possible to avoid issuing invoices: the obligation depends on tax rules and the type of transaction, not the mode of transport.
It is false that road transport is always the cheapest solution: cost depends on distance, quantity and how transport is organized, and other modes may be more economical.

The quiz considers it true that road transport operators are specialized. The wording is too absolute, however: transport can also be carried out on own account by businesses whose main activity is something other than transport.
ITS systems can improve freight transport: for example, they help manage fleets and traffic and track shipments.
Intermodality combines different modes, using their strengths and making the transport chain more efficient, including its road legs.

In the historical context of the quiz, road freight was expected to grow more than rail freight in the absence of corrective measures. This was a forecast from that time, not a certainty about the future today.

The quiz considers false the forecast of a decline in road transport in favour of air transport: the historical reference scenario instead predicted growth in road transport. The wording “could” does not, however, rule out other scenarios.
The quiz considers the forecast of a sharp decline in road transport relative to rail false: the historical scenario without intervention predicted stronger growth in road transport.

The quiz considers false the forecast of a decline in road transport due to traffic: the historical scenario instead predicted growth in road transport and greater congestion. “Could decrease” remains, however, a possibility stated in general terms.

The quiz considers the increase in road freight transport to be true. However, the phrase ‘the last ten years’ does not identify the period, and ‘growth’ may refer to volume or its rate: the result therefore depends on the years and indicator chosen.
More goods vehicles or more kilometres travelled can increase exposure to accident risk; this does not mean that every increase automatically causes more accidents.
A greater number of freight vehicles uses road network capacity and can contribute to congestion, especially on already busy stretches.
It is false that there is no effect: an increase in transport using vehicles that burn fuel can increase CO₂ emissions, which contribute to the greenhouse effect.
It is false that growth has no effect on the environment: more transport can increase consumption, emissions and other impacts, depending on the vehicles and conditions of use.
It is false that growth has no effect on safety: increased goods vehicle traffic can increase exposure to accident risk, although infrastructure and prevention also matter.
Intermodality contributes to sustainability by combining transport modes and reducing dependence on road transport and pollution.
Sustainability also considers environmental impact, so reducing pollutant emissions is part of the issue.

The quiz considers the role of international cooperation on infrastructure true: connecting networks in different countries facilitates sustainable transport. “Requires an agreement” is, however, an absolute formulation, not a single condition for every intervention.
Being able to choose between different modes helps organize transport according to the needs of the shipment and the strengths of each mode.
Combining modes appropriately makes it possible to use their respective strengths and improve the efficiency of the logistics chain.
It is wrong to say there is no link: efficient logistics can coordinate transport modes and contribute to more sustainable transport.
It is wrong to rule out a link: using alternative energy and fuels in vehicles can help reduce the environmental impact of transport.
It is wrong to say that trans-European networks have no influence: connections and intelligent systems on the network can support sustainable multimodal transport.
It is wrong to attribute optimization solely to the use of ships: maritime transport can be useful, but the choice depends on the needs and the combination of transport modes.
It is wrong to limit it exclusively to inland waterway transport: optimization can also use and combine road, rail and sea transport according to the route and the goods.
Logistics organizes the flow of goods in the supply chain, including transport, storage and distribution.
Logistics coordinates flows, vehicles and deliveries to make better use of resources and organize transport efficiently.
A logistics platform can consolidate goods and coordinate deliveries, reducing the number of trips needed and therefore traffic; the result depends on how it is organized.
The quiz marks this false on the understanding that logistics is not limited to particular goods. The statement is ambiguous, however: a logistics system can certainly also transfer specific goods.

The quiz marks this false because logistics comprises more than the physical distribution of goods: it also includes organization, inventory management and information. The word ‘only’, however, makes the statement ambiguous.

The quiz marks this false because logistics is not limited to physical transfer: it also includes storage and inventory management. The word ‘only’, however, may refer to the goods rather than the activities.
It is false that logistics platforms are necessarily inefficient when speed is required: they can coordinate collection, sorting and delivery, although the result depends on how they are organized.
It is wrong to rule out this function: a platform can also organize return flows, such as the collection of discarded packaging or products and their dispatch for recovery.
FALSO. Logistics platforms can integrate several services, such as storage, handling and distribution, offering a complete range; the actual services offered vary from one platform to another.

Galileo provides positioning signals that can be used to follow goods along their route through a tracking system. ‘At any point’ is not an absolute guarantee: reception and communications must be available.
It is false that Galileo measures the pressure of containers: the system provides positioning signals; a separate sensor is needed to measure pressure.
It is false that Galileo checks every vehicle parameter: it provides positioning and timing; other data require dedicated sensors or onboard systems.
It is false that Galileo cannot reduce costs: position information can help manage the fleet and optimize routes, although savings depend on how the system is used.
VERO. Compared with similar conventional vehicles, low-impact vehicles can have a higher initial price, which may be partly offset by lower running costs. This is not, however, true of every model.

VERO. Compared with similar conventional vehicles, hybrids can consume less fuel, partly thanks to energy recovery; electric vehicles consume no fuel on board. The result depends on the technology and how the vehicle is used.
FALSO. Road transport has a significant impact, and reducing its consumption can help reduce demand for oil. The percentage depends on the location, period and scope: 10% is not a universal figure.
