FALSO. High energy consumption is not an inherent characteristic of low-impact vehicles: electric propulsion, for example, is efficient. Actual consumption depends on the vehicle and how it is used.
FALSO. Low-impact vehicles are intended to reduce emissions: electric vehicles, for example, produce no tailpipe CO2 emissions. Overall emissions also depend on energy production.
ADR regulates the international carriage of dangerous goods by road, setting conditions for their transport and providing for specific exemptions.
ADR regulates the carriage of dangerous goods by road: these include fuels such as gasoline and diesel. Its application in practice also depends on any applicable exemptions.
Crude oil is a dangerous good covered by ADR. The application of individual requirements depends on the transport conditions and any applicable exemptions.

Controlled temperature and perishability do not in themselves make ADR applicable, as it concerns dangerous goods. ATP applies to certain perishable foods instead; goods may nevertheless be subject to ADR if they are also dangerous.

The exceptional nature of a work vehicle does not in itself make ADR applicable, as it concerns dangerous goods. ADR requirements may still apply if the transport includes goods classified as dangerous.

Being construction materials is not enough to make ADR applicable: what matters is whether the goods are classified as dangerous. Some products used in construction may nevertheless fall within its scope.
FALSO. ADR concerns the carriage of dangerous goods by road, not food as such. A food product falls under ADR only if it has characteristics that classify it as dangerous goods.
FALSO. ADR governs the carriage of dangerous goods by road; maritime transport is subject to separate rules.
VERO. Under ADR, a transport unit can be a truck on its own or a truck with a trailer attached.
VERO. A tractor with a semitrailer attached forms a combination consisting of a motor vehicle and a trailer, and therefore a transport unit.
FALSO. A container is an item intended to hold goods, not the transport unit: the latter is the motor vehicle on its own or the combination with a trailer attached.
FALSO. Under the ADR definition, a transport unit consists of a motor vehicle on its own or a motor vehicle with one trailer attached, not two.

FALSO according to the quiz. Note that the ADR definition of a transport unit also includes a motor vehicle without a trailer; read in this context, it can include a road tractor on its own. The official verdict is therefore ambiguous.
FALSO. A detached trailer or semitrailer does not by itself constitute a transport unit: a motor vehicle is needed, either on its own or with a trailer attached.
VERO. For ADR vehicles, the ABS requirement depends on the rules applicable to the type of vehicle and transport, its mass and the provisions linked to first registration.
ABS detects slipping and automatically adjusts braking to counter wheel lockup, helping the driver maintain directional control.

The quiz considers the requirement to apply to categories M2, M3, N2 and N3. However, the wording ‘all’ is absolute: the directive has a defined scope and specific exceptions, including ones based on the vehicle's characteristics or use.

The quiz considers the requirement to apply to trucks over 3.5 tonnes, which normally belong to categories N2 or N3. However, ‘all’ should be understood with caution: the rules have limits to their application and exceptions.
FALSO. The requirement does not apply only to the listed categories of motor vehicles: certain trailers must also be equipped with ABS.
It is incorrect to say that ABS is always optional: type-approval rules make it mandatory for certain categories of new vehicles.

It is not true that ABS is mandatory on every vehicle: the requirement depends on the category and the applicable rules. For example, a combined braking system is also permitted for some new motorcycles.
FALSO. For heavy vehicles, the requirement is not independent of the date: the rules provide for effective dates linked to registration and specific exceptions.

FALSO according to the quiz. N2 vehicles registered after 2006 are generally subject to the requirement, but ‘all’ is too absolute: the directive provides for exceptions, for example for certain emergency service vehicles.
FALSO. The registration date alone is not enough: the requirement depends on the vehicle's category and mass, as well as any applicable exceptions.
It is incorrect to consider the speed limiter merely recommended for N2 and N3: the rules also require it for these categories in cases that fall within their scope.
VERO. A vehicle with a bare platform, without a superstructure or sides, is an example of an open vehicle; a platform fitted with sides can also be one.
VERO. An open vehicle has a platform without a superstructure or fitted only with sides.
A flatbed fitted only with sideboards can constitute an open vehicle. Sideboards are not essential, however: the flatbed may also have no superstructure.

A load compartment with rigid walls and roof is an example of a closed vehicle. The ADR definition is broader: it requires a body that can be closed, without specifying here that all walls must be rigid.
VERO. A sheeted vehicle is an open vehicle, with or without sides, fitted with a sheet to protect the load.
A sheeted vehicle is an open vehicle fitted with a tarpaulin to protect the load.
VERO. A sheeted vehicle may have hoops that support the sheet protecting the load.
FALSO. The lack of insulation concerns the tank's insulation; an open vehicle, on the other hand, is defined by the open configuration of its platform.

The quiz distinguishes an open vehicle from a sheeted vehicle: the latter is an open vehicle fitted with a tarpaulin to protect the load. The statement is ambiguous if the tarpaulin is merely laid on the flatbed and is not used to cover the goods.
A van body encloses the load compartment; an open vehicle, by contrast, has a flatbed with no superstructure or fitted only with sideboards.
FALSO. Sides alone do not make a vehicle closed: a closed vehicle has a body that can be closed.
A platform covered by a sheet identifies a sheeted vehicle. A closed vehicle, on the other hand, has a body consisting of a box that can be closed.
Removable hoops and a sheet characterize a sheeted body; a closed vehicle has a box that can be closed.
Rigid walls and a rigid roof describe a closed compartment, not a sheeted vehicle. A sheeted vehicle is an open vehicle fitted with a tarpaulin to protect the goods.
A sheeted vehicle is not defined as a fireproofed battery vehicle: it is an open vehicle fitted with a sheet to protect the goods.
A sheeted vehicle is not a tank insulated with fabric: it is an open vehicle with a sheet that protects the goods.

The quiz refers to certification of the vehicle's suitability: an ADR certificate of approval is generally not required for ordinary packages. The statement does not remove the other ADR documents and obligations applicable to the transport.
For an ordinary goods vehicle carrying benzene in packages, no specific ADR suitability endorsement is required on the registration certificate; the transport requirements still apply.

An ADR suitability endorsement on the registration certificate is not generally required for every vehicle carrying dangerous goods in packages. Certain specific categories, however, require a certificate of approval.
The ATP certificate concerns vehicles for perishable foodstuffs; it does not certify suitability for carrying dangerous goods in packages.
The ADR certificate with a pink diagonal stripe is not required for every carriage of dangerous goods in packages: it applies to specific categories of vehicles.
For an ordinary goods vehicle carrying benzene in packages, that specific endorsement is not required on the registration certificate.
The specific endorsement is not required for an ordinary goods vehicle carrying benzene in packages, even simply because the transport is domestic.
For an ordinary goods vehicle carrying benzene in packages, no specific ADR suitability endorsement is required on the registration certificate.

Units subject to ADR requirements must have suitable fire extinguishers; their number and capacity depend on the transport conditions and the mass of the unit. Simplified provisions apply to certain quantities.
ADR requires safety equipment for the unit and crew members, selected with regard to the hazards of the goods and the applicable regime, among other factors.

Some motor vehicles carrying ADR goods in packages must have a speed limiter according to their category and the applicable rules; the requirement does not depend solely on the load being in packages.

ADR transport in packages does not impose an ABS requirement on every unit without distinction. Braking requirements depend on the type of vehicle and the applicable technical rules; ABS may be mandatory for some vehicles.
Not all units carrying ADR packages always require a special electrical system: construction requirements vary according to the type of vehicle and the goods carried.
It is incorrect to require a retarder on every unit carrying ADR packages regardless of mass: braking requirements depend on the type and characteristics of the vehicle.

The transport of an indivisible item that causes the dimensional limits to be exceeded falls under transport in exceptional conditions, subject to the conditions of Article 10; the prescribed authorization is required.
For a single truck, the standard length limit is 12 metres: an indivisible beam whose projection causes that limit to be exceeded makes the transport exceptional in size.

If the loaded beam causes the vehicle or vehicle combination to exceed its maximum permitted length, the load exceeds the dimensional limits and the transport may be considered exceptional. The conditions applicable to the load must be met and authorization obtained.
The beam is an indivisible load: if it projects beyond the front of the truck's outline, the transport is considered exceptional and requires the corresponding authorization.

Exceeding 11 metres does not automatically make the transport exceptional. For the overall length, what matters is the dimensional limit applicable to the vehicle and its configuration, as well as the rules on projecting loads.
The standard limit for a single truck is 12 metres, not 16.50. However, the statement is ambiguous: exceeding 16.50 metres also means exceeding 12 metres, so the transport is exceptional in any case.

A rear projection of 20% does not in itself make the transport exceptional: an indivisible load may project up to three tenths of the vehicle's length, provided the dimensional limits and other requirements are met.

A rear projection of 10% does not in itself make the transport exceptional: an indivisible load may project up to three tenths of the vehicle's length, provided the dimensional limits and other requirements are met.

A projection of one quarter alone does not automatically make the transport exceptional: an indivisible item may project at the rear by up to three tenths, provided the dimensional limits are also respected.

In the ordinary case of a change to the vehicle's characteristics, the modification requires an inspection and test to update the documents; the regulations provide exceptions for specific modifications.
ATP refers to the international agreement on the transport of perishable foodstuffs and the special equipment used to transport them.

The quiz considers a simple notification insufficient: a change to the vehicle's characteristics normally requires an inspection and test. The wording is imprecise because it does not expressly say that notification is the only formality.
It is incorrect to rule out an inspection and test: one is normally required for a change to the vehicle's characteristics, subject to the exceptions provided for.
The fact that the vehicle is already in use does not eliminate the formalities: a change to its characteristics normally requires an inspection and test and an update to the documents.
ATP does not mean an authorisation for agricultural products: it is the international agreement on perishable foodstuffs and special transport equipment.
ATP concerns perishable foodstuffs; the agreement on the road transport of dangerous goods is ADR.
ATP is not an authorisation for petroleum products: it is the international agreement on perishable foodstuffs and special transport equipment.
Quick-frozen products are among the foodstuffs for which the ATP sets temperature conditions and vehicle requirements when the transport falls within the scope of the agreement.
The ATP applies to certain perishable foodstuffs and to transport governed by the agreement: it does not require an ATP-compliant vehicle for every food product.
Even for non-perishable food, the load compartment must meet hygiene requirements, for example by being clean and kept in good condition to prevent contamination.
It is not true that there are no requirements: even for non-perishable food, the load compartment must be clean and in good condition to protect the food from contamination.
Not all food requires an ATP-compliant vehicle: the agreement governs certain perishable foodstuffs, while the fact that a non-perishable product is food does not by itself trigger this requirement.
Dangerous goods do not fall under the ATP simply because they are dangerous: the agreement concerns the transport of certain perishable foodstuffs. Dangerous goods are governed by separate rules.
False: special waste does not fall under ATP as such. The agreement concerns the transport of certain perishable foodstuffs.
False: metallurgical waste is not perishable food; ATP regulates the transport of certain foodstuffs.
False: not all food requires an ATP vehicle. The requirements concern certain perishable foodstuffs and the conditions specified for their transport.
False: ATP-compliant vehicles are required for certain perishable foodstuffs in the cases specified; it is not true that they are never needed.
False: ATP compliance may also be required for domestic transport of perishable foodstuffs, not just international transport.
True: ATP regulates the transport of certain perishable foodstuffs and the special equipment to be used.
True: the competent authority issues a certificate of conformity for a vehicle that complies with ATP standards.
True: during certain operations, such as defrosting, a brief increase of up to 3 °C is permitted on the surface of products in part of the load.
False: ATP concerns certain perishable foodstuffs and the equipment used to transport them; dangerous goods are not its subject.
False: ATP concerns certain perishable foodstuffs, not the transport of waste as a category.
False: ATP concerns certain perishable foodstuffs, not goods identified by their risk of contaminating water.
False: bodies used for foodstuffs under ATP are classified according to ATP categories, not ADR.

False according to the quiz: ATP compliance is certified by the certificate or the corresponding ATP plate; the VIN identifies the vehicle. The wording is ambiguous because the presence of a VIN on the vehicle does not rule out ATP certification.
False: ATP vehicles are not exclusively mechanically refrigerated; other categories are also provided for, including insulated, refrigerated and heated vehicles.
False: for the operations specified, the maximum permitted brief increase on the surface of part of the load is 3 °C, not 4 °C.
False according to the quiz: the specified threshold is 3 °C, not 2 °C. The statement is ambiguous when read literally: an increase of 2 °C still falls within the 3 °C limit.
False according to the quiz: the specified threshold is 3 °C, not 1 °C. The statement is ambiguous when read literally: an increase of 1 °C still falls within the 3 °C limit.
The stated limit is a maximum temperature for the foodstuff: it must be respected at every point in the load, subject to the tolerances provided for by the ATP for particular operations.
This is not a minimum temperature below which the foodstuff cannot fall: the stated value is the maximum limit to be respected at every point in the load, subject to the permitted tolerances.

The limit does not apply only to the central area: it must be respected at every point in the load, subject to the permitted tolerances. The statement is ambiguous because the centre is also included; the FALSO verdict should be understood as rejecting a check limited to the centre.

The limit does not apply only to the side area: it must be respected at every point in the load, subject to the permitted tolerances. The statement is ambiguous because the side is also included; the FALSO verdict should be understood as rejecting a check limited to the side.
True: the choice and combination of available modes affect the network's costs, times and organisation.
The type of transport matters because different goods and services require suitable vehicles, personnel and procedures.
False: there is no predominantly road-based choice that works for every network. Optimisation requires evaluating and combining the available modes according to the service.
False: inland waterway transport is not always the mode to favour. Optimisation depends on the combination of available modes and the needs of the service.
False: maritime transport is not always the mode to favour. Optimisation depends on the combination of available modes and the needs of the service.
It is false to exclude the economic decision-maker: both the party that assumes rights and obligations and the party that directs the company's economic decisions matter.
It is false to exclude the legal entity: both the party that directs economic decisions and the party that assumes the company's rights and obligations matter.
The organizational structure matters: assigning tasks, responsibilities and resources makes it possible to coordinate transport.
To carry goods by road for third parties, the business must be registered in the road haulage register, subject to the conditions laid down by law.

Professional carriage of goods using category C vehicles requires driver qualification and periodic training. VERO expresses the general rule: the law also provides for specific exemptions and different ways of certifying the qualification.

Being employed by a business registered in the road haulage register does not exempt a driver from driving and rest time rules: these apply to transport covered by the regulation, subject to the specific exceptions provided for.

The legal form affects the configuration of the business: for example, the activity may be carried out by an individual or a company, with different organizational structures and responsibilities. The question does not specify which configurations it means.
False. The legal form does not depend solely on the type of transport: the organisational choice may also take account of the size and needs of the business.
True. In the context of the quiz, carriers are normally private businesses that offer transport services; the wording indicates a general rule, not an exclusive one.
True. A carrier undertakes transport on behalf of a customer: in road haulage for third parties, it provides the service as part of its business activity.
True. A carrier may operate as a sole trader or as a company and may vary in size according to its organisation.
True. A joint-stock company may operate as a road carrier, provided it meets the requirements for the activity.
True. In road haulage of goods for third parties, the carrier provides the transport service for payment.
True. In subcontracted carriage, the appointed carrier entrusts the performance of the transport to another carrier under a further contract.
False. For businesses subject to European rules, at least one vehicle must be available after authorisation; however, it need not be owned, and a large fleet is not required.
False. A carrier does not always have to be a corporation: the activity may also be carried out by an individual or other eligible entities.
False. A limited liability company may also carry out road haulage if it meets the requirements for the activity.
False. As used in the quiz, a carrier provides transport for third parties; own-account transport is carried out for the needs of one's own business, subject to legal conditions.
True. The freight forwarder organises the shipment for the principal and concludes the transport contract with the carrier, thus acting as an intermediary.
True. A freight forwarder may also undertake to perform the transport: in that case, they are a forwarding carrier and assume the carrier's rights and obligations.

True according to the historical quiz. The provision is outdated: the register of freight forwarders has been abolished, and the activity is now subject to SCIA and the formalities with the Business Register.
True. The freight forwarder receives the assignment specified in the forwarding contract from the principal and acts on their behalf.
True. Under the forwarding contract, the freight forwarder undertakes to conclude the transport contract in their own name and on behalf of the principal.
VERO. A freight forwarding contract is a form of agency: the freight forwarder acts on behalf of the principal to arrange transport.
FALSO. The freight forwarder arranges the shipment and may be distinct from the carrier; they are the same only when the forwarder also undertakes to carry out the transport.
FALSO according to the quiz, but the statement is ambiguous. The freight forwarder accounts to the principal; if the sender is also the principal, the forwarder accounts to the sender.
FALSO. The freight forwarder is the agent: the forwarder concludes the freight forwarding contract with the principal, who assigns the task.
FALSO as a general rule. The freight forwarder has the carrier's rights and obligations only if the forwarder also undertakes to carry out the transport.
FALSO. Freight forwarding as such does not require registration in the drivers' register: it is subject to the rules and formalities specific to freight forwarding.

FALSO. Freight forwarding alone does not require registration in the road haulage operators' register, which is required for those who transport goods by road for third parties; registration may be necessary if the forwarder also carries out that activity.

FALSO according to the historical quiz, which referred to the obligation to register in the list. The list has since been abolished: the SCIA and the formalities with the Business Register still apply.
FALSO. The freight forwarder concludes the freight forwarding contract with the principal, who entrusts the forwarder with arranging the transport.
It is false that the freight forwarder never asks for payment: remuneration is due for carrying out the assignment.
Vehicles serving people with limited or impaired mobility are among the exceptions to the ban on traffic in a pedestrian area, subject to any further restrictions indicated by signs.
Vehicles on emergency duty are allowed to travel in the pedestrian area.

The supplementary panel may indicate exemptions for certain categories of vehicles. However, the word ‘only’ in the question should be read with caution: the law also provides for exceptions, such as emergency vehicles, and possible local restrictions.
Vehicles serving people with limited mobility are among those allowed in a pedestrian area, subject to any further restrictions indicated by signs.

There is no parking ban extending 15 metres before and after the boundaries of a pedestrian area. The 15-metre distance instead applies to a public transport stop sign where the stop is not marked out.
A pedestrian area is not normally intended for buses: vehicles are prohibited, with exceptions including bicycles, and further restrictions may be indicated by signs.
It is false that a pedestrian area is identified by curbs painted black and white: its beginning and end are indicated by the appropriate signs.
A pedestrian area does not exclude pedestrians: it restricts vehicle traffic, subject to the specified exceptions. It is not defined by a yellow and black kerb.
The prohibition does not always apply to bicycles: cycles are allowed, subject to any additional municipal restrictions indicated by signs.
A pedestrian crossing is a part of the carriageway marked and arranged for pedestrians to cross.
A pedestrian crossing is part of the carriageway, where it is designated for pedestrians to cross.
The crossing is on the carriageway used by vehicles; pedestrians crossing have priority there, subject to traffic control.
Pedestrian crossings can also be found outside built-up areas, on roads where they are permitted.
It is false that pedestrians do not have priority: at a crossing, drivers must give way to pedestrians, subject to traffic control by officers or traffic lights.
It is false that the crossing prohibits passage: it allows pedestrians to cross the carriageway from one side to the other.
Traffic includes the movement, stopping and parking of pedestrians, vehicles and animals on the road.
The movement of pedestrians on the road falls within the definition of traffic.
A road is defined as an area for public use intended for the movement of pedestrians, vehicles and animals.
It is false that traffic concerns only motor vehicles: it includes pedestrians, vehicles and animals, even when they stop or remain stationary.
It is false that traffic concerns only pedestrians: it also includes the movement, stopping and parking of vehicles and animals.
It is false that traffic concerns only vehicles: it also includes the movement, stopping and remaining stationary of pedestrians and animals.
A lane is a longitudinal part of the road, running along its length.
A lane is wide enough for a single line of vehicles to travel along it.
A lane is a longitudinal part of the road suitable for a single line of vehicles.
A specialized lane is intended for specific maneuvers, such as turning or overtaking.
A reserved lane may be designated for the exclusive use of one or more categories of vehicles.
A lane may be reserved for buses in public service, excluding other unauthorized categories.
It is false that a lane is reserved only for motor vehicles: other vehicles, such as bicycles, may also use it, according to the signs.
It is false that a lane runs across the road: it runs lengthwise along it.
An acceleration lane makes it easier for vehicles to enter the carriageway.
It is a specialized lane because it is intended for the maneuver of entering the carriageway.
Overtaking is prohibited in an acceleration lane; on motorways and major roads outside built-up areas, parking is also prohibited except in an emergency.
It is a specialized lane for entering the carriageway, and overtaking is prohibited in it.
It is a specialized lane for entering; on motorways and major roads outside built-up areas, stopping in it is prohibited except in an emergency.
It is not used to exit: the acceleration lane makes it easier to enter the carriageway; the deceleration lane is used to exit.
A reserved lane is characterized by being set aside for certain categories of vehicles. An acceleration lane is intended for the maneuver of entering.
It is not intended for overtaking: it is used to enter the carriageway, and overtaking in it is prohibited.
A deceleration lane allows those exiting to slow down outside the main traffic flow, without slowing vehicles continuing onward.
It is a specialized lane intended for vehicles preparing to leave the carriageway.
Overtaking is prohibited in a deceleration lane; on motorways and major roads outside built-up areas, parking is also prohibited except in an emergency.
It is a specialized lane for leaving the carriageway, and overtaking is prohibited in it.
It is a specialized lane for exiting; on motorways and major roads outside built-up areas, stopping in it is prohibited except in an emergency.
It makes it easier to leave the carriageway, not to enter it. An acceleration lane is used to enter.
A reserved lane is characterized by being set aside for certain categories. A deceleration lane is intended for the maneuver of exiting.
It is not intended for broken-down vehicles: the deceleration lane is used to leave the carriageway; the emergency lane is intended for emergency stops.
The carriageway consists of one or more traffic lanes, so the lane is part of it.
A traffic lane is normally bounded by road markings, but those markings are not necessarily always present.
A traffic lane is intended for the movement of vehicles. VERO should be understood in general terms: prohibitions or restrictions may exclude certain categories, even if they are motor vehicles.
A lane is wide enough for a single line of vehicles to pass.
A traffic lane is part of the carriageway intended for moving traffic; a deceleration lane facilitates leaving it.
A traffic lane is part of the carriageway; an acceleration lane facilitates entering it.
It is not intended only for pedestrians: a traffic lane is part of the carriageway, which is intended for the movement of vehicles.
A traffic lane is not necessarily reserved: it is reserved when it is intended exclusively for one or more categories of vehicles. A reserved lane is nevertheless a type of traffic lane.
It is not always bounded by solid lines: the markings may be broken, and boundaries are normally provided but are not necessarily always present.
A reserved lane is a traffic lane intended exclusively for vehicles in the indicated categories.
When it is not protected by raised elements, a reserved lane is separated from the other lanes by a yellow line alongside a white one.
A reserved lane is intended for one or more categories of vehicles, which may include buses in public service.
The boundary includes a yellow longitudinal line alongside a white one. This rule applies when the lane is not protected by raised elements.
An acceleration lane facilitates entry onto the carriageway. A reserved lane, by contrast, is intended for specific categories of vehicles.
A deceleration lane facilitates exit from the carriageway. A reserved lane is intended for specific categories of vehicles.
A reserved lane is intended for certain categories of vehicles; a lane intended for overtaking is a lane specialized for a maneuver.
Taxis may use the bus lane when they are among the categories authorized by the signs.
Buses in public service may use lanes reserved for them, according to the categories and any conditions indicated by signs.
A reserved lane may be separated from other lanes by two solid lines side by side: the yellow line is on the reserved lane side.
A short duration does not authorize all vehicles to park in the bus lane: the lane is reserved for the permitted categories.
Not all buses are automatically allowed: the lane is reserved for the categories indicated by signs, for example public service buses.
A reserved lane does not permit driving at high speed: the driver must obey speed limits and adjust speed to road and traffic conditions.

The quiz indicates FALSO because a bus lane is not automatically open to bicycles. Today, however, the municipality may authorize bicycles to use such lanes under the prescribed conditions, so the prohibition is not absolute.
A specialized lane is intended for vehicles performing particular maneuvers or traveling at low speed.
A specialized lane is intended for vehicles. The statement is general: the precise definition concerns particular maneuvers or slow-moving vehicles.
Acceleration and overtaking are both maneuvers for which a specialized lane may be provided.
Turning is one of the maneuvers for which a specialized lane may be provided.
Acceleration and deceleration lanes are both specialized lanes: they are used to enter and leave the carriageway, respectively.
An acceleration lane helps vehicles merge onto the motorway carriageway.
A deceleration lane allows vehicles to leave the motorway carriageway without slowing vehicles continuing ahead.
A specialized lane does not always grant right of way: it is intended for particular maneuvers or slow-moving vehicles. Right of way depends on the rules applicable to the situation.
A specialized lane is intended for vehicles performing certain maneuvers or traveling slowly, not for pedestrian traffic.
A specialized lane is not limited to public vehicles: it is intended for vehicles based on their maneuver or low speed.
A deceleration lane is used to leave the motorway; an acceleration lane is used to merge onto the carriageway.
An acceleration lane is used to enter the motorway; a deceleration lane is used to leave the carriageway.
A bus bay is a part of the road outside the carriageway, intended for scheduled public transport vehicles to stop.
A bus bay is outside the carriageway, serves scheduled public transport stops and is next to the pavement or a pedestrian waiting area.
A bus bay is an area outside the carriageway intended for scheduled public transport vehicles to stop.
A bus bay is outside the carriageway and is intended for scheduled public transport vehicles to stop.
The stopping area for scheduled public transport is marked by yellow lines; in a bus bay, the transverse lines may be omitted.
It is incorrect to say that the bus bay is within the carriageway: it is outside it, next to the pavement or a waiting area.
The wording is too general: the bay is not intended for vehicles of all kinds to stop, but for scheduled public transport vehicles.
A bus bay is not limited to roads outside built-up areas: its definition concerns the space for scheduled services to stop and does not require that location.
The bay is not a general parking area: it is intended for scheduled public transport vehicles to stop and serve passengers.
The bay is not a shelter for buses: it is a space outside the carriageway intended for scheduled public transport vehicles to stop.
The sidewalk is the part of the road intended for pedestrians.
The sidewalk is outside the carriageway and is raised or otherwise marked off and protected for pedestrians.
Parking on the sidewalk is prohibited unless signs indicate otherwise, so it is permitted in specifically marked spaces.

The verdict is VERO in the sense that the sidewalk is intended for pedestrians, not for vehicles to travel along. The phrase ‘any vehicle’ is absolute, however: it does not rule out, for example, crossing the sidewalk to access a driveway.
The curb may have alternating yellow and black segments, indicating a stretch where parking is prohibited.
The function attributed to the sidewalk is incorrect: it is intended for pedestrians, not to help vehicles leave the carriageway.
It is incorrect to say that the sidewalk is intended for vehicle parking: it is intended for pedestrians.
Leaving space for pedestrians is not enough: parking on the sidewalk is prohibited unless signs indicate otherwise.
A parking area is intended for vehicle parking, which may or may not be regulated.
A parking area is an area or facility outside the carriageway intended for vehicle parking.
A parking area may be reserved for particular vehicles: the relevant signs must be observed.
It is incorrect to say that a parking area is intended for pedestrians: it is intended for vehicle parking.
It is incorrect to say that a parking area is intended for exclusive circulation: it is used for vehicle parking.
The definition limited to motorhomes and a fixed period is incorrect: a parking area is intended for vehicle parking, whether regulated or not.
A park-and-ride facility is located near local public transport or railway stations or stops to make it easier to change modes of transport.
A park-and-ride facility makes it easier to transfer from a parked vehicle to public transport: this is intermodality.

The verdict is VERO because transferring to public transport can reduce traffic heading into the city. ‘Prevents’ should be understood as contributing to limiting congestion, not as a guarantee of eliminating it.
The claim that it is intended for pedestrians is false: it is a car park for vehicles, located near public transport to make transfers easier.
It is false that it does not facilitate intermodal travel: a park-and-ride facility is specifically designed to make changing modes of transport easier.
The claim that it is exclusively for cycles is false: a park-and-ride facility makes transfers to public transport easier and is not defined as reserved only for bicycles.
A pedestrian walkway is separated from the carriageway by a continuous white line or a parallel barrier.
A pedestrian walkway is intended for pedestrian traffic.
Where there is no sidewalk, the pedestrian walkway serves the same function.
In the absence of a sidewalk, the pedestrian walkway serves the same function.
The claim that it serves intermodal travel is false: a pedestrian walkway is for pedestrian traffic and takes the place of a sidewalk where there is none.
A pedestrian walkway is intended for pedestrian traffic, not for vehicles to park.
A driveway is an entrance to an adjoining area suitable for parking vehicles.
Parking is prohibited at the entrance to a driveway; stopping is not prohibited for that reason alone, provided no other prohibition applies.
A driveway provides access to an adjoining area for vehicles, and parking in front of its entrance is prohibited.
A driveway is not intended for pedestrian traffic: it is an entrance to an adjoining area suitable for parking vehicles.
A driveway is not a parking space: it is an entrance to an adjoining area where vehicles can park.
A driveway is not a parking area, regulated or otherwise: it is an entrance to an adjoining area suitable for parking vehicles.
A lay-by is a marked-off part of the road intended for parking vehicles.
A lay-by is a part of the road adjacent to the outer edge of the shoulder.
Special road signs give advance notice of the lay-by, allowing it to be identified ahead of time.
A lay-by is not intended for pedestrian traffic, but for parking vehicles.
Motorway lay-bys do not have intermodal travel as their specific function: they are spaces intended for parking vehicles.
A lay-by is not a space intended specifically for scheduled bus passengers: it is used for parking vehicles.
A pedestrian refuge offers pedestrians a protected space to shelter and wait near crossings or public transport stops.
A pedestrian refuge is a part of the road that is raised or marked off and protected, intended for pedestrians.
At a stop, a pedestrian refuge protects pedestrians and makes it easier for bus passengers to board and get off.
At a stop, a pedestrian refuge protects pedestrians and makes it easier for trolleybus passengers to board and get off.
A pedestrian refuge may be located near a pedestrian crossing and provide shelter for pedestrians.
A pedestrian refuge is a protected space intended for pedestrians to shelter and wait.
A pedestrian refuge is not intended for parking vehicles, but for pedestrians to shelter and wait.
A pedestrian refuge is not reserved for tram traffic: it is a protected space for pedestrians. The tramway, on the other hand, is intended for trams.
Flashing red lights are not the marking that defines a pedestrian refuge: it is a protected space where pedestrians can shelter and wait.
A pedestrian refuge is not an officer: it is a protected part of the road intended for pedestrians to shelter and wait.
Buses do not travel on the pedestrian refuge: it is a protected space intended for pedestrians, including near public transport stops.
The road area is the surface within the road boundaries and includes the carriageway and the adjoining strips of land.
The road area is the surface within the road boundaries and includes both the carriageway and the adjoining strips of land.
A bus bay is part of the road, outside the carriageway, and forms part of the road area within its boundaries.
The reservation for trams and similar vehicles applies to the tramway; the road area, on the other hand, includes the entire surface within the road boundaries.
Separating streams of traffic is the function of a traffic divider. The road area, on the other hand, is the entire surface within the road boundaries.
A bus bay is part of the road and therefore of the road area, even though it is outside the carriageway.
The tramway is the part of the road reserved for trams and similar vehicles.
The tramway is a part of the road that runs lengthwise and is suitably marked off for trams and similar vehicles.
The tramway may have its own track, separated from the area used by vehicles, or a shared track.
The tramway is a longitudinal part of the road intended for trams and similar vehicles.
In a shared tramway, the tracks are embedded in the carriageway, which is shared with other permitted vehicles.
The tramway is for trams and similar vehicles; sheltering pedestrians and providing a place for them to wait are functions of a pedestrian refuge.
The tramway is intended for trams and similar vehicles. Separating traffic flows is the function of a traffic divider.
Buses cannot always use it: the tramway is reserved for trams and similar vehicles; any rules applying to the section must be followed.
A dedicated tramway is reserved for trams; the legal definition also includes similar vehicles.
A dedicated tramway is reserved for tram traffic: other vehicles cannot occupy it to stop or park.
A dedicated tramway is reserved for trams and similar vehicles, so ordinary road vehicles cannot travel on it.
A dedicated tramway is marked off and reserved for trams and similar vehicles; ordinary rubber-tyred vehicles cannot travel on it.
It is not enough to avoid obstructing the tram: a dedicated tramway is reserved for tram traffic, not for other vehicles to park.
A dedicated tramway is appropriately marked off, but not necessarily by road signs: these may accompany the boundary without forming it.
Even if the tracks were flush with the road, a dedicated tramway remains reserved for tram traffic; sharing is a feature of a shared tramway.
A dedicated tramway is not open to ordinary road vehicles: it is reserved for trams and similar vehicles.
A shared tramway is open to other vehicles, but stopping and parking are prohibited on the tracks and close enough to obstruct the tram.
On a shared tramway, the tracks are embedded in the carriageway and traffic shares it with other permitted vehicles.
On a shared tramway, the tracks are flush with the carriageway, which may also be used by other permitted vehicles.
Buses may use the shared tramway because it is shared with other vehicles, subject to any local restrictions.
Not obstructing the tram is not enough: parking on the tracks is prohibited even when the vehicle does not obstruct its movement.
A shared tramway is identified by the tracks embedded in the carriageway; it is not necessarily marked by specific road signs.
A shared tramway is shared with other permitted vehicles: it is not reserved exclusively for trams.
Flashing yellow bollards do not identify a shared tramway, which can be recognised by the tracks embedded in the carriageway.
A traffic divider is a longitudinal part of the road that is not intended for vehicles to travel on.
A traffic divider separates streams of vehicles and is a part of the road that is not intended for driving on.
A traffic divider separates streams of vehicles and is a part of the road that is not intended for driving on: it is not intended for parking vehicles.
A traffic divider separates streams of vehicles; providing shelter and a place for pedestrians to wait are instead functions of a pedestrian refuge.
A traffic divider is not intended for pedestrians: it separates streams of vehicle traffic.
A traffic divider is an area not intended for driving on, designed to separate streams of vehicles: stopping there is not allowed.
In a limited traffic zone (ZTL), access and circulation may be restricted to certain categories of users or vehicles, according to the permits provided for.
A ZTL is not necessarily reserved solely for public transport vehicles: other authorised categories may also enter. This does not rule out public transport vehicles using it.
In a ZTL, vehicle access and circulation may be restricted to certain hours or to particular categories of users and vehicles.
A ZTL is identified by signs marking its beginning and end; any access conditions are shown on the signs.
A ZTL does not necessarily coincide with the city centre: it is an area designated by the competent authority where specific traffic restrictions apply.
A ZTL restricts vehicle access and circulation; this does not mean that pedestrians are excluded.
A ZTL does not exclude every vehicle: circulation is restricted at certain times or to certain categories, according to the rules indicated.
A ZTL is not necessarily reserved for pedestrians and bicycles: vehicles permitted under local rules may also use it.
Well-designed stops and bus stations organise vehicle manoeuvres and passenger access, promoting safety and service efficiency. The economic benefits, however, depend on their design and use.
Stop infrastructure can serve different categories of public transport, such as buses, trolleybuses and trams, depending on the intended use of the space.
Well-organised stops and bus stations can make service operations more regular and reduce delays, helping vehicles keep to schedule; the result depends on local conditions.
It is not true that these facilities necessarily increase environmental impact: better organisation can reduce delays and consumption, although the effect depends on the design and the service.
It is incorrect to say that they offer no benefits: stops and bus stations organise access to services and transfers, making it easier for people to travel.
Reserved lanes reduce interference from general traffic and can make journey times more consistent, helping vehicles keep to schedule. They do not guarantee this in every situation.
A reserved lane can reduce queues and stops, potentially saving fuel and lowering emissions from combustion-engine vehicles. The effect depends on operating conditions; trolleybuses use electricity.
A reserved route can make a journey smoother and more comfortable by reducing interference from traffic; the benefit also depends on the quality of the route and the vehicle.
Smoother travel can reduce stops and restarts and therefore wear on components such as brakes. The actual savings depend on operating conditions.
A reserved lane does not in itself create greater risks: by separating public transport vehicles from some traffic, it can reduce interference. Safety nevertheless depends on design and management.
A bus bay is outside the carriageway and is intended for scheduled public transport vehicles to stop.
The stopping area includes space to pull in and space to rejoin traffic, as well as the central section where the vehicle stops.
The bay helps traffic flow because it allows a scheduled service vehicle to stop outside the carriageway, leaving more of it clear.
False. The bay is outside the carriageway and reserved for scheduled public transport vehicles to stop.
False. The bay is intended for scheduled public transport vehicles to stop, not for other vehicles to park.
False. The bay allows vehicles to stop outside the carriageway, reducing obstruction to traffic while they are stopped.
A scheduled public transport stop is normally identified by yellow lines marking the space reserved for vehicles.
The stop is also marked by the appropriate road sign, making its location recognisable.
The word BUS is normally painted in yellow on the road surface in the stop area, identifying the space intended for the service.
The prescribed marking is yellow, not white.
The prescribed marking is yellow, not blue.
The area is normally marked by yellow lines; kerbs are not the boundary prescribed by the road markings.
True. The stop is indicated by the prescribed vertical signs, such as a stop pole or stop sign.
Private vehicles may pass through the stop area on the carriageway, obeying the signs and without obstructing the service. This answer does not authorise them to use any reserved lanes.
The rule prohibits parking in spaces reserved for buses; a brief stop remains possible if there are no other prohibitions and no obstruction is caused.
True. The beginning and end of the stopping area, intended for pulling in and rejoining traffic, may be marked with yellow zigzags.
True. A stop may be near spaces for other transport services, making transfers easier; each space retains its intended use.
True. The stop is the place designated for passengers to board and alight, and where they access the service.
When several routes serve the same stop area, passengers can get off one vehicle and continue on another, making transfers easier.
False. A stop may occupy part of the carriageway: other vehicles may pass through if they obey the signs and do not obstruct the service.
It is not true that they are always absent: the lines prescribed to mark the stop are yellow.
False. The ban applies to parking; a brief stop may be allowed if it causes no obstruction and no other applicable prohibitions are in force.
The rule is the reverse: parking is prohibited in the stop area; a brief stop may be permitted if there are no other prohibitions and no obstruction is caused.
False. A shelter may be provided, but it is not required at every stop; the appropriate vertical sign is required.
These areas are intended for scheduled public transport vehicles to stop so passengers can board and alight.
There may be a pedestrian refuge, which provides pedestrians with a protected space near the stop.
They are not structures closed to the public: they are places intended for passengers waiting for, boarding or alighting from vehicles.
The claim that it is never marked is incorrect: the stop may also be identified by a stop pole or a road sign.
True. The service operator installs the vertical sign after reaching an agreement with the road-owning authority.
True. The BUS STOP sign is provided for interurban bus services; the TRAM STOP sign indicates tram stops.
True. The stop sign may display information about routes and any timetables.
False. The sign is installed by the service operator after reaching an agreement with the road-owning authority.
False. The stop is indicated by the appropriate vertical sign, not by a general danger sign.
False. The stop is indicated by the appropriate vertical sign, not by a flashing yellow light.
The lines marking the stop, when painted, are yellow.
The official answer is true, but zigzag markings are not mandatory: they can highlight the two manoeuvring areas on either side, before and after the central area.
The word BUS is prescribed on the road surface within the marked stop area.
The central area must be at least as long as the longest vehicle that stops there, plus 2 metres.
The two end sections of the stop area are each 12 metres long; the central section lies between them.
The two end sections are used respectively for the bus to pull in and rejoin traffic.
The prescribed lines are yellow, not blue.
The prescribed longitudinal line is broken, but it is yellow, not light blue.
The 12 metres refers to each of the two end sections. The central section must instead be at least as long as the longest vehicle, plus 2 metres.
The zigzag marking is not always present: it may be painted in the two end sections of the stop.
The prescribed marking inside the area is BUS, not AUTOBUS.
Parking in the stop area is prohibited: suspension of the service alone does not automatically turn it into a parking area.
Being five metres from the sign is not enough to make parking legal in the marked area, where it is prohibited. If the area is not marked, the prohibition applies within 15 metres of the sign.
The prescribed minimum distance between stops on opposite sides is 50 metres.
Thirty metres is not enough: the prescribed minimum is 50 metres.
Forty metres is not enough: the prescribed minimum is 50 metres.
The quiz marks this FALSO because the prescribed minimum is 50 metres, not 70. The wording is ambiguous: a distance of at least 70 metres still meets the legal minimum.
An integrated network connects and coordinates several transport systems or services, making it easier to travel between them.

The quiz considers it VERO that a journey on an integrated network often involves changing vehicles. The actual frequency depends on the route, however: integration does not make a transfer necessary on every journey.
By connecting and coordinating services, an integrated network aims to make public transport more effective.
It is not true that the network excludes transfers: it connects services, including different types, and allows passengers to move from one to another.
It is not true that transfers never occur: a journey may require changing from one vehicle to another.
There do not always have to be exactly two systems: an integrated network can connect more than two.
A bus station is a hub where passengers, with their luggage, can board, alight and continue their journey.
The functional layout of a bus station distinguishes the forecourt, passenger areas and vehicle areas; the actual facilities vary from one station to another.
The forecourt allows buses and, when permitted, service vehicles to circulate.
A bus station is a dedicated facility off the roadway, organised for buses and passengers.
A bus station brings together spaces and services for the arrival, departure and transfer of passengers with their luggage.
A bus station has spaces for buses to stop or park and for passengers to wait.
When connected to other modes of transport, a bus station can make it easier for passengers to transfer between them.
It does not consist only of a forecourt: it can also have spaces and services for passengers and vehicles.
It is not used solely for the transfer of goods: it is primarily intended for passengers and their luggage.
The function of a bus station is to organise bus services and passenger access, not simply to provide parking for cars. It may nevertheless include car parks.

The quiz considers it FALSO to reduce a bus station to a simple parking area: it is a complex serving buses and passengers. The statement is ambiguous because urban or suburban routes may also serve it.
They do not have to be located inside a railway station: they are separate facilities that may be connected to one for transfers.
It is false that a ticket office is prohibited: a bus station may include one among its passenger services.
It is false that the law prohibits workshops in bus stations: there may be spaces for vehicle maintenance and repair.
They are not dedicated exclusively to vehicle storage and maintenance: they also serve bus circulation and the reception and transfer of passengers.
In this layout, the building occupies one side of the forecourt and the platforms run parallel to that side.
The quiz considers the number of platforms unlimited in the sense that the layout does not impose a fixed maximum. In an actual station, however, the number is still limited by the available space.
In the quiz's layout, placing the building on one side with parallel platforms represents a compromise between bus and passenger circulation.

The quiz marks this false because it means that the layout does not impose a fixed maximum number of platforms. The wording is ambiguous: an individual bus station can naturally have a limited number of them.
The U shape is incorrect: in the layout described, the building is on one side of the forecourt, with platforms parallel to that side.
It is not true that the number is always very limited: the layout allows multiple platforms and sets no maximum of its own.
True. Buses operate in the station forecourt, and passengers move through the designated spaces and along the designated routes.
True. Moving buses and passengers may cross paths: the designated routes and signs must be followed.
True. Use of the forecourt is governed by the bus station regulations, which regulate movement and safety.
False. The forecourt is not reserved exclusively for passengers: buses also drive and park there.
False. Passengers also use the forecourt, following the designated pedestrian routes.
False. Buses and passengers may cross paths as they move; this is why routes and signs must be followed.
True. The prescribed ordinary maximum length for a two-axle bus is 13.50 m.
Buses and trolleybuses on scheduled urban and suburban public services following predetermined routes may be up to 4.30 m high.
True. The prescribed ordinary maximum width for buses is 2.55 m.
True. For a bus with more than two axles, including a three-axle bus, the prescribed ordinary maximum length is 15 m.
The stated limit is not the prescribed one: for these services, the maximum permitted height is 4.30 m. A bus that is 4.20 m high can still be within the limit.
The figure of 12 m is not the specific maximum limit: the directive provides for 13.50 m for a two-axle bus. A bus that is 12 m long can still be within the limit.
The standard maximum width is 2.55 m, not 2.60 m; movable rear-view mirrors are excluded from the measurement.
The brake lights are incorrect: the hazard warning signal makes all the direction indicators flash simultaneously.
The manoeuvrability test requires the bus to be able to travel within the annular space bounded by an outer radius of 12.50 m and an inner radius of 5.30 m.
When cornering, the part of the body beyond the rear axle may swing outward: this widening must be taken into account when manoeuvring.
Overhangs are the parts that extend beyond the axles: their length changes the space occupied by the ends of the bus during manoeuvres.
It is incorrect to say they can never fit: buses must be able to manoeuvre within the specified annular space, with an outer radius of 12.50 m and an inner radius of 5.30 m.
It is incorrect to rule out the widening: when cornering, the rear overhang of the body may swing outward from the path.
A long wheelbase increases off-tracking: when turning, the rear wheels follow a path further inward than the front wheels.
If the driver does not account for the wheelbase, they may take the turn without leaving enough room for the rear wheels' more inward path.
A long wheelbase increases the difference between the paths of the axles and therefore the amount of off-tracking in a turn.
Scraping against the road surface is a different phenomenon: off-tracking results from the rear wheels following a more inward path when turning.
The rear overhang can cause the tail to swing outward; inward off-tracking, on the other hand, depends on the paths of the axles and the wheelbase.
Low ground clearance concerns the risk of contact with the road surface, not off-tracking in a turn, which is related to the paths of the axles.
The part beyond the rear axle can swing sideways outward during a turn, so a long overhang requires greater attention to the available space.
The portion extending beyond the rear axle is the rear overhang: the tail can swing outward during a turn.
Scraping against the road is a different phenomenon: the sideways swing of the tail in a turn concerns the movement of the rear overhang.
The wheelbase affects the inward off-tracking of the rear wheels; the quiz links the sideways swing of the tail to the rear overhang. The actual path also depends on the geometry and the maneuver.
Low ground clearance concerns possible contact with the road surface; the sideways swing of the tail, on the other hand, concerns the rear overhang.
The portion extending in front of the front axle is the front overhang; the swing of the tail, on the other hand, involves the part beyond the rear axle.
When pulling in, the part in front of the front axle can extend toward the sidewalk: it must be watched and the vehicle straightened in time.
The portion extending in front of the front axle is the front overhang, which can occupy the space above the sidewalk when pulling in.
Low ground clearance concerns contact with the road surface; when pulling in, the front overhang can instead extend over the sidewalk.
The quiz attributes the front of the vehicle encroaching on the sidewalk to the front overhang, not the wheelbase. The bus's actual path also depends on the line chosen.
The rear overhang concerns the tail; when pulling in at a stop, it is the front overhang that can encroach on the space above the sidewalk.
The portion extending beyond the rear axle concerns the tail; when pulling in, the portion in front of the front axle must also be watched.
On a hump or a change in gradient, an inappropriate speed can make contact between the overhang and the road more likely; the risk also depends on the road profile and the vehicle.
A heavy load can lower the body, reducing ground clearance: the rear overhang may then touch the road, especially at changes in gradient.
A long rear overhang can bring the tail close to the ground when the bus crosses a hump or a change in gradient.
A short overhang does not increase the risk: all else being equal, a longer rear overhang can come closer to the ground at changes in gradient.
False: on a level road, the risk to the rear overhang does not increase for this reason. It is mainly abrupt changes in gradient that reduce ground clearance.
False: the absence of changes in gradient does not in itself increase the risk. An abrupt transition between gradients, however, can bring the rear overhang closer to the road.
Doors and steps that project outward require attention to the available space and nearby people, to avoid collisions during the stop.
The position relative to the sidewalk must allow safe access, especially when a ramp must be used or a wheelchair user needs assistance.
Mirrors and, where fitted, cameras and monitors help the driver monitor the door areas and passengers during the stop.
Objects left near doors or passageways can obstruct passengers or cause them to trip: access areas must remain clear.
False: during a normal stop, the main focus is on the service doors and passengers boarding and getting off. Emergency exits are intended for emergencies and must be kept usable.
False: passengers getting off require attention because they may trip or find themselves in a dangerous position.
Canopies can cover the platforms and shelter passengers while they wait.
The platform provides an access area beside the bus and makes it easier for passengers to board and alight.
The claim that they are reserved exclusively for articulated buses is incorrect: a herringbone layout does not in itself identify bays reserved only for that type of bus.
In the quiz's model, straight, parallel platforms are suitable for quick boarding and alighting; they are not chosen for long stops. The actual duration nevertheless depends on the service.
The passenger building also provides a place for people to wait before the buses arrive.
The passenger building normally houses public facilities, such as a waiting room and ticket office; it may also include a café.
The functional connection allows passengers to reach the bus station forecourt and the buses from the building.
Boards or screens in the building can inform passengers about arrival and departure times.
It is incorrect to assign those areas to the passenger building: garaging, parking, cleaning and refuelling belong to the part intended for vehicles.
Maintenance and repair spaces belong to the vehicle building, not the building intended for passengers.
The vehicle building serves the needs of buses and includes areas for garaging, parking, cleaning and refuelling.
The vehicle building may include equipped spaces for bus maintenance and repair.
The vehicle building is intended for activities involving buses, such as garaging and maintenance; for this reason it is usually reserved for staff.
The waiting room, ticket office and café are normally in the passenger building, not the building intended for vehicles.
The statement confuses the two buildings: public facilities may be found in the passenger building; the vehicle building serves the buses.
Passengers are meant to wait in the passenger building; the vehicle building is intended for activities involving buses.
A speed suited to the radius of the curve limits lateral forces on passengers and contributes to a comfortable ride.
Anticipating maneuvers allows them to be performed gradually and reduces jolts for passengers.
Smooth driving, with gradual acceleration and braking, reduces jolts and improves comfort; speed must always be adjusted for safety.
Gradual acceleration and braking reduce jolts and help passengers keep their balance.
Braking early and moderately, when possible, limits sudden deceleration and makes the ride more comfortable.
False: starting and braking should also be gradual whenever possible, to limit jolts and losses of balance.
False: sudden changes in speed and abrupt steering cause jolts. The driver should use smooth movements suited to the conditions.
False: sudden starts and hard braking can throw passengers off balance. For comfort, starting and braking should be gradual unless necessary otherwise.
The driver must act fairly and responsibly even in difficult situations, protecting people and the safety of the service.
Passenger safety requires attention both while driving and during boarding and getting off.
It is wrong to accommodate every individual request even to the detriment of others: the driver must treat all passengers fairly and protect their safety.
False: mobility aids must not be refused simply because they are mobility aids; their transport must be facilitated in accordance with the applicable accessibility conditions.

There is no general obligation to interrupt the service whenever the driver considers it necessary. In the event of actual danger, however, the driver must stop and take the measures needed for safety.
False: not every object can be transported; safety conditions must be observed and passageways and exits must not be obstructed.
The required interior lighting must work so that passengers can see the access areas and steps.
Checking the lighting periodically makes it possible to identify faults and keep it working properly.
Interior lighting is provided to make steps and access to exits visible, among other things.

False according to the quiz: the required interior lighting is not an accessory reserved for only some buses. The statement is ambiguous: taken literally, ‘some’ does not rule out the others being equipped with it too.
It is false that interior lighting is optional: the bus must illuminate the areas intended for passengers.
It is false that it is not checked: during the vehicle inspection, the interior lighting is visually examined and tested for operation.
Before setting off, the driver checks that the required fire extinguishers are on board so they can be used in an emergency.
The windscreen, windows and indirect vision devices must be clean and in working order: they are needed to see the road and the areas around the vehicle.
The driver checks that the warning triangle is present; it is needed to give advance warning of the stopped vehicle in the prescribed circumstances.
The first aid kit is an item of equipment to be checked before departure, as required for the bus.
The driver checks the label: under the quiz criterion, fire extinguishers must be inspected every six months.
Before departure, the driver checks that the fire extinguishers are up to date with their periodic inspections; the technical inspection is entrusted to competent personnel.
The driver checks that the wheel chocks required for the vehicle are present; they help prevent it from moving when stationary.
The first aid kit is an item of equipment to be checked before departure, as required for the bus.
If the emergency windows require hammers, the driver checks that they are present: they must be available so the exits can be used in an emergency.
The projecting-load warning panel is not an item of equipment that must always be checked: it is needed when a load projects lengthwise and must be marked.
The quiz considers checking the rear panels false because such panels are not generally mandatory equipment on buses. The devices actually required for the vehicle must still be checked.

The quiz considers the twelve-month interval false: it requires fire extinguishers to be checked every six months. Note: periodic checks and servicing are distinct operations; the statement uses ‘serviced’ ambiguously.
Checking the ignition distributor is not a routine check required of the driver before every departure; the driver must instead check the equipment and devices needed for safety.
Measuring exhaust gases is not a routine check required of the driver before every departure: emissions are subject to periodic technical inspections.
The number of seated passengers must not exceed the maximum number of seats stated on the vehicle registration document.
Standing passengers may be carried only if the vehicle is authorised to do so and within the limits stated on the vehicle registration document.
The authorised load combinations must be respected, including any different allocations of seated and standing places.
To transport a person in a wheelchair, a bus equipped with the prescribed spaces and accommodation systems is required.
If S.2 does not indicate standing places, they are not authorised: the seats indicated in S.1 are used.
Field S.2 indicates the authorised standing places, where provided; their number must not be exceeded.
People with reduced mobility can also travel on the bus, under the conditions and with the assistance provided for the service and the vehicle.
Free space in the aisle is not enough: standing places must be authorised and must respect the number specified on the vehicle registration document.
Placing the wheelchair near the front door is not enough: the designated space and systems on the equipped bus must be used.
S.1 indicates seated places, not standing places. For the latter, S.2 must be checked.
Service requirements do not authorise exceeding the capacity stated on the vehicle registration document.
The number of people authorised on the registration certificate must not be exceeded, and any load combinations must also be respected.
Standing places must be authorised on the registration certificate and occupied only up to the number indicated.
Standing passengers distribute themselves along the aisle or in the designated spaces, avoiding crowding and keeping boarding and alighting areas clear.
With standing passengers, the driver must pay more attention: sudden braking and manoeuvres can cause them to lose their balance.
With standing passengers, the driver must anticipate manoeuvres and drive carefully, avoiding sudden changes that could cause them to fall.
Standing passengers must hold on to the designated supports to reduce the risk of falling during braking and manoeuvres.
Standing passengers are not required to gather at the rear: they must occupy the designated spaces without obstructing driving or the exits.
FALSO. Free space does not authorise exceeding the permitted capacity: standing places must also remain within the limits prescribed for the bus.
FALSO. People travelling standing up can lose their balance: the driver must take particular care, avoiding sudden acceleration and braking.
S.1 concerns seated places; any authorisation for standing places appears in field S.2.
Standing passengers must also follow safety rules, for example by holding on to supports and keeping the doors clear.
Holding on to supports helps maintain balance if the vehicle brakes or changes direction suddenly.
Not pushing or leaning on seated passengers avoids disturbing or endangering others during the journey.
Following the signs on the doors makes boarding and alighting more orderly and safer, subject to any exceptions provided by the service.
Keeping the doors clear allows other passengers to board and alight without obstruction.
Not leaning out of or throwing objects from the windows protects both passengers and people outside.
Passengers are not required to clean the seat after sitting down; instead, they must help keep the vehicle clean by not making it dirty.
Emergency windows are not broken during a normal journey: they are used for evacuation when an emergency requires it.
The hammers must remain on board, available to break the emergency windows when needed; they are not objects to take away.
VERO. To transport a person in a wheelchair, a bus with suitable access and space to accommodate the wheelchair safely is required.
FALSO. Transport on a scheduled bus is not prohibited: it is possible on vehicles that are accessible and equipped for wheelchairs.
FALSO. Buses and minibuses can transport people in wheelchairs if they are equipped for access and safe accommodation.
The vehicle must remain securely braked while passengers board and alight, to prevent movement while they use the doors.
VERO. If present, a lift or platform allows a wheelchair user to safely overcome the difference in height while boarding and alighting.
While passengers board and alight, the driver must remain attentive to the operation and their safety, avoiding distracting activities.
FALSO. Hazard warning lights are not mandatory every time passengers board or alight: they are used in the prescribed circumstances, for example during a dangerous emergency stop.
FALSO. The service doors are used for normal boarding and alighting; emergency exits are intended for emergency situations.
A personal need does not require the driver to make a phone call while passengers board and alight: the driver must instead supervise the operation without being distracted.
VERO. While driving, the driver must keep their attention on the road and the vehicle so they can respond promptly to hazards.
VERO. The stop must allow passengers to alight without being exposed to danger, taking account of the location and traffic.
Before moving off again, the driver must check that boarding and alighting have finished and that people are safe.
VERO. The driver provides the assistance needed for a person with a disability to board, for example by correctly using the aids available on the vehicle.
An absolute ban on speaking even when the vehicle is stationary is incorrect: the driver may communicate with passengers when doing so does not compromise attention and safety.

FALSO. The driver must not ignore passenger safety: where seat belt use is required, passengers must be informed of that obligation. This does not mean that the driver is automatically responsible for every adult's seat belt.

VERO. A lift, including one operated electrically or hydraulically, can move the wheelchair between street level and the level of the bus. It is not the only possible device, however: a suitable ramp can also be used.
VERO. A manually operated ramp can connect street level to the vehicle and allow wheelchair access, provided it is suitable and correctly positioned.
VERO. A portable ramp can also be positioned by hand for boarding and alighting; it must be stable and safe when in use.

FALSO according to the quiz. The wording is ambiguous, however: the mere fact that a lift is removable does not show that it is unsuitable. For access, what matters is that the device is provided for and used safely; other aids, such as ramps, are also permitted.
FALSO. The person with a disability is not necessarily required to bring their own ramp: access is provided using suitable aids prescribed for the service and the vehicle.
FALSO. The tachograph records driving and activity data: it does not lift the wheelchair. A suitable device, such as a ramp or lift, is used to access the bus.
Before opening or closing the doors, the driver must check that the operation will not endanger passengers.
After a stop, the driver moves off again only with the doors closed, after checking that passengers are safe.
If the company provides a service uniform, the driver wears it in accordance with company rules.
Informing passengers of the diversion allows them to understand how the unforeseen event affects their journey.

The quiz considers it false that eating or smoking on board is permitted even when off duty. The wording is ambiguous: company rules may regulate eating and smoking differently; a general ban on eating while off duty cannot be inferred.
Hot weather does not justify driving with the doors open: the doors must be kept closed while the bus is moving for passenger safety.
It is false that the driver is not required to provide assistance: the driver must help passengers when necessary, within the limits of their duties and safety.

The driver must concentrate on driving: talking to reassure passengers is not an obligation while the vehicle is moving. The driver may give information when doing so does not distract from driving, for example when the vehicle is stopped.
The driver checks the vehicle's condition and helps keep it clean and in good working order, reporting any problems.
The timetable at stops is a reference for the service: the driver must follow it as far as possible without compromising safety.
In an emergency, the driver may use the service communication equipment to contact the control centre, in a way that is compatible with safe driving.
Before leaving the stop, the driver checks that the doors are closed to prevent danger to passengers while the vehicle is moving.

The quiz considers it false that eating on board at the terminus is permitted: stopping alone does not automatically make eating on the vehicle permissible. However, the applicable rules may depend on the company and the circumstances.
Two-tone horns should not be preferred: the horn must be used only in permitted circumstances and without excessive use.
On a scheduled service, passengers normally board and get off at designated stops: a passenger's request does not authorise the driver to stop elsewhere.
On a hired service with a driver, the driver does not smoke during the journey, to protect the travel environment.
According to the rule referred to in the quiz, the driver does not eat in the passenger area while stopped. The specific requirements also depend on the applicable regulations.
The driver maintains professional and respectful behaviour; improper conduct and vulgar language are incompatible with the service.
The hire service is provided for the group that requested it: as a rule, outsiders are not allowed on board without agreement from the customer.
The driver must not entrust the driving to people unconnected with the service: the vehicle must be driven by authorised and qualified personnel.
As a rule, the driver does not bring their own animals on board. The prohibition concerns the driver's animals; it does not amount to a general ban on passengers' animals.
At the end of the journey, the driver checks the interior for forgotten items and starts the process of returning them. The handover procedures depend on the applicable rules.
There is no general obligation to transport municipal employees free of charge. The hire service is arranged with the customer on agreed terms.
It is false that eating is prohibited throughout working hours: a meal may be eaten during an appropriate break, in accordance with the applicable rules.
There is no absolute ban on speaking to people other than passengers; however, communications must not distract the driver from driving.
